requirements.lead_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a managed public or private forest area with the manager or a forester who is familiar with it. Write a brief report describing the type of forest, the management objectives, and the forestry techniques used to achieve the objectives. (b) With a knowledgeable individual, visit a current or past logging operation or wood-using manufacturing plant. Write a brief report describing the following: (1) The species and size of trees harvested or used (2) The origin of the forest or stands of trees utilized (e. g., planted or natural) (3) The forest's successional stage, its future, and, if it is a past logging operation, the regeneration that is occurring, whether planted or natural (4) Where the trees are coming from (land ownership) or where they are going (type of mill or processing plant) (5) The products that are made from the trees (6) How the products are made and used (7) How waste materials from the logging operation or manufacturing plant are or were disposed of or utilized (c) Take part in a forest-fire prevention campaign in cooperation with your local fire warden, state wildfire agency, forester, or counselor. Write a brief report describing the campaign, how it will help prevent wildfires, and your part in it.

pamphlet_excerpts: Coordinating Forestry Site Visits: Your merit badge counselor and parents can help you arrange a visit to a managed forest, a logging operation, or a manufacturing plant that uses wood (p. 71).
Observing Field Operations Firsthand: You can see for yourself how the work of forestry is carried (p. 71).
Meeting Professional Forest Managers: You also will have opportunities to visit with forestry professionals and learn more about their backgrounds, training, and responsibilities (p. 71).
Advance Scheduling with Hosts: Plan the trip well in advance so that the forestry professionals will have time to prepare for your visit (p. 71).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Interview Working Forestry Specialists: You also will have opportunities to visit with forestry professionals and learn more about their backgrounds, training, and responsibilities (p. 71).
Step 2 - Schedule Visits Well Ahead: Plan the trip well in advance so that the forestry professionals will have time to prepare for your visit (p. 71).
Step 3 - Request Photo Permission First: Get permission in advance if you want to take photographs during your visit (p. 71).

Step 4 - Research Operations and Questions: Do some research on the forest, logging operation, or manufacturing plant you plan to visit, and think about some of the questions you want answered (p. 71).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When preparing a field notebook of local trees for Forestry Requirement 1, which combination of botanical characteristics allows you to accurately identify a tree species in the field?
options: A. Counting the number of birds perched in the upper branches and measuring the shadow length at noon.
B. Tasting unknown berries and chewing raw inner bark from every tree along the trail.
C. Measuring only the total height of the trunk without examining the leaves, twigs, buds, or fruit.

D. Examining whether branching and leaf arrangement are opposite (such as maple, ash, dogwood) or alternate (such as oak, birch, hickory), whether leaves are simple or compound with lobed or toothed margins, along with bark texture, winter buds, and seeds/cones.
choices: A. Counting the number of birds perched in the upper branches and measuring the shadow length at noon.
B. Tasting unknown berries and chewing raw inner bark from every tree along the trail.
C. Measuring only the total height of the trunk without examining the leaves, twigs, buds, or fruit.

D. Examining whether branching and leaf arrangement are opposite (such as maple, ash, dogwood) or alternate (such as oak, birch, hickory), whether leaves are simple or compound with lobed or toothed margins, along with bark texture, winter buds, and seeds/cones.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Examining whether branching and leaf arrangement are opposite (such as maple, ash, dogwood) or alternate (such as oak, birch, hickory), whether leaves are simple or compound with lobed or toothed margins, along with bark texture, winter buds, and seeds/cones.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Dendrology (tree identification) relies on systematic keys comparing opposite vs. alternate twig arrangement, simple vs. compound leaf structure, leaf margins, bark patterns, buds, and reproductive structures (acorns, samaras, or cones).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why does the wood formed by the cambium in the spring look lighter in color than the wood formed later in the summer?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why does the wood formed by the cambium in the spring look lighter in color than the wood formed later in the summer?
options: A. Spring wood absorbs bleaching minerals from melting snow before the roots warm up.
B. The cambium grows rapidly in the spring, producing large, thin-walled cells that appear light in color.
C. Sunlight penetrates through the outer bark in spring and fades the outer sapwood.
D. Spring wood contains no water or sap until late summer when the leaves mature.
choices: A. Spring wood absorbs bleaching minerals from melting snow before the roots warm up.
B. The cambium grows rapidly in the spring, producing large, thin-walled cells that appear light in color.
C. Sunlight penetrates through the outer bark in spring and fades the outer sapwood.
D. Spring wood contains no water or sap until late summer when the leaves mature.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. The cambium grows rapidly in the spring, producing large, thin-walled cells that appear light in color.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): During the rapid growth of spring, the cambium produces large cells that form light-colored springwood, whereas slower summer growth creates smaller, denser, darker cells (p. 28).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: During photosynthesis, what raw materials does a tree combine using sunlight and chlorophyll to produce simple sugars and release oxygen?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: During photosynthesis, what raw materials does a tree combine using sunlight and chlorophyll to produce simple sugars and release oxygen?
options: A. Nitrogen from the air and minerals from decaying bedrock
B. Oxygen from the atmosphere and sap from the heartwood
C. Water and carbon dioxide
D. Methane gas and rainwater collected on the bark
choices: A. Nitrogen from the air and minerals from decaying bedrock
B. Oxygen from the atmosphere and sap from the heartwood
C. Water and carbon dioxide
D. Methane gas and rainwater collected on the bark
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Water and carbon dioxide
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Charged by sunlight, chlorophyll enables leaves to combine water with absorbed carbon dioxide to manufacture simple sugars, releasing oxygen as a by-product (p. 45).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which silvicultural approach is designed to regenerate tree species that require full, direct sunlight and grow best alongside trees of approximately the same age?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which silvicultural approach is designed to regenerate tree species that require full, direct sunlight and grow best alongside trees of approximately the same age?
options: A. Single-tree selection in a shaded, uneven-aged canopy
B. Salvage pruning of lower branches on old-growth trees
C. Even-aged management using systems such as clear-cutting, seed-tree, or shelterwood
D. Complete fire and harvest exclusion across the entire stand
choices: A. Single-tree selection in a shaded, uneven-aged canopy
B. Salvage pruning of lower branches on old-growth trees
C. Even-aged management using systems such as clear-cutting, seed-tree, or shelterwood
D. Complete fire and harvest exclusion across the entire stand
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Even-aged management using systems such as clear-cutting, seed-tree, or shelterwood
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Even-aged systems create open, sunlit conditions where a new generation of trees begins growing at the same time, suiting species that cannot tolerate heavy shade (p. 55).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When conducting a hazard tree inventory in a camp or park, what two factors determine whether a defective tree poses an actual hazard?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When conducting a hazard tree inventory in a camp or park, what two factors determine whether a defective tree poses an actual hazard?
options: A. The commercial lumber value of the wood and the age of the tree
B. Structural defects in the tree and its proximity to a target such as a campsite, trail, road, or building
C. Whether the tree has simple leaves or compound leaves
D. How much carbon dioxide the tree absorbs during the summer
choices: A. The commercial lumber value of the wood and the age of the tree
B. Structural defects in the tree and its proximity to a target such as a campsite, trail, road, or building
C. Whether the tree has simple leaves or compound leaves
D. How much carbon dioxide the tree absorbs during the summer
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Structural defects in the tree and its proximity to a target such as a campsite, trail, road, or building
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): A hazard tree assessment looks for structural weaknesses like dead limbs, fungal rot, or leaning trunks located where a failure could strike people, roads, trails, or structures (p. 65).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does carefully planned prescribed burning help protect a forest ecosystem?
options: A. It permanently sterilizes the topsoil so no new seeds or insects can ever sprout
B. It reduces dangerous fuel buildup, recycles nutrients into the soil, and removes undesirable brush and pests
C. It dries out nearby streams so heavy logging trucks can drive up the streambeds
D. It replaces native fire-adapted pines with shade-loving invasive vines
choices: A. It permanently sterilizes the topsoil so no new seeds or insects can ever sprout
B. It reduces dangerous fuel buildup, recycles nutrients into the soil, and removes undesirable brush and pests

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Set under strict weather and fuel guidelines, prescribed fires reduce fuel loads that feed severe wildfires while exposing mineral soil, releasing nutrients, and controlling pests and brush (p. 36).

C. Games of emergence have no rules at all, whereas games of progression never allow a player to make choices.
D. Game balance means ensuring that the player who goes first automatically wins every match regardless of skill.

quiz_item.question: How does a game designer distinguish between a game's difficulty and its depth?
options: A. Difficulty measures how hard it is to complete objectives, while depth measures the richness of strategic choices available to master
B. Difficulty applies only to single-player electronic games, while depth applies only to multiplayer board games
C. Difficulty is determined by the age rating of the game, while depth is determined by the length of the rulebook
D. Difficulty measures how fast turns move, while depth measures how many times a player wants to replay the game
choices: A. Difficulty measures how hard it is to complete objectives, while depth measures the richness of strategic choices available to master
B. Difficulty applies only to single-player electronic games, while depth applies only to multiplayer board games
C. Difficulty is determined by the age rating of the game, while depth is determined by the length of the rulebook
D. Difficulty measures how fast turns move, while depth measures how many times a player wants to replay the game
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Difficulty measures how hard it is to complete objectives, while depth measures the richness of strategic choices available to master
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Difficulty describes how easy or hard it is to achieve an objective, whereas depth refers to the layers of strategy and decision-making that keep a game rewarding as players improve (p. 49).

C. To register a federal patent on the game's title before anyone else can use it
D. To replace the need for a written rulebook during blind playtesting
choices: A. To lock in the final retail price and box dimensions for manufacturing
B. To define the core medium, player format, objectives, theme, and play value that guide all design decisions
C. To register a federal patent on the game's title before anyone else can use it
D. To replace the need for a written rulebook during blind playtesting
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. To define the core medium, player format, objectives, theme, and play value that guide all design decisions
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): A vision statement captures the core concept, medium, player format, objectives, and theme so your design stays focused as you draft rules and components (p. 22).

requirements.lead_text: Do the following: Note: You must have your counselor's approval of your concept before you begin creating the prototype.
requirements.req_text: Do the following: Note: You must have your counselor's approval of your concept before you begin creating the prototype. (a) Prototype your game from requirement 5. If applicable, demonstrate to your counselor that you have addressed player safety through the rules and equipment. Record your work in your game design notebook. (b) Test your prototype with as many other people as you need to meet the player format. Compare the play experience to your descriptions from requirement 5(b). Correct unclear rules, holes in the rules, dead ends, and obvious rule exploits. Change at least one rule, mechanic, or objective from your first version of the game, and describe why you are making the change. Play the game again. Record in your game design notebook whether or not your change had the expected effect. (c) Repeat 6(b) at least two more times and record the results in your game design notebook.

requirements.lead_text: Blind test your game. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Blind test your game. Do the following: (a) Write an instruction sheet that includes all of the information needed to play the game. Clearly describe how to set up the game, play the game, and end the game. List the game objectives. (b) Share your prototype from requirement 6 with a group of players that has not played it or witnessed a previous playtest. Provide them with your instruction sheet(s) and any physical components. Watch them play the game, but do not provide them with instruction. Record their feedback in your game design notebook. (c) Share your game design notebook with your counselor. Discuss the player reactions to your project and what you learned about the game design process. Based on your testing, determine what you like most about your game and suggest one or more changes.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why should you play a familiar game under its standard rules first and then test only one rule or objective change at a time?
options: A. Official board game publishers prohibit changing more than one rule in a home game
B. Players will forget the objective if they do not play the standard version for at least three hours first
C. Testing multiple changes at once makes it impossible to tell which specific rule change caused the shift in player behavior
D. Changing two rules simultaneously always resets the game's balance back to normal
choices: A. Official board game publishers prohibit changing more than one rule in a home game
B. Players will forget the objective if they do not play the standard version for at least three hours first
C. Testing multiple changes at once makes it impossible to tell which specific rule change caused the shift in player behavior
D. Changing two rules simultaneously always resets the game's balance back to normal
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Testing multiple changes at once makes it impossible to tell which specific rule change caused the shift in player behavior
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Playing the baseline game and then isolating a single rule or objective modification lets you compare your prediction directly against how players actually adapt their actions and emotions (p. 78).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: If 82 out of 100 seeds sprout during your germination test, what is the germination rate and a likely reason the remaining 18 failed?
quiz_item.question: If 82 out of 100 seeds sprout during your germination test, what is the germination rate and a likely reason the remaining 18 failed?
options: A. 18 percent germination rate, caused by excessive moonlight
B. 100 percent germination rate, because unsprouted seeds do not count
C. 41 percent germination rate, because you must divide the sprouted total in half
D. 82 percent germination rate, with failures likely due to seed age, storage conditions, or moisture levels
choices: A. 18 percent germination rate, caused by excessive moonlight
B. 100 percent germination rate, because unsprouted seeds do not count
C. 41 percent germination rate, because you must divide the sprouted total in half
D. 82 percent germination rate, with failures likely due to seed age, storage conditions, or moisture levels
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. 82 percent germination rate, with failures likely due to seed age, storage conditions, or moisture levels
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): When 82 of 100 tested seeds sprout, the germination rate is 82 percent, and non-germinating seeds typically fail due to age, damaged embryos, or improper moisture and warmth (p. 72).

Pollinator Importance for Food: Without these winged creatures, many of our food sources would be in great peril (p. 59).
Crop and Feed Pollination: We rely on honeybees not only for the sweet honey they make, but more importantly for their ability to pollinate many of the crops and livestock feed (p. 59).
Cross Pollination for Seeds: Some plants can produce seeds only if pollen is exchanged between flowers on the same plant, or from flowers of different plants from the same variety (p. 59).

Step 2 - Observe Flower Pollen Transfer: Some plants can produce seeds only if pollen is exchanged between flowers on the same plant, or from flowers of different plants from the same variety (p. 59).
Step 3 - Identify Diverse Native Pollinators: Birds, bats, bumblebees, butterflies, and many other creatures help transfer pollen as they flit from flower to flower or feed on the nectar (p. 59).
Step 4 - Compare Honeybee Pollination Advantages: Honey bees, however, have three advantages over all of these other pollinators (p. 59).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following and record weekly observations. Discuss the results of your project with your counselor.
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following and record weekly observations. Discuss the results of your project with your counselor. (a) Build a compost bin and maintain it for 90 days. (b) Build a vermicompost bin (worm compost bin) and maintain it for 90 days. (c) Build a hydroponic garden containing three vegetables or herbs, or three ornamental plants. Maintain this garden through harvest or flowering, or for 90 days. (d) Build one water garden, either in a container (at least 12 by 6 inches and 6 inches deep), or in the ground as a small, decorative pond no larger than 6 by 3 feet and 24 inches deep. Maintain the water garden for 90 days. (e) Prepare a honey super for use on a hive or colony. Remove a filled honey super from the hive or colony and prepare the honey for sale. (f) Grow a garden of your own using soil from seed or plantings to harvest or for 90 days, whichever is earlier. This can be an outdoor garden or indoors using appropriate containers, and should include at least three types of plants approved by your counselor.

B. Act like a detective to determine what went wrong and try again without getting discouraged
C. Pour undiluted household bleach over the remaining plants
D. Assume that seeds can never grow in that climate
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Act like a detective to determine what went wrong and try again without getting discouraged
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Setbacks happen to everyone in gardening; the best response is to act as a detective, diagnose what went wrong, and try again (p. 64).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: While preparing soil beds and applying fertilizers or pest controls for Gardening Requirement 1, which health and safety practices are essential?
options: A. Leave metal garden rakes and hoes lying face-up in tall grass with the sharp tines pointing skyward so you can spot them easily.
B. Lift heavy bags of compost by bending straight over at the waist with locked knees and twisting your spine.

C. Wear work gloves, sturdy closed-toe shoes, sun protection, and updated tetanus immunization; lift heavy loads with your legs while keeping your back straight; store rakes and hoes with tines turned down or hung on racks; and strictly follow all product label directions and PPE rules when handling fertilizers or pesticides.
D. Mix double the recommended concentration of garden pesticide in an unlabeled drinking cup and spray it upwind on a gusty afternoon.
choices: A. Leave metal garden rakes and hoes lying face-up in tall grass with the sharp tines pointing skyward so you can spot them easily.

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Safe gardening prevents puncture wounds and tetanus (gloves, shoes, rakes stored tines-down), avoids back strain (lifting with the legs), protects against sun/heat, and follows exact label safety instructions for any soil amendments or pest treatments.

options: A. Seedlings never require watering after being placed in soil
B. Seedlings are completely immune to all garden insects
C. Seedlings already have established roots that improve outdoor survival
D. Seedlings can grow without sunlight during their first month
choices: A. Seedlings never require watering after being placed in soil
B. Seedlings are completely immune to all garden insects
C. Seedlings already have established roots that improve outdoor survival
D. Seedlings can grow without sunlight during their first month
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Seedlings already have established roots that improve outdoor survival
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Planting seedlings that already have roots gives your outdoor garden a much better chance of surviving than raw seeds alone (p. 45).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How can a gardener use tall, sun-tolerant crops to help cool-season vegetables thrive in the same bed?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How can a gardener use tall, sun-tolerant crops to help cool-season vegetables thrive in the same bed?
options: A. Plant cool-season crops beneath the vines or stalks of taller sun-tolerant crops
B. Harvest the tall crops before planting any seeds in the soil
C. Tie the roots of both crops together before placing them in the ground
D. Cover the tall crops with plastic tarps to block out all sunlight
choices: A. Plant cool-season crops beneath the vines or stalks of taller sun-tolerant crops
B. Harvest the tall crops before planting any seeds in the soil
C. Tie the roots of both crops together before placing them in the ground
D. Cover the tall crops with plastic tarps to block out all sunlight
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Plant cool-season crops beneath the vines or stalks of taller sun-tolerant crops
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Crops that prefer cooler temperatures can be planted beneath the natural shade of taller vines or stalks that thrive in full sun (p. 41).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: If 82 out of 100 seeds sprout during your germination test, what is the germination rate and a likely reason the remaining 18 failed?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: If 82 out of 100 seeds sprout during your germination test, what is the germination rate and a likely reason the remaining 18 failed?
options: A. 18 percent germination rate, caused by excessive moonlight
B. 100 percent germination rate, because unsprouted seeds do not count
C. 41 percent germination rate, because you must divide the sprouted total in half
D. 82 percent germination rate, with failures likely due to seed age, storage conditions, or moisture levels
choices: A. 18 percent germination rate, caused by excessive moonlight
B. 100 percent germination rate, because unsprouted seeds do not count
C. 41 percent germination rate, because you must divide the sprouted total in half
D. 82 percent germination rate, with failures likely due to seed age, storage conditions, or moisture levels
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. 82 percent germination rate, with failures likely due to seed age, storage conditions, or moisture levels
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): When 82 of 100 tested seeds sprout, the germination rate is 82 percent, and non-germinating seeds typically fail due to age, damaged embryos, or improper moisture and warmth (p. 72).

choices: A. It magnifies the bees so you can count their wings

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It keeps the mesh standing out away from your face to prevent stings

choices: A. Their ability to pollinate food crops and livestock feed

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): While honeybees produce sweet honey, we rely on them most importantly to pollinate human food crops and livestock feed (p. 59).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
quiz_item.question: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
options: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
B. A primary source is any story repeated at a family reunion fifty years later, whereas a secondary source is a courthouse marriage license signed by the officiating judge.
C. A primary source refers only to relatives on your father's side, whereas a secondary source refers to relatives on your mother's side.
D. Secondary sources are always 100 percent error-free and never need to be verified against vital records or federal census schedules.
choices: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
B. A primary source is any story repeated at a family reunion fifty years later, whereas a secondary source is a courthouse marriage license signed by the officiating judge.
C. A primary source refers only to relatives on your father's side, whereas a secondary source refers to relatives on your mother's side.
D. Secondary sources are always 100 percent error-free and never need to be verified against vital records or federal census schedules.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Genealogists distinguish original, contemporaneous primary records (vital certificates, wills, census returns) from derivative or secondary compilations, cross-checking facts to build an accurate pedigree and family group record.

pamphlet_excerpts: Unique Search Keyword Selection: Keywords are words that are unique to what you are searching (p. 16).
Broad Search Query Overload: If you just typed in grave and Rose Goldman, you would get thousands of hits (p. 16).
Place and Date Filters: To do this, you might add the name of the place Rose Goldman died or the year of her death to your search terms (p. 16).
Same Name Identity Traps: Remember, however, that not all the Rose Gold mans you find will be your ancestor (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Add Place and Year: To do this, you might add the name of the place Rose Goldman died or the year of her death to your search terms (p. 16).
Step 2 - Distinguish Matching Ancestor Names: Remember, however, that not all the Rose Gold mans you find will be your ancestor (p. 16).
Step 3 - Rule Out False Matches: In fact, it is possible that none of the matches you get will be your ancestor (p. 16).
Step 4 - Check Computer Search Results: Remember, too, that computers are not as smart (p. 16).

quiz_item.question: How can you narrow an online genealogy search when typing an ancestor's name returns thousands of results?
options: A. Remove the surname and search only by the ancestor's first name
B. Accept the first result listed at the top of the search engine page
C. Add unique keywords such as the place or year of the ancestor's death
D. Search only for living relatives instead of historical records
choices: A. Remove the surname and search only by the ancestor's first name
B. Accept the first result listed at the top of the search engine page
C. Add unique keywords such as the place or year of the ancestor's death
D. Search only for living relatives instead of historical records
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Add unique keywords such as the place or year of the ancestor's death
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Adding specific keywords like the place or year an ancestor died narrows thousands of broad hits down to records that are much more likely to match the right person (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Adding Small Ancestor Photographs: Adding small photographs to your pedigree chart can make it more interesting (p. 44).
Commercial or Custom Charts: You can buy charts with spaces built in for photos, or you can design your own (p. 44).
Handling Missing Ancestor Photos: Place a photo of each ancestor near his or her space on the chart; do not worry if you don't have a photo of each one (p. 44).
Direct Ancestor Chart Scope: Your pedigree chart contains information about your parents, grandparents, and other direct ancestors (p. 44).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Add Photos Where Available: Place a photo of each ancestor near his or her space on the chart; do not worry if you don't have a photo of each one (p. 44).
Step 2 - Verify Direct Line Entries: Your pedigree chart contains information about your parents, grandparents, and other direct ancestors (p. 44).
Step 3 - List Siblings and Aunts: But what about other relatives such as brothers, sisters, uncles, aunts, and cousins (p. 44).
Step 4 - Complete Both Family Forms: They, too, are an important part of your genealogy (p. 44).

quiz_item.question: How have microfilming and record indexing worked together to transform genealogical research?
options: A. Microfilming preserved copies of fragile records worldwide, while indexing made those millions of pages searchable by name
B. Indexing replaced the need to ever read original birth or census certificates
C. Microfilming automatically translates handwritten foreign records into modern English
D. Family History Centers charge a per-page fee to index private family diaries
choices: A. Microfilming preserved copies of fragile records worldwide, while indexing made those millions of pages searchable by name
B. Indexing replaced the need to ever read original birth or census certificates
C. Microfilming automatically translates handwritten foreign records into modern English
D. Family History Centers charge a per-page fee to index private family diaries
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Microfilming preserved copies of fragile records worldwide, while indexing made those millions of pages searchable by name
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Microfilming preserved over two million rolls of fragile records at institutions like the Family History Library, and record indexing allows researchers to locate specific ancestors across those vast collections in seconds (p. 20).

pamphlet_excerpts: Confirming Accurate Research Answers: Then you must know where to go to find accurate answers (p. 17).
Tracing Immigrant Family Roots: If your family moved to the United States from another country, it is important to ask your parents or guardians and other relatives (p. 17).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Genealogy Requirement 1, what is the difference between a primary genealogical source and a secondary source when researching your family's pedigree chart?
options: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
B. A primary source is any story repeated at a family reunion fifty years later, whereas a secondary source is a courthouse marriage license signed by the officiating judge.
C. A primary source refers only to relatives on your father's side, whereas a secondary source refers to relatives on your mother's side.
D. Secondary sources are always 100 percent error-free and never need to be verified against vital records or federal census schedules.
choices: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
B. A primary source is any story repeated at a family reunion fifty years later, whereas a secondary source is a courthouse marriage license signed by the officiating judge.
C. A primary source refers only to relatives on your father's side, whereas a secondary source refers to relatives on your mother's side.
D. Secondary sources are always 100 percent error-free and never need to be verified against vital records or federal census schedules.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. A primary source is an original record created at or near the time of the event by a direct participant or official witness (such as an original birth certificate, parish baptismal register, or contemporaneous ship manifest), whereas a secondary source is compiled later from other accounts (such as a published county history or an unsourced online family tree).
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Genealogists distinguish original, contemporaneous primary records (vital certificates, wills, census returns) from derivative or secondary compilations, cross-checking facts to build an accurate pedigree and family group record.

options: A. Your own history is the easiest place to start and builds habits for recording facts and stories
B. Public archives require a personal biography before granting access to census rolls
C. Genealogy software programs lock out ancestor entries until a six-week diary is uploaded
D. Personal timelines automatically verify the birth certificates of your great-grandparents
choices: A. Your own history is the easiest place to start and builds habits for recording facts and stories
B. Public archives require a personal biography before granting access to census rolls

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Your own history is the easiest place to start and builds habits for recording facts and stories
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Starting with your own history is the easiest entry point into genealogy and lets you practice organizing timelines, biographies, and journals using events you already know firsthand (p. 11).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: When interviewing relatives about family history, which type of information is most likely to be remembered accurately compared to specific dates and places?
options: A. Exact street addresses from childhood homes
B. Precise years of marriage and naturalization
C. Family relationships, such as who was a grandparent's sibling
D. Original spellings of towns in foreign countries
choices: A. Exact street addresses from childhood homes
B. Precise years of marriage and naturalization
C. Family relationships, such as who was a grandparent's sibling
D. Original spellings of towns in foreign countries
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Family relationships, such as who was a grandparent's sibling
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): In oral interviews, family relationships (such as knowing that great-uncle Ralph was Grandpa Erickson's brother) are usually reliable, whereas exact names, places, and dates are more often misremembered (p. 17).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In the United States today, which level of government is primarily responsible for creating and issuing official birth, marriage, and death vital records?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In the United States today, which level of government is primarily responsible for creating and issuing official birth, marriage, and death vital records?
options: A. The federal National Archives
B. Each individual state government
C. The U.S. Census Bureau
D. International lineage societies
choices: A. The federal National Archives
B. Each individual state government
C. The U.S. Census Bureau
D. International lineage societies
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Each individual state government
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): In the United States, each state creates and maintains the basic vital records for births, marriages, and deaths occurring within its borders (p. 20).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the main purpose of an ancestral family organization built around an early founding couple?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the main purpose of an ancestral family organization built around an early founding couple?
options: A. Issuing legal birth and marriage certificates on behalf of state governments
B. Charging mandatory membership fees to anyone born with that surname
C. Replacing federal census records with private family guesswork
D. Researching the ancestry and descendants of that couple and sharing the verified information
choices: A. Issuing legal birth and marriage certificates on behalf of state governments
B. Charging mandatory membership fees to anyone born with that surname
C. Replacing federal census records with private family guesswork
D. Researching the ancestry and descendants of that couple and sharing the verified information
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Researching the ancestry and descendants of that couple and sharing the verified information
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Ancestral family organizations bring together descendants of a specific couple to conduct quality research into the couple's ancestry and descendants and share those records (p. 19).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How can you narrow an online genealogy search when typing an ancestor's name returns thousands of results?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How can you narrow an online genealogy search when typing an ancestor's name returns thousands of results?
options: A. Remove the surname and search only by the ancestor's first name
B. Accept the first result listed at the top of the search engine page
C. Add unique keywords such as the place or year of the ancestor's death
D. Search only for living relatives instead of historical records
choices: A. Remove the surname and search only by the ancestor's first name
B. Accept the first result listed at the top of the search engine page
C. Add unique keywords such as the place or year of the ancestor's death
D. Search only for living relatives instead of historical records
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Add unique keywords such as the place or year of the ancestor's death
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Adding specific keywords like the place or year an ancestor died narrows thousands of broad hits down to records that are much more likely to match the right person (p. 16).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How have microfilming and record indexing worked together to transform genealogical research?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How have microfilming and record indexing worked together to transform genealogical research?
options: A. Microfilming preserved copies of fragile records worldwide, while indexing made those millions of pages searchable by name
B. Indexing replaced the need to ever read original birth or census certificates
C. Microfilming automatically translates handwritten foreign records into modern English
D. Family History Centers charge a per-page fee to index private family diaries
choices: A. Microfilming preserved copies of fragile records worldwide, while indexing made those millions of pages searchable by name
B. Indexing replaced the need to ever read original birth or census certificates
C. Microfilming automatically translates handwritten foreign records into modern English
D. Family History Centers charge a per-page fee to index private family diaries
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Microfilming preserved copies of fragile records worldwide, while indexing made those millions of pages searchable by name
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Microfilming preserved over two million rolls of fragile records at institutions like the Family History Library, and record indexing allows researchers to locate specific ancestors across those vast collections in seconds (p. 20).

options: A. Keep your eyes glued to the GPS screen while walking briskly near cliff edges, talus slopes, and busy roadways.
B. Reach bare-handed deep into dark rock crevices, hollow logs, and stone walls without looking first, and pry apart historic cemetery masonry to find micro-caches.
C. Cross fenced private ranch land with 'No Trespassing' signs whenever the GPS arrow points straight across the pasture.

D. Look up from the GPS screen whenever moving to watch your footing and surroundings, never thrust bare hands into blind crevices where snakes or spiders may shelter, respect private property and park permissions, and practice Cache In Trash Out (CITO) by packing out litter.

pamphlet_excerpts: Continuous Global Satellite Coverage: GPS technology can be used anywhere in the world 24 hours a day because the system of satellites circles Earth all the time, and some number of them (p. 11).
All Weather Free Operation: The system works in any kind of weather and does not require any setup fee or subscription charge (p. 11).
Timing Orbiting Satellite Signals: A GPS receiver (GPSr) calculates its position by carefully timing the signals sent by the 24 to 30 GPS satellites high above Earth (p. 11).
Multiple Satellites Overhead Everywhere: At any given time, there are usually several satellites over any given place on Earth (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Calculate Position From Signals: A GPS receiver (GPSr) calculates its position by carefully timing the signals sent by the 24 to 30 GPS satellites high above Earth (p. 11).
Step 2 - Track Multiple Overhead Satellites: At any given time, there are usually several satellites over any given place on Earth (p. 11).
Step 3 - Receive Satellite Time Data: Each satellite continually transmits data that indicates its location and the current time (p. 11).
Step 4 - Compare Signal Arrival Times: All GPS satellites transmit signals at the same instant, but the signals arrive at a GPS receiver at slightly different times (p. 11).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) If a Cache to Eagle® series exists in your council, visit at least three of the locations in the series. Describe the projects that each cache you visit highlights, and explain how the Cache to Eagle® program helps share our Scouting service with the public. (b) Create a Scouting-related Travel Bug® that promotes one of the values of Scouting. Release your Travel Bug into a public geocache and, with your parent or guardian's permission, monitor its progress at www. geocaching. com for 30 days. Keep a log, and share this with your counselor at the end of the 30-day period. (c) Set up and hide a public geocache, following the guidelines in the Geocaching merit badge pamphlet. Before doing so, share with your counselor a three-month maintenance plan for the geocache where you are personally responsible for those three months. After setting up the geocache, with your parent or guardian's permission, follow the logs online for 30 days and share them with your counselor. You must archive the geocache when you are no longer maintaining it. (d) Explain what Cache In Trash Out (CITO) means, and describe how you have practiced CITO at public geocaches or at a CITO event. Then, either create CITO containers to leave at public caches, or host a CITO event for your unit or for the public.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does a GPS receiver calculate its position on Earth?
options: A. By measuring variations in Earth's magnetic field and local barometric air pressure
B. By bouncing a laser beam off cell phone towers within five miles of the trailhead
C. By taking high-resolution photographs of the ground from orbit and matching landmarks
D. By timing the slight differences in arrival times of radio signals sent by multiple orbiting satellites
choices: A. By measuring variations in Earth's magnetic field and local barometric air pressure
B. By bouncing a laser beam off cell phone towers within five miles of the trailhead
C. By taking high-resolution photographs of the ground from orbit and matching landmarks

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. By timing the slight differences in arrival times of radio signals sent by multiple orbiting satellites
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): All GPS satellites transmit their location and current time simultaneously, and the receiver calculates its position by measuring the slight differences in arrival times from 24 to 30 orbiting satellites (p. 11).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
quiz_item.question: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
options: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
choices: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Uniformitarianism holds that ongoing geologic processes (magma crystallization, erosion, sedimentation, lithification, and metamorphism) explain the rock structures and stratigraphic record formed over geologic time.

pamphlet_excerpts: Grain Size Cooling Depth: Rock texture, or grain size, provides information about the depth at which the minerals in the magma began to cool, forming igneous rocks (p. 66).
Fine Grained Extrusive Rocks: As an example, if you find a fine-grainedigneous rock, you interpret the rock to be an extrusive rock that cooled at or near the surface (p. 66).
Coarse Grained Intrusive Rocks: Coarse-grained igneous rocks are intrusive rocks that cooled over very long periods of time (p. 66).
Tectonic Uplift and Erosion: These deep rocks get to the surface when tectonic (mountain-building) forces uplift the area and the material covering the intrusive rock is eroded away by wind (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Slow Cooling Intrusive Rocks: Coarse-grained igneous rocks are intrusive rocks that cooled over very long periods of time (p. 66).

Step 2 - Trace Uplift and Weathering Exposure: These deep rocks get to the surface when tectonic (mountain-building) forces uplift the area and the material covering the intrusive rock is eroded away by wind (p. 66).
Step 3 - Inspect Rock Color for Minerals: Another important characteristic of igneous rocks is color, which indicates the kinds of rock minerals (p. 66).
Step 4 - Recognize Quartz Rich Silicic Granite: Lighter colored igneous rocks such as granite are usually formed fromsialic or silicic magmas, rich in quartz and feldspar (p. 66).

quiz_item.question: How do coarse-grained intrusive igneous rocks that formed deep underground eventually become exposed at Earth's surface?
options: A. They float upward through solid crust like bubbles in water without any erosion
B. Burrowing animals dig them up from several miles beneath the crust
C. Ocean tides wash deep magma chambers onto beaches every spring
D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
choices: A. They float upward through solid crust like bubbles in water without any erosion
B. Burrowing animals dig them up from several miles beneath the crust

quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Deep intrusive rocks reach Earth's surface when mountain-building tectonic forces uplift the area and wind and water erode away the overlying material (p. 66).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Surface and Sedimentary Processes. Do ALL of the following: (1) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that demonstrates how sediments settle from suspension in water. Explain to your counselor what the exercise shows and why it is important. (2) Using topographical maps provided by your counselor, plot the stream gradients (different elevations divided by distance) for four different stream types (straight, meandering, dendritic, trellis). Explain which ones flow fastest and why, and which ones will carry larger grains of sediment and why. (3) On a stream diagram, show areas where you will find the following features: cut bank, fill bank, point bar, medial channel bars, and lake delta. Describe the relative sediment grain size found in each feature. (4) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that shows how some sedimentary material carried by water may be too small for you to see without a magnifier. (5) Visit a nearby stream. Find clues that show the direction of water flow, even if the water is missing. Record your observations in a notebook, and sketch those clues you observe. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (b) Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site. (c) Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (d) Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site.

sub_requirements.text: Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

sub_requirements.label: (d)
sub_requirements.text: Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

Step 3 - Trace Shale to Gneiss Progression: Depending on the degree of metamorphism, shale may be altered to form slate, schist, or gneiss, all of which exhibit foliation but varying grain sizes (p. 68).
Step 4 - Recognize Metamorphosed Igneous Rocks: Even igneous rocks can be altered by metamorphic conditions (p. 68).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
options: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
choices: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Uniformitarianism holds that ongoing geologic processes (magma crystallization, erosion, sedimentation, lithification, and metamorphism) explain the rock structures and stratigraphic record formed over geologic time.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What three stages must all Earth natural resources go through before people can use them in daily life?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What three stages must all Earth natural resources go through before people can use them in daily life?
options: A. They must be found, extracted, and processed before they can be used
B. They must be synthesized in laboratories before being buried in mines
C. They can be pumped or dug directly into finished consumer products without refinement
D. They are gathered exclusively from surface riverbeds without geological exploration
choices: A. They must be found, extracted, and processed before they can be used
B. They must be synthesized in laboratories before being buried in mines
C. They can be pumped or dug directly into finished consumer products without refinement
D. They are gathered exclusively from surface riverbeds without geological exploration
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. They must be found, extracted, and processed before they can be used
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): All natural resources must follow a three-stage sequence: they must be found (discovered), extracted (removed from Earth), and processed before they can be used (p. 37).

options: A. They float upward through solid crust like bubbles in water without any erosion
B. Burrowing animals dig them up from several miles beneath the crust
C. Ocean tides wash deep magma chambers onto beaches every spring
D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
choices: A. They float upward through solid crust like bubbles in water without any erosion
B. Burrowing animals dig them up from several miles beneath the crust
C. Ocean tides wash deep magma chambers onto beaches every spring

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Deep intrusive rocks reach Earth's surface when mountain-building tectonic forces uplift the area and wind and water erode away the overlying material (p. 66).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Your patrol is on the 6th fairway when dark thunderclouds build and you hear thunder 20 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. What must your group do immediately?
quiz_item.question: Your patrol is on the 6th fairway when dark thunderclouds build and you hear thunder 20 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. What must your group do immediately?
options: A. Finish playing the current hole quickly while holding metal golf umbrellas overhead.
B. Take shelter together under the tallest oak tree along the fairway edge until the rain passes.

C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
D. Sit inside an open-sided golf cart parked on the elevated 7th tee box while holding a 1-iron.
choices: A. Finish playing the current hole quickly while holding metal golf umbrellas overhead.
B. Take shelter together under the tallest oak tree along the fairway edge until the rain passes.

C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
D. Sit inside an open-sided golf cart parked on the elevated 7th tee box while holding a 1-iron.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A 20-second flash-to-bang count means lightning is 4 miles away (within the 6-mile / 30-second strike zone); isolated trees and metal clubs/umbrellas are acute lightning hazards.

requirements.lead_text: Complete ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Traditional Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the USGA Rules of Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the three categories of golf etiquette. (b) Demonstrate that you understand the definitions of golf terms. (c) Show that you understand the Rules of Amateur Status. (2) Tell about your understanding of the World Handicap System. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the early history of golf. (b) Describe golf's early years in the United States. (c) Tell about the accomplishments of a top golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) The proper grip, stance, posture, and key fundamentals of a good swing (b) Driver played from a tee (c) The fairway wood shot (d) The long iron shot (e) The short iron shot (f) The approach, chip-and-run, and pitch shots (g) A recovery shot from a bunker or heavy rough (h) A sound putting stroke (6) Play a minimum of two nine-hole rounds or one 18-hole round of golf with another golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the Rules of Golf. (b) Practice good golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow golfers, committee, sponsor, and gallery. (7) Find out about three careers related to traditional golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you. (b) Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you.
