requirements.lead_text: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement:
requirements.req_text: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement: (a) Option A, Agronomy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Describe how to prepare a seedbed. (2) Make and use a seed germination tester to test 50 seeds of four of the following plants: corn, cotton, alfalfa, soybeans, clover, wheat, rice, rye, or barley. Determine the percentage of live seeds. (3) Explain one important insect pest and one important disease that damage each of the following: corn, small grains, and cotton. Collect and name five weeds that compete with crops in your locality. Tell how to control these weeds without harming people, wildlife, or useful insects. (4) On a map of the United States, identify the chief regions where corn, cotton, forage crops, small grain crops, and oil crops grow. Tell how the climate and location of these regions make them leaders in the production of these crops. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Corn (1) Grow a plot of corn and have your plot inspected by your counselor. Record seed variety or experimental code number. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial corn farming and the contributions that corn makes to today's food and fuel supply. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage corn, and explain how it affects corn production and how it is controlled. (5) (b) Cotton (1) Grow a plot of cotton and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial cotton farming, and about the uses of cotton fiber and seed and the economic value of this crop. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage cotton, and explain how it affects cotton production and how it is controlled. (5) (c) Forage Crops (1) Collect, count, and label samples of each for display: perennial grasses, annual grasses, legumes, and broadleaf weeds. Indicate how each grass and legume is used. Keep a log of the site where you found each sample and share it with your counselor. (2) Explain how legumes can be used to enrich the soil and how they may deplete it under certain conditions. Explain how livestock may enrich or deplete the soil. (3) Name five poisonous plants that are dangerous to livestock, and tell the different ways of using forage crops as feed for livestock. (5) (d) Small Grains (1) Give production figures for small grain crops listed in the U. S. Statistical Report or Agricultural Statistics Handbook for the latest year available. (2) Help in harvesting a crop of grain. Tell how to reduce harvesting losses and about modern methods of growing one small grain crop. (3) Visit a grain elevator, flour mill, cereal plant, feed or seed company. Talk with the operator. Take notes, and describe the processes used and tell your patrol, troop, or class about your visit. (5) (e) Oil Crops (1) Grow a plot of soybeans and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of growing soybeans on a commercial scale, and discuss the contributions soybeans make to our food supply. (3) Explain why a hard frost can be dangerous to soybeans just after emergence. (b) Option B, Horticulture. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit one of the following places and tell what you learned about horticulture there: public garden, arboretum, retail nursery, wholesale nursery, production greenhouse, or conservatory greenhouse. (2) Explain the following terms: hardiness zone, shade tolerance, pH, moisture requirement, native habitat, texture, cultivar, ultimate size, disease resistance, habit, evergreen, deciduous, annual, and perennial. Find out what hardiness zone you live in and list 10 landscape plants you like that are suitable for your climate, giving the common name and scientific name for each. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Explain the difference between vegetative and sexual propagation methods, and tell some horticultural advantages of each. Grow a plant from a stem or root cutting or graft. (b) Transplant 12 seedlings or rooted cuttings to larger containers and grow them for at least one month. (c) Demonstrate good pruning techniques and tell why pruning is important. (d) After obtaining permission, plant a tree or shrub properly in an appropriate site. (4) Do the following: (a) Explain the importance of good landscape design and selection of plants that are suitable for particular sites and conditions. (b) Tell why it is important to know how big a plant will grow. (c) Tell why slower-growing landscape plants are sometimes a better choice than faster-growing varieties. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. Explain why you chose the mix and tell what is in it. (2) Transplant plants to a bed in the landscape and maintain the bed until the end of the growing season. Record your activities, observations, materials used, and costs. (3) Demonstrate mulching, fertilizing, watering, weeding, and deadheading, and tell how each practice helps your plants. (4) Tell some differences between gardening with annuals and perennials. (5) (b) Fruit, Berry, and Nut Crops (1) Plant five fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants that are suited to your area. Take full care of fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants through one season. (2) Prune a tree, vine, or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) Demonstrate one type of graft and tell why this method is useful. (4) Describe how one fruit, nut, or berry crop is processed for use. (5) (c) Woody Ornamentals (1) Plant five or more trees or shrubs in a landscape setting. Take full care of the trees or shrubs you have planted for one growing season. (2) Prune a tree or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) List 10 trees (in addition to those listed in general requirement 6 above) and tell your counselor how each is used in the landscape. Give the common and scientific names. (4) Describe the size, texture, color, flowers, leaves, fruit, hardiness, cultural requirements, and any special characteristics that make each type of tree or shrub attractive or interesting. (5) Tell five ways trees help improve the quality of our environment. (5) (d) Home Gardening (1) Design and plant a garden or landscape that is at least 10 by 10 feet. (2) Plant 10 or more different types of plants in your garden. Tell why you selected particular varieties of vegetables and flowers. Take care of the plants in your garden for one season. (3) Demonstrate soil preparation, staking, watering, weeding, mulching, composting, fertilizing, pest management, and pruning. Tell why each technique is used. (4) Tell four types of things you could provide to make your home landscape or park a better place for birds and wildlife. List the common and scientific names of 10 kinds of native plants that are beneficial to birds and wildlife in your area. (c) Option C, Field Botany. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a park, forest, Scout camp, or other natural area near your home. While you are there: (a) Determine which species of plants are the largest and which are the most abundant. Note whether they cast shade on other plants. (b) Using information from maps, textbooks, or the internet, describe the environmental factors that may influence the presence of plants on your site, including latitude, climate, air and soil temperature, soil type and pH, geology, hydrology, and topography. (c) Record any differences in the types of plants you see at the edge of a forest, near water, in burned areas, or near a road or railroad. (2) Select a study site that is at least 100 by 100 feet. Make a list of 10 woody plants (trees and shrubs) and 10 non-woody plants in the study site. Find out which of these are native plants and which are exotic (or non-native). (3) Tell how an identification key works and use a simple key to identify 10 kinds of plants (in addition to those in general requirement 5 above). Tell the difference between common and scientific names and tell why scientific names are important. (4) After gaining permission, collect, identify, press, mount, and label 10 different plants that are common in your area. Tell why voucher specimens are important for documentation of a field botanist's discoveries. (5) Obtain a list of rare plants of your state. Tell what is being done to protect rare plants and natural areas in your state. Write a paragraph about one of the rare plants in your state. (6) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (a) Tree Inventory (1) Identify the trees of your neighborhood, a park, a section of your town, or a Scout camp. (2) Collect, press, and label leaves, flowers, or fruits to document your inventory. (3) List the types of trees by scientific name and give common names. Note the number and size (diameter at 4½ feet above ground) of trees observed and determine the largest of each species in your study area. (4) Show two or more people how to use a leaf or twig key to identify at least five species of trees or shrubs. (b) Transect Study (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Use the transect method to study the two different kinds of plant communities. The transects should be at least 500 feet long. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify each tree within 10 feet of the transect line. (b) Measure the diameter of each tree at 4½ feet above the ground, and map and list each tree. (c) Nested Plot (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Mark off nested plots and inventory two different kinds of plant communities. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify, measure, and map each tree in a 100-by-100-foot plot. (Measure the diameter of each tree larger than 3 inches in diameter at 4½ feet above the ground.) (b) Identify and count all trees and shrubs in a 10-by-10-foot plot within each of the larger areas. (c) Identify and count all broad-leaved plants (trees, shrubs, vines, and herbaceous plants) and all plants (wildflowers, ferns, grasses, mosses, etc.) of a 4-by-4-foot plot within the 10-by-10-foot plot. Note: If individual plants like ferns, grasses, and mosses cannot be clearly distinguished, make a reasonable estimate of area (square inches of cover) for each species and record that as an estimate within the 4 x 4 subplot. (d) Herbarium Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit an herbarium at a university, park, or botanical garden; OR, visit an herbarium website (with your parent or guardian's permission). (2) Tell how the specimens are arranged and how they are used by researchers. If possible, observe voucher specimens of a plant that is rare in your state. (3) Tell how a voucher specimen is mounted and prepared for permanent storage. Tell how specimens should be handled so that they will not be damaged. (4) Tell about the tools and references used by botanists in an herbarium. (e) Plant Conservation Organization Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit a private conservation organization or government agency that is concerned with protecting rare plants and natural areas. (2) Tell about the activities of the organization in studying and protecting rare plants and natural areas. (3) If possible, visit a nature preserve managed by the organization. Tell about land management practices such as controlled burning, or measures to eradicate invasive (non-native) plants or other threats to the plants that are native to the area.

children.text: Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Corn (1) Grow a plot of corn and have your plot inspected by your counselor. Record seed variety or experimental code number. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial corn farming and the contributions that corn makes to today's food and fuel supply. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage corn, and explain how it affects corn production and how it is controlled. (5) (b) Cotton (1) Grow a plot of cotton and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial cotton farming, and about the uses of cotton fiber and seed and the economic value of this crop. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage cotton, and explain how it affects cotton production and how it is controlled. (5) (c) Forage Crops (1) Collect, count, and label samples of each for display: perennial grasses, annual grasses, legumes, and broadleaf weeds. Indicate how each grass and legume is used. Keep a log of the site where you found each sample and share it with your counselor. (2) Explain how legumes can be used to enrich the soil and how they may deplete it under certain conditions. Explain how livestock may enrich or deplete the soil. (3) Name five poisonous plants that are dangerous to livestock, and tell the different ways of using forage crops as feed for livestock. (5) (d) Small Grains (1) Give production figures for small grain crops listed in the U. S. Statistical Report or Agricultural Statistics Handbook for the latest year available. (2) Help in harvesting a crop of grain. Tell how to reduce harvesting losses and about modern methods of growing one small grain crop. (3) Visit a grain elevator, flour mill, cereal plant, feed or seed company. Talk with the operator. Take notes, and describe the processes used and tell your patrol, troop, or class about your visit. (5) (e) Oil Crops (1) Grow a plot of soybeans and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of growing soybeans on a commercial scale, and discuss the contributions soybeans make to our food supply. (3) Explain why a hard frost can be dangerous to soybeans just after emergence.

children.sub_req_text: Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Corn (1) Grow a plot of corn and have your plot inspected by your counselor. Record seed variety or experimental code number. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial corn farming and the contributions that corn makes to today's food and fuel supply. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage corn, and explain how it affects corn production and how it is controlled. (5) (b) Cotton (1) Grow a plot of cotton and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial cotton farming, and about the uses of cotton fiber and seed and the economic value of this crop. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage cotton, and explain how it affects cotton production and how it is controlled. (5) (c) Forage Crops (1) Collect, count, and label samples of each for display: perennial grasses, annual grasses, legumes, and broadleaf weeds. Indicate how each grass and legume is used. Keep a log of the site where you found each sample and share it with your counselor. (2) Explain how legumes can be used to enrich the soil and how they may deplete it under certain conditions. Explain how livestock may enrich or deplete the soil. (3) Name five poisonous plants that are dangerous to livestock, and tell the different ways of using forage crops as feed for livestock. (5) (d) Small Grains (1) Give production figures for small grain crops listed in the U. S. Statistical Report or Agricultural Statistics Handbook for the latest year available. (2) Help in harvesting a crop of grain. Tell how to reduce harvesting losses and about modern methods of growing one small grain crop. (3) Visit a grain elevator, flour mill, cereal plant, feed or seed company. Talk with the operator. Take notes, and describe the processes used and tell your patrol, troop, or class about your visit. (5) (e) Oil Crops (1) Grow a plot of soybeans and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of growing soybeans on a commercial scale, and discuss the contributions soybeans make to our food supply. (3) Explain why a hard frost can be dangerous to soybeans just after emergence.

(2) Make and use a seed germination tester to test 50 seeds of four of the following plants: corn, cotton, alfalfa, soybeans, clover, wheat, rice, rye, or barley. Determine the percentage of live seeds. (3) Explain one important insect pest and one important disease that damage each of the following: corn, small grains, and cotton. Collect and name five weeds that compete with crops in your locality. Tell how to control these weeds without harming people, wildlife, or useful insects. (4) On a map of the United States, identify the chief regions where corn, cotton, forage crops, small grain crops, and oil crops grow. Tell how the climate and location of these regions make them leaders in the production of these crops. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Corn (1) Grow a plot of corn and have your plot inspected by your counselor. Record seed variety or experimental code number. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial corn farming and the contributions that corn makes to today's food and fuel supply. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage corn, and explain how it affects corn production and how it is controlled. (5) (b) Cotton (1) Grow a plot of cotton and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial cotton farming, and about the uses of cotton fiber and seed and the economic value of this crop. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage cotton, and explain how it affects cotton production and how it is controlled. (5) (c) Forage Crops (1) Collect, count, and label samples of each for display: perennial grasses, annual grasses, legumes, and broadleaf weeds. Indicate how each grass and legume is used. Keep a log of the site where you found each sample and share it with your counselor. (2) Explain how legumes can be used to enrich the soil and how they may deplete it under certain conditions. Explain how livestock may enrich or deplete the soil. (3) Name five poisonous plants that are dangerous to livestock, and tell the different ways of using forage crops as feed for livestock. (5) (d) Small Grains (1) Give production figures for small grain crops listed in the U. S. Statistical Report or Agricultural Statistics Handbook for the latest year available. (2) Help in harvesting a crop of grain. Tell how to reduce harvesting losses and about modern methods of growing one small grain crop. (3) Visit a grain elevator, flour mill, cereal plant, feed or seed company. Talk with the operator. Take notes, and describe the processes used and tell your patrol, troop, or class about your visit. (5) (e) Oil Crops (1) Grow a plot of soybeans and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of growing soybeans on a commercial scale, and discuss the contributions soybeans make to our food supply. sub_requirements.text: Option B, Horticulture. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit one of the following places and tell what you learned about horticulture there: public garden, arboretum, retail nursery, wholesale nursery, production greenhouse, or conservatory greenhouse. (2) Explain the following terms: hardiness zone, shade tolerance, pH, moisture requirement, native habitat, texture, cultivar, ultimate size, disease resistance, habit, evergreen, deciduous, annual, and perennial. Find out what hardiness zone you live in and list 10 landscape plants you like that are suitable for your climate, giving the common name and scientific name for each. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Explain the difference between vegetative and sexual propagation methods, and tell some horticultural advantages of each. Grow a plant from a stem or root cutting or graft. (b) Transplant 12 seedlings or rooted cuttings to larger containers and grow them for at least one month. (c) Demonstrate good pruning techniques and tell why pruning is important. (d) After obtaining permission, plant a tree or shrub properly in an appropriate site. (4) Do the following: (a) Explain the importance of good landscape design and selection of plants that are suitable for particular sites and conditions. (b) Tell why it is important to know how big a plant will grow. (c) Tell why slower-growing landscape plants are sometimes a better choice than faster-growing varieties. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. Explain why you chose the mix and tell what is in it. (2) Transplant plants to a bed in the landscape and maintain the bed until the end of the growing season. Record your activities, observations, materials used, and costs. (3) Demonstrate mulching, fertilizing, watering, weeding, and deadheading, and tell how each practice helps your plants. (4) Tell some differences between gardening with annuals and perennials. (5) (b) Fruit, Berry, and Nut Crops (1) Plant five fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants that are suited to your area. Take full care of fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants through one season. (2) Prune a tree, vine, or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) Demonstrate one type of graft and tell why this method is useful. (4) Describe how one fruit, nut, or berry crop is processed for use. (5) (c) Woody Ornamentals (1) Plant five or more trees or shrubs in a landscape setting. Take full care of the trees or shrubs you have planted for one growing season. (2) Prune a tree or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) List 10 trees (in addition to those listed in general requirement 6 above) and tell your counselor how each is used in the landscape. Give the common and scientific names. (4) Describe the size, texture, color, flowers, leaves, fruit, hardiness, cultural requirements, and any special characteristics that make each type of tree or shrub attractive or interesting. (5) Tell five ways trees help improve the quality of our environment. (5) (d) Home Gardening (1) Design and plant a garden or landscape that is at least 10 by 10 feet. (2) Plant 10 or more different types of plants in your garden. Tell why you selected particular varieties of vegetables and flowers. Take care of the plants in your garden for one season. (3) Demonstrate soil preparation, staking, watering, weeding, mulching, composting, fertilizing, pest management, and pruning. Tell why each technique is used. (4) Tell four types of things you could provide to make your home landscape or park a better place for birds and wildlife. List the common and scientific names of 10 kinds of native plants that are beneficial to birds and wildlife in your area.

children.text: Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. Explain why you chose the mix and tell what is in it. (2) Transplant plants to a bed in the landscape and maintain the bed until the end of the growing season. Record your activities, observations, materials used, and costs. (3) Demonstrate mulching, fertilizing, watering, weeding, and deadheading, and tell how each practice helps your plants. (4) Tell some differences between gardening with annuals and perennials. (5) (b) Fruit, Berry, and Nut Crops (1) Plant five fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants that are suited to your area. Take full care of fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants through one season. (2) Prune a tree, vine, or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) Demonstrate one type of graft and tell why this method is useful. (4) Describe how one fruit, nut, or berry crop is processed for use. (5) (c) Woody Ornamentals (1) Plant five or more trees or shrubs in a landscape setting. Take full care of the trees or shrubs you have planted for one growing season. (2) Prune a tree or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) List 10 trees (in addition to those listed in general requirement 6 above) and tell your counselor how each is used in the landscape. Give the common and scientific names. (4) Describe the size, texture, color, flowers, leaves, fruit, hardiness, cultural requirements, and any special characteristics that make each type of tree or shrub attractive or interesting. (5) Tell five ways trees help improve the quality of our environment. (5) (d) Home Gardening (1) Design and plant a garden or landscape that is at least 10 by 10 feet. children.sub_req_text: Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. Explain why you chose the mix and tell what is in it. (2) Transplant plants to a bed in the landscape and maintain the bed until the end of the growing season. Record your activities, observations, materials used, and costs. (3) Demonstrate mulching, fertilizing, watering, weeding, and deadheading, and tell how each practice helps your plants. (5) (b) Fruit, Berry, and Nut Crops (1) Plant five fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants that are suited to your area. (3) Demonstrate one type of graft and tell why this method is useful. (4) Describe how one fruit, nut, or berry crop is processed for use. (5) (c) Woody Ornamentals (1) Plant five or more trees or shrubs in a landscape setting. Take full care of the trees or shrubs you have planted for one growing season. (2) Prune a tree or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) List 10 trees (in addition to those listed in general requirement 6 above) and tell your counselor how each is used in the landscape. Give the common and scientific names. (4) Describe the size, texture, color, flowers, leaves, fruit, hardiness, cultural requirements, and any special characteristics that make each type of tree or shrub attractive or interesting. (5) Tell five ways trees help improve the quality of our environment. (5) (d) Home Gardening (1) Design and plant a garden or landscape that is at least 10 by 10 feet. Find out what hardiness zone you live in and list 10 landscape plants you like that are suitable for your climate, giving the common name and scientific name for each. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Explain the difference between vegetative and sexual propagation methods, and tell some horticultural advantages of each. (c) Demonstrate good pruning techniques and tell why pruning is important. (d) After obtaining permission, plant a tree or shrub properly in an appropriate site. (4) Do the following: (a) Explain the importance of good landscape design and selection of plants that are suitable for particular sites and conditions. (b) Tell why it is important to know how big a plant will grow. (c) Tell why slower-growing landscape plants are sometimes a better choice than faster-growing varieties. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. sub_requirements.text: Option C, Field Botany. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a park, forest, Scout camp, or other natural area near your home. While you are there: (a) Determine which species of plants are the largest and which are the most abundant. Note whether they cast shade on other plants. (b) Using information from maps, textbooks, or the internet, describe the environmental factors that may influence the presence of plants on your site, including latitude, climate, air and soil temperature, soil type and pH, geology, hydrology, and topography. (c) Record any differences in the types of plants you see at the edge of a forest, near water, in burned areas, or near a road or railroad. (2) Select a study site that is at least 100 by 100 feet. Make a list of 10 woody plants (trees and shrubs) and 10 non-woody plants in the study site. Find out which of these are native plants and which are exotic (or non-native). (3) Tell how an identification key works and use a simple key to identify 10 kinds of plants (in addition to those in general requirement 5 above). Tell the difference between common and scientific names and tell why scientific names are important. (4) After gaining permission, collect, identify, press, mount, and label 10 different plants that are common in your area. Tell why voucher specimens are important for documentation of a field botanist's discoveries. (5) Obtain a list of rare plants of your state. Tell what is being done to protect rare plants and natural areas in your state. Write a paragraph about one of the rare plants in your state. (6) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (a) Tree Inventory (1) Identify the trees of your neighborhood, a park, a section of your town, or a Scout camp. (2) Collect, press, and label leaves, flowers, or fruits to document your inventory. (3) List the types of trees by scientific name and give common names. Note the number and size (diameter at 4½ feet above ground) of trees observed and determine the largest of each species in your study area. (4) Show two or more people how to use a leaf or twig key to identify at least five species of trees or shrubs. (b) Transect Study (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Use the transect method to study the two different kinds of plant communities. The transects should be at least 500 feet long. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify each tree within 10 feet of the transect line. (b) Measure the diameter of each tree at 4½ feet above the ground, and map and list each tree. (c) Nested Plot (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Mark off nested plots and inventory two different kinds of plant communities. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify, measure, and map each tree in a 100-by-100-foot plot. (Measure the diameter of each tree larger than 3 inches in diameter at 4½ feet above the ground.) (b) Identify and count all trees and shrubs in a 10-by-10-foot plot within each of the larger areas. (c) Identify and count all broad-leaved plants (trees, shrubs, vines, and herbaceous plants) and all plants (wildflowers, ferns, grasses, mosses, etc.) of a 4-by-4-foot plot within the 10-by-10-foot plot. Note: If individual plants like ferns, grasses, and mosses cannot be clearly distinguished, make a reasonable estimate of area (square inches of cover) for each species and record that as an estimate within the 4 x 4 subplot. (d) Herbarium Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit an herbarium at a university, park, or botanical garden; OR, visit an herbarium website (with your parent or guardian's permission). (2) Tell how the specimens are arranged and how they are used by researchers. If possible, observe voucher specimens of a plant that is rare in your state. (3) Tell how a voucher specimen is mounted and prepared for permanent storage. Tell how specimens should be handled so that they will not be damaged. (4) Tell about the tools and references used by botanists in an herbarium. (e) Plant Conservation Organization Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit a private conservation organization or government agency that is concerned with protecting rare plants and natural areas. (2) Tell about the activities of the organization in studying and protecting rare plants and natural areas. (3) If possible, visit a nature preserve managed by the organization. Tell about land management practices such as controlled burning, or measures to eradicate invasive (non-native) plants or other threats to the plants that are native to the area.

children.text: Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (a) Tree Inventory (1) Identify the trees of your neighborhood, a park, a section of your town, or a Scout camp. (2) Collect, press, and label leaves, flowers, or fruits to document your inventory. (3) List the types of trees by scientific name and give common names. Note the number and size (diameter at 4½ feet above ground) of trees observed and determine the largest of each species in your study area. (4) Show two or more people how to use a leaf or twig key to identify at least five species of trees or shrubs. (b) Transect Study (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Use the transect method to study the two different kinds of plant communities. The transects should be at least 500 feet long. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify each tree within 10 feet of the transect line. (b) Measure the diameter of each tree at 4½ feet above the ground, and map and list each tree. (c) Nested Plot (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Mark off nested plots and inventory two different kinds of plant communities. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify, measure, and map each tree in a 100-by-100-foot plot. (Measure the diameter of each tree larger than 3 inches in diameter at 4½ feet above the ground.) (b) Identify and count all trees and shrubs in a 10-by-10-foot plot within each of the larger areas. (c) Identify and count all broad-leaved plants (trees, shrubs, vines, and herbaceous plants) and all plants (wildflowers, ferns, grasses, mosses, etc.) of a 4-by-4-foot plot within the 10-by-10-foot plot. Note: If individual plants like ferns, grasses, and mosses cannot be clearly distinguished, make a reasonable estimate of area (square inches of cover) for each species and record that as an estimate within the 4 x 4 subplot. (d) Herbarium Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit an herbarium at a university, park, or botanical garden; OR, visit an herbarium website (with your parent or guardian's permission). (2) Tell how the specimens are arranged and how they are used by researchers. If possible, observe voucher specimens of a plant that is rare in your state. (3) Tell how a voucher specimen is mounted and prepared for permanent storage. Tell how specimens should be handled so that they will not be damaged. (4) Tell about the tools and references used by botanists in an herbarium. (e) Plant Conservation Organization Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit a private conservation organization or government agency that is concerned with protecting rare plants and natural areas. (2) Tell about the activities of the organization in studying and protecting rare plants and natural areas. (3) If possible, visit a nature preserve managed by the organization. Tell about land management practices such as controlled burning, or measures to eradicate invasive (non-native) plants or other threats to the plants that are native to the area.

children.label: (c)
children.text: Nested Plot (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Mark off nested plots and inventory two different kinds of plant communities. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify, measure, and map each tree in a 100-by-100-foot plot. (Measure the diameter of each tree larger than 3 inches in diameter at 4½ feet above the ground.) (b) Identify and count all trees and shrubs in a 10-by-10-foot plot within each of the larger areas. (c) Identify and count all broad-leaved plants (trees, shrubs, vines, and herbaceous plants) and all plants (wildflowers, ferns, grasses, mosses, etc.) of a 4-by-4-foot plot within the 10-by-10-foot plot. Note: If individual plants like ferns, grasses, and mosses cannot be clearly distinguished, make a reasonable estimate of area (square inches of cover) for each species and record that as an estimate within the 4 x 4 subplot.

children.label: (d)
children.text: Herbarium Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit an herbarium at a university, park, or botanical garden; OR, visit an herbarium website (with your parent or guardian's permission). children.sub_req_text: Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (a) Tree Inventory (1) Identify the trees of your neighborhood, a park, a section of your town, or a Scout camp. (2) Collect, press, and label leaves, flowers, or fruits to document your inventory. (3) List the types of trees by scientific name and give common names. Note the number and size (diameter at 4½ feet above ground) of trees observed and determine the largest of each species in your study area. (4) Show two or more people how to use a leaf or twig key to identify at least five species of trees or shrubs. (b) Transect Study (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Use the transect method to study the two different kinds of plant communities. The transects should be at least 500 feet long. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify each tree within 10 feet of the transect line. (b) Measure the diameter of each tree at 4½ feet above the ground, and map and list each tree. (c) Nested Plot (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Mark off nested plots and inventory two different kinds of plant communities. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify, measure, and map each tree in a 100-by-100-foot plot. (Measure the diameter of each tree larger than 3 inches in diameter at 4½ feet above the ground.) (b) Identify and count all trees and shrubs in a 10-by-10-foot plot within each of the larger areas. (c) Identify and count all broad-leaved plants (trees, shrubs, vines, and herbaceous plants) and all plants (wildflowers, ferns, grasses, mosses, etc.) of a 4-by-4-foot plot within the 10-by-10-foot plot. Note: If individual plants like ferns, grasses, and mosses cannot be clearly distinguished, make a reasonable estimate of area (square inches of cover) for each species and record that as an estimate within the 4 x 4 subplot. (d) Herbarium Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit an herbarium at a university, park, or botanical garden; OR, visit an herbarium website (with your parent or guardian's permission). (2) Tell how the specimens are arranged and how they are used by researchers. If possible, observe voucher specimens of a plant that is rare in your state. (3) Tell how a voucher specimen is mounted and prepared for permanent storage. Tell how specimens should be handled so that they will not be damaged. (4) Tell about the tools and references used by botanists in an herbarium. (e) Plant Conservation Organization Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit a private conservation organization or government agency that is concerned with protecting rare plants and natural areas. (2) Tell about the activities of the organization in studying and protecting rare plants and natural areas. (3) If possible, visit a nature preserve managed by the organization. Tell about land management practices such as controlled burning, or measures to eradicate invasive (non-native) plants or other threats to the plants that are native to the area.

(2) Tell how the specimens are arranged and how they are used by researchers. If possible, observe voucher specimens of a plant that is rare in your state. (3) Tell how a voucher specimen is mounted and prepared for permanent storage. Tell how specimens should be handled so that they will not be damaged. (4) Tell about the tools and references used by botanists in an herbarium. (e) Plant Conservation Organization Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit a private conservation organization or government agency that is concerned with protecting rare plants and natural areas. (2) Tell about the activities of the organization in studying and protecting rare plants and natural areas. (3) If possible, visit a nature preserve managed by the organization. Tell about land management practices such as controlled burning, or measures to eradicate invasive (non-native) plants or other threats to the plants that are native to the area.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In a flowering vascular plant, what are the distinct roles of xylem and phloem tissues inside the roots, stems, and leaves?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In a flowering vascular plant, what are the distinct roles of xylem and phloem tissues inside the roots, stems, and leaves?
options: A. Xylem produces pollen grains in the anther, while phloem captures sunlight in the epidermis.
B. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the leaves, while phloem distributes sugars produced during photosynthesis throughout the plant.
C. Xylem carries sugars downward from flowers to the soil, while phloem absorbs carbon dioxide through root hairs.
D. Xylem and phloem are reproductive organs located inside the pistil that fertilize ovules.
choices: A. Xylem produces pollen grains in the anther, while phloem captures sunlight in the epidermis.
B. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the leaves, while phloem distributes sugars produced during photosynthesis throughout the plant.
C. Xylem carries sugars downward from flowers to the soil, while phloem absorbs carbon dioxide through root hairs.
D. Xylem and phloem are reproductive organs located inside the pistil that fertilize ovules.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the leaves, while phloem distributes sugars produced during photosynthesis throughout the plant.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Vascular plants rely on xylem to conduct water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots and phloem to transport photosynthetic sugars (food) to growing tissues and storage organs.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why are honeybees and other pollinating insects critical to the life cycle of many flowering plants?
options: A. They carry pollen from the male anthers to the female pistils so fertilization and seed production can occur
B. They chew through thick seed coats so dormant seeds can sprout in spring
C. They inject chlorophyll into flower petals to start photosynthesis
D. They loosen compacted clay around deep taproots during dry weather
choices: A. They carry pollen from the male anthers to the female pistils so fertilization and seed production can occur
B. They chew through thick seed coats so dormant seeds can sprout in spring
C. They inject chlorophyll into flower petals to start photosynthesis
D. They loosen compacted clay around deep taproots during dry weather
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. They carry pollen from the male anthers to the female pistils so fertilization and seed production can occur
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): As honeybees and other insects forage among blossoms, they transfer pollen grains to the pistil, enabling fertilization and the development of fertile seeds and fruit (p. 21).

options: A. Horizons or bedrock layers
B. Peds or aggregates
C. Silts or leached sediments
D. Stomata or root nodules
choices: A. Horizons or bedrock layers
B. Peds or aggregates
C. Silts or leached sediments
D. Stomata or root nodules
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Peds or aggregates
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Soil particles cling together in clusters known as peds or aggregates, and the arrangement of these clumps determines the soil structure (p. 22).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What is the primary purpose of the curved P-trap installed directly beneath every household sink, shower, and floor drain?
quiz_item.question: What is the primary purpose of the curved P-trap installed directly beneath every household sink, shower, and floor drain?
options: A. To boost incoming municipal water pressure before it reaches the hot and cold faucet valves.
B. To grind up solid food waste so it does not enter the septic tank or city sewer main.
C. To hold a standing water seal that blocks toxic, flammable, and foul-smelling sewer gases from rising out of the drain-waste-vent system into the building.
D. To filter dissolved calcium and magnesium minerals out of potable drinking water.
choices: A. To boost incoming municipal water pressure before it reaches the hot and cold faucet valves.
B. To grind up solid food waste so it does not enter the septic tank or city sewer main.
C. To hold a standing water seal that blocks toxic, flammable, and foul-smelling sewer gases from rising out of the drain-waste-vent system into the building.
D. To filter dissolved calcium and magnesium minerals out of potable drinking water.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. To hold a standing water seal that blocks toxic, flammable, and foul-smelling sewer gases from rising out of the drain-waste-vent system into the building.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A P-trap retains a small volume of water after each use, creating an airtight liquid barrier that prevents hazardous sewer gases (such as methane and hydrogen sulfide) from entering living spaces.

requirements.lead_text: Do FOUR of the following, each under the supervision of a knowledgeable adult:
requirements.req_text: Do FOUR of the following, each under the supervision of a knowledgeable adult: (a) Visit the plumbing section of a hardware store or home center and identify: (1) PVC pipe and fittings (2) CPVC pipe and fittings (3) PEX pipe and fittings (4) Copper pipe and fittings (5) Steel pipe and fittings (6) Specialty plumbing tools (b) Cut, clean (deburr), PVC or CPVC pipe; solvent weld at least three connections to include a coupling, tee, and elbow. patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the primary purpose of the curved P-trap installed directly beneath every household sink, shower, and floor drain?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the primary purpose of the curved P-trap installed directly beneath every household sink, shower, and floor drain?
options: A. To boost incoming municipal water pressure before it reaches the hot and cold faucet valves.
B. To grind up solid food waste so it does not enter the septic tank or city sewer main.
C. To hold a standing water seal that blocks toxic, flammable, and foul-smelling sewer gases from rising out of the drain-waste-vent system into the building.
D. To filter dissolved calcium and magnesium minerals out of potable drinking water.
choices: A. To boost incoming municipal water pressure before it reaches the hot and cold faucet valves.
B. To grind up solid food waste so it does not enter the septic tank or city sewer main.
C. To hold a standing water seal that blocks toxic, flammable, and foul-smelling sewer gases from rising out of the drain-waste-vent system into the building.
D. To filter dissolved calcium and magnesium minerals out of potable drinking water.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. To hold a standing water seal that blocks toxic, flammable, and foul-smelling sewer gases from rising out of the drain-waste-vent system into the building.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A P-trap retains a small volume of water after each use, creating an airtight liquid barrier that prevents hazardous sewer gases (such as methane and hydrogen sulfide) from entering living spaces.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What happens to a home drainage system if it lacks properly installed air vents?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What happens to a home drainage system if it lacks properly installed air vents?
options: A. The water heater automatically shuts off its burner
B. The pipes become air-bound like a narrow-necked bottle, slowing drainage
C. Cold supply water reverses direction and flows back to the city main
D. The water meter records double the actual household water usage
choices: A. The water heater automatically shuts off its burner
B. The pipes become air-bound like a narrow-necked bottle, slowing drainage
C. Cold supply water reverses direction and flows back to the city main
D. The water meter records double the actual household water usage
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. The pipes become air-bound like a narrow-necked bottle, slowing drainage
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Without air vents to admit atmospheric air behind flowing wastewater, the drainage system becomes air-bound like an inverted small-necked bottle (p. 9).

options: A. It threads the outside of the copper pipe while cutting
B. It melts the copper edge so no soldering flux is required
C. It makes a straight, square cut and avoids bending or crushing the pipe
D. It automatically flares the end of the tubing for compression nuts
choices: A. It threads the outside of the copper pipe while cutting
B. It melts the copper edge so no soldering flux is required

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. It makes a straight, square cut and avoids bending or crushing the pipe
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A pipe cutter rolls smoothly around the tubing to produce a straight, square cut while preventing soft copper pipe from bending or crushing (p. 23).

options: A. The rubber force cup plunger
B. The municipal water meter dial
C. The cast-iron drainpipe coupling
D. The temperature and pressure-relief valve
choices: A. The rubber force cup plunger
B. The municipal water meter dial
C. The cast-iron drainpipe coupling
D. The temperature and pressure-relief valve
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. The temperature and pressure-relief valve
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): All hot-water heating systems use a temperature and pressure-relief valve to release expanding water and steam before dangerous pressure causes an explosion (p. 13).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why should a pottery studio always be cleaned with wet sponges and mops rather than dry sweeping or blowing away dried clay scraps?
quiz_item.question: Why should a pottery studio always be cleaned with wet sponges and mops rather than dry sweeping or blowing away dried clay scraps?
options: A. Dry sweeping launches fine crystalline silica dust into the air, which can cause permanent lung damage (silicosis) when inhaled over time.
B. Broom bristles scratch the glaze off bisque-fired pottery sitting on drying shelves.
C. Dry clay dust reacts with room humidity to make the potter's wheel motor overheat.
D. Wet mopping is the only way to dissolve lead oxide out of raw earthenware clay bodies.
choices: A. Dry sweeping launches fine crystalline silica dust into the air, which can cause permanent lung damage (silicosis) when inhaled over time.
B. Broom bristles scratch the glaze off bisque-fired pottery sitting on drying shelves.
C. Dry clay dust reacts with room humidity to make the potter's wheel motor overheat.
D. Wet mopping is the only way to dissolve lead oxide out of raw earthenware clay bodies.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Dry sweeping launches fine crystalline silica dust into the air, which can cause permanent lung damage (silicosis) when inhaled over time.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Clay and glaze powders contain fine silica particles that stay suspended in the air when dry-swept; wiping surfaces and mopping floors with water traps dust safely.

pamphlet_excerpts: Ancient Czech Ceramic Artifacts: Archaeologists in the Czech Republic have uncovered human made ceramics that they believe date to at least 24,000 (p. 13).
Prehistoric Clay Figure Composition: These artifacts are in the form of slabs, balls, and animal- and human-shaped figures, and are made of animal fat, bone, bone ash, and a clay like (p. 13).
Unfired Sun Dried Vessels: The earliest clay vessels were sun-dried, not fired (p. 13).
Dry Grain Storage Limits: They probably were used to store only grain and other dry foods, because filling them with water would have caused the clay to absorb the liquid (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Compare Sun Dried and Fired Clay: The earliest clay vessels were sun-dried, not fired (p. 13).
Step 2 - Understand Unfired Water Absorption: They probably were used to store only grain and other dry foods, because filling them with water would have caused the clay to absorb the liquid (p. 13).
Step 3 - Fire Clay for Permanent Strength: Not long after these first crude Neolithic means clay vessels were made, people learned how to use fire to make "new stone" them stronger, harder (p. 13).
Step 4 - Apply Surface Texturing and Glazes: This pottery is called Jomon, which means "cord markings," because much of it was decorated with cord patterns (p. 13).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why should a pottery studio always be cleaned with wet sponges and mops rather than dry sweeping or blowing away dried clay scraps?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why should a pottery studio always be cleaned with wet sponges and mops rather than dry sweeping or blowing away dried clay scraps?
options: A. Dry sweeping launches fine crystalline silica dust into the air, which can cause permanent lung damage (silicosis) when inhaled over time.
B. Broom bristles scratch the glaze off bisque-fired pottery sitting on drying shelves.
C. Dry clay dust reacts with room humidity to make the potter's wheel motor overheat.
D. Wet mopping is the only way to dissolve lead oxide out of raw earthenware clay bodies.
choices: A. Dry sweeping launches fine crystalline silica dust into the air, which can cause permanent lung damage (silicosis) when inhaled over time.
B. Broom bristles scratch the glaze off bisque-fired pottery sitting on drying shelves.
C. Dry clay dust reacts with room humidity to make the potter's wheel motor overheat.
D. Wet mopping is the only way to dissolve lead oxide out of raw earthenware clay bodies.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Dry sweeping launches fine crystalline silica dust into the air, which can cause permanent lung damage (silicosis) when inhaled over time.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Clay and glaze powders contain fine silica particles that stay suspended in the air when dry-swept; wiping surfaces and mopping floors with water traps dust safely.

C. Stoneware melts at room temperature when mixed with water

choices: A. Stoneware never requires kiln firing to become waterproof
B. Stoneware is more plastic than porcelain and holds its shape better during forming
C. Stoneware melts at room temperature when mixed with water
D. Stoneware contains no silica or alumina minerals
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Stoneware is more plastic than porcelain and holds its shape better during forming
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Stoneware has greater plasticity than porcelain, making it much easier to manipulate without slumping when throwing on the wheel or hand-building (p. 32).

C. The importation of Roman terra-cotta amphorae from Italy

choices: A. The invention of the electric silicon-carbide kiln in Tokyo
B. The discovery of porcelain clays in Arita by Korean craftsmen

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. The discovery of porcelain clays in Arita by Korean craftsmen
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Imariware dates from around 1616, when Korean craftsmen discovered suitable porcelain clays in Arita, Japan (p. 20).

B. Hidden underneath an inverted stoneware bowl on the bottom shelf
C. Clearly visible through the peephole against a plain, solid background

choices: A. Pressed tightly against the inside of the peephole plug

C. Clearly visible through the peephole against a plain, solid background

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why were the earliest prehistoric sun-dried clay vessels used only to store grain and other dry foods?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why were the earliest prehistoric sun-dried clay vessels used only to store grain and other dry foods?
options: A. Unfired sun-dried clay absorbs water and softens if filled with liquid
B. Prehistoric glazes reacted explosively with fresh drinking water
C. Ancient potters only knew how to throw flat plates on electric wheels
D. Sun-dried clay vessels were too heavy to lift when filled with water
choices: A. Unfired sun-dried clay absorbs water and softens if filled with liquid
B. Prehistoric glazes reacted explosively with fresh drinking water
C. Ancient potters only knew how to throw flat plates on electric wheels
D. Sun-dried clay vessels were too heavy to lift when filled with water
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Unfired sun-dried clay absorbs water and softens if filled with liquid
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Because sun-dried vessels were not fired in a kiln, filling them with water would cause the raw clay to absorb the liquid and break down (p. 13).

B. Refining crude oil into flexible polyethylene plumbing pipes
C. Spinning organic cotton fibers for summer camp uniforms
D. Brewing synthetic rubber adhesives for woodworking clamps
choices: A. Packaging uranium oxide fuel in ceramic rods for nuclear power plants
B. Refining crude oil into flexible polyethylene plumbing pipes
C. Spinning organic cotton fibers for summer camp uniforms
D. Brewing synthetic rubber adhesives for woodworking clamps
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Packaging uranium oxide fuel in ceramic rods for nuclear power plants
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Beyond craft pottery, the industrial ceramics sector produces silica abrasives, specialized glass, and ceramic rods used to package uranium oxide fuel in nuclear power plants (p. 89).

B. It evaporates completely unless salt is thrown into the firebox
C. It produces greens in an oxidation firing and brilliant red in a reduction firing
D. It melts at room temperature when the kiln dampers are opened wide
choices: A. It turns bright yellow in both electric and wood kilns
B. It evaporates completely unless salt is thrown into the firebox

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. It produces greens in an oxidation firing and brilliant red in a reduction firing
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Copper oxide reacts to the kiln atmosphere by producing green colors in an oxygen-rich oxidation firing and a brilliant red in a reduction firing (p. 25).

pamphlet_excerpts: Unexpected Programming Injuries: You might not think that writing programs could cause injuries (p. 88).
Athletic Prevention Techniques: But in fact, injuries from programming have much in common with sports injuries and can be prevented using some of the same techniques that athletes use (p. 88).
Repetitive Stress Injuries: The main programming-related injuries are repetitive stress injuries, or RSIs (p. 88).
Joint and Tendon Stress: Just as in athletic activities, an RSI occurs when stress is placed on a joint, pulling on the tendons and muscles around the joint (p. 88).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Repetitive Stress: The main programming-related injuries are repetitive stress injuries, or RSIs (p. 88).
Step 2 - Protect Joints and Tendons: Just as in athletic activities, an RSI occurs when stress is placed on a joint, pulling on the tendons and muscles around the joint (p. 88).
Step 3 - Allow Tissue Recovery Time: When the stress happens repeatedly, the body does not have time to recover and becomes irritated (p. 88).
Step 4 - Monitor Swelling and Irritation: The body reacts to the irritation by increasing the amount of fluid in that area to reduce the stress placed on the tendon or muscle (p. 88).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While writing code for several hours and incorporating third-party libraries into your project, how should you protect both your physical health and software intellectual property?
quiz_item.question: While writing code for several hours and incorporating third-party libraries into your project, how should you protect both your physical health and software intellectual property?
options: A. Work in a dark room without breaks to maintain focus, and remove copyright headers from open-source files so your repository looks uniform.
B. Hold your wrists bent upward against the desk edge, and copy proprietary source code from commercial apps as long as your program is free.
C. Sit with the monitor 6 inches from your eyes, and assume any code posted on a public forum is in the public domain.
D. Maintain neutral wrist and back posture, follow the 20-20-20 rule to prevent eye strain, and respect software licenses by keeping required open-source attributions.
choices: A. Work in a dark room without breaks to maintain focus, and remove copyright headers from open-source files so your repository looks uniform.
B. Hold your wrists bent upward against the desk edge, and copy proprietary source code from commercial apps as long as your program is free.
C. Sit with the monitor 6 inches from your eyes, and assume any code posted on a public forum is in the public domain.
D. Maintain neutral wrist and back posture, follow the 20-20-20 rule to prevent eye strain, and respect software licenses by keeping required open-source attributions.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Maintain neutral wrist and back posture, follow the 20-20-20 rule to prevent eye strain, and respect software licenses by keeping required open-source attributions.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Safe programming combines ergonomic posture and regular 20-20-20 visual breaks with ethical adherence to open-source and commercial software licensing rules.

Mid-Century Language Pioneers: By the 1950s and 1960s, many new languages were being introduced, including BASIC, Fortran, and LISP (p. 18).
Moving Beyond Machine Assembly: These languages took programming beyond binary and assembly to allow portability of languages beyond just the processor hardware of the time (p. 18).
Cross-Platform Program Portability: That is, programs written in these languages could runon two or more kinds of processors or with two or more kinds of operating systems (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Trace Early Assembly Roots: These languages took programming beyond binary and assembly to allow portability of languages beyond just the processor hardware of the time (p. 18).
Step 2 - Compare Cross-Platform Portability: That is, programs written in these languages could runon two or more kinds of processors or with two or more kinds of operating systems (p. 18).
Step 3 - Examine Computer Science Concepts: Many languages, such as Pascal, we recreated to capture new concepts of computer science (p. 18).
Step 4 - Match Languages to Industries: Others, such as Fortran and COBOL, were developed to meet specific needs of science or business (p. 18).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What major advantage did 1950s and 1960s languages like BASIC, Fortran, and LISP introduce over earlier binary and assembly coding?
quiz_item.question: What major advantage did 1950s and 1960s languages like BASIC, Fortran, and LISP introduce over earlier binary and assembly coding?
options: A. They eliminated the need for a central processing unit inside the computer.
B. They allowed programs to be portable across multiple types of processors and operating systems.
C. They restricted software so it could only run on one custom-built mainframe processor.
D. They replaced all mathematical operations with spoken voice commands.
choices: A. They eliminated the need for a central processing unit inside the computer.
B. They allowed programs to be portable across multiple types of processors and operating systems.
C. They restricted software so it could only run on one custom-built mainframe processor.
D. They replaced all mathematical operations with spoken voice commands.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. They allowed programs to be portable across multiple types of processors and operating systems.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): High-level languages took programming beyond hardware-specific binary and assembly, enabling programs to run on two or more processor types or operating systems (p. 18).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While writing code for several hours and incorporating third-party libraries into your project, how should you protect both your physical health and software intellectual property?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While writing code for several hours and incorporating third-party libraries into your project, how should you protect both your physical health and software intellectual property?
options: A. Work in a dark room without breaks to maintain focus, and remove copyright headers from open-source files so your repository looks uniform.
B. Hold your wrists bent upward against the desk edge, and copy proprietary source code from commercial apps as long as your program is free.
C. Sit with the monitor 6 inches from your eyes, and assume any code posted on a public forum is in the public domain.
D. Maintain neutral wrist and back posture, follow the 20-20-20 rule to prevent eye strain, and respect software licenses by keeping required open-source attributions.
choices: A. Work in a dark room without breaks to maintain focus, and remove copyright headers from open-source files so your repository looks uniform.
B. Hold your wrists bent upward against the desk edge, and copy proprietary source code from commercial apps as long as your program is free.
C. Sit with the monitor 6 inches from your eyes, and assume any code posted on a public forum is in the public domain.
D. Maintain neutral wrist and back posture, follow the 20-20-20 rule to prevent eye strain, and respect software licenses by keeping required open-source attributions.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Maintain neutral wrist and back posture, follow the 20-20-20 rule to prevent eye strain, and respect software licenses by keeping required open-source attributions.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Safe programming combines ergonomic posture and regular 20-20-20 visual breaks with ethical adherence to open-source and commercial software licensing rules.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What major advantage did 1950s and 1960s languages like BASIC, Fortran, and LISP introduce over earlier binary and assembly coding?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What major advantage did 1950s and 1960s languages like BASIC, Fortran, and LISP introduce over earlier binary and assembly coding?
options: A. They eliminated the need for a central processing unit inside the computer.
B. They allowed programs to be portable across multiple types of processors and operating systems.
C. They restricted software so it could only run on one custom-built mainframe processor.
D. They replaced all mathematical operations with spoken voice commands.
choices: A. They eliminated the need for a central processing unit inside the computer.
B. They allowed programs to be portable across multiple types of processors and operating systems.
C. They restricted software so it could only run on one custom-built mainframe processor.
D. They replaced all mathematical operations with spoken voice commands.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. They allowed programs to be portable across multiple types of processors and operating systems.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): High-level languages took programming beyond hardware-specific binary and assembly, enabling programs to run on two or more processor types or operating systems (p. 18).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does mobile application development typically differ from traditional standalone programming?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does mobile application development typically differ from traditional standalone programming?
options: A. Mobile applications must be wired directly into the battery with a soldering iron.
B. Mobile applications cannot use loops, variables, or conditional statements.
C. The mobile operating system is designed as a framework within which apps are built and run.
D. Mobile devices can only execute programs written in 1950s punch-card Fortran.
choices: A. Mobile applications must be wired directly into the battery with a soldering iron.
B. Mobile applications cannot use loops, variables, or conditional statements.
C. The mobile operating system is designed as a framework within which apps are built and run.
D. Mobile devices can only execute programs written in 1950s punch-card Fortran.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. The mobile operating system is designed as a framework within which apps are built and run.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Most mobile applications differ from traditional programming because the mobile operating system is designed as a framework that manages app lifecycle and device features (p. 35).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why does the Programming merit badge pamphlet compare software licensing to renting a bicycle rather than buying one?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why does the Programming merit badge pamphlet compare software licensing to renting a bicycle rather than buying one?
options: A. Because all computer programs automatically delete themselves after twenty-four hours.
B. Because software companies require users to mail back their computer hard drives every month.
C. Because open-source software is illegal to install on a personal home computer.
D. Because the user receives permission to use the software under set restrictions rather than owning the program outright.
choices: A. Because all computer programs automatically delete themselves after twenty-four hours.
B. Because software companies require users to mail back their computer hard drives every month.
C. Because open-source software is illegal to install on a personal home computer.
D. Because the user receives permission to use the software under set restrictions rather than owning the program outright.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Because the user receives permission to use the software under set restrictions rather than owning the program outright.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): When you license software, you purchase permission to use the program subject to restrictions, just like renting a bike gives you riding rights without outright ownership (p. 84).

intro_notes: Scouts BSA Test Lab Pilot Badge (Valid through 2026-12-31). This badge takes you on an exciting journey to understand how psychology impacts everyday life and leadership. You’ll learn about famous psychologists and their contributions, create and perform a skit showing psychology in action, explore mental health and resilience, and track your own activities and emotions to see how they shape your well-being. Along the way, you’ll practice empathy, reflect on the Scout Oath and Law, and even design your own pledge to inspire hope and support in your community. Finally, dive into career paths in psychology and discover what it takes to succeed in this fascinating field. Expand your mind, build resilience, and make a difference, start your Psychology Badge adventure today!

NOTE: Any registered adult Scouting America volunteer may serve as the counselor/reviewer for a Test Lab badge. Upon completion of all requirements and the official Scouting America Test Lab survey, Scouts receive an official Certificate of Completion that converts to Merit Badge credit if the badge graduates to permanent status.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While preparing for a high-adventure trek, a patrol leader notices a Scout becoming overwhelmed when trying to memorize 15 wilderness safety rules all at once. Using cognitive psychology principles of working memory, what teaching strategy works best?
quiz_item.question: While preparing for a high-adventure trek, a patrol leader notices a Scout becoming overwhelmed when trying to memorize 15 wilderness safety rules all at once. Using cognitive psychology principles of working memory, what teaching strategy works best?
options: A. Read all 15 rules faster without pausing so they enter long-term memory immediately.
B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
C. Skip practice and rely only on passive re-reading right before the trek.
D. Test the Scout on all 15 rules simultaneously while playing loud background distractions.
choices: A. Read all 15 rules faster without pausing so they enter long-term memory immediately.
B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
C. Skip practice and rely only on passive re-reading right before the trek.
D. Test the Scout on all 15 rules simultaneously while playing loud background distractions.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Human working memory holds only a few chunks at once; grouping items into meaningful frameworks and practicing active recall builds durable neural pathways.

quiz_item.question: In youth mental health, what is the difference between a risk factor and a protective factor?
options: A. Risk factors are physical helmets, while protective factors are outdoor camping hazards.
B. Risk factors only affect adults over sixty, while protective factors only apply to toddlers.
C. Risk factors increase the likelihood of stress or struggle, while protective factors provide support, connection, and coping strength that build resilience.
D. Risk factors and protective factors mean the exact same thing in community psychology.
choices: A. Risk factors are physical helmets, while protective factors are outdoor camping hazards.
B. Risk factors only affect adults over sixty, while protective factors only apply to toddlers.
C. Risk factors increase the likelihood of stress or struggle, while protective factors provide support, connection, and coping strength that build resilience.
D. Risk factors and protective factors mean the exact same thing in community psychology.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Risk factors increase the likelihood of stress or struggle, while protective factors provide support, connection, and coping strength that build resilience.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Risk factors increase vulnerability to emotional distress, whereas protective factors like supportive peers, mentors, and healthy habits help youth build resilience (p. 16).

options: A. They guarantee that a Scout will never feel tired or frustrated again in adulthood.
B. They teach Scouts to quit an activity immediately whenever the first attempt fails.
C. They eliminate the need for empathy toward younger patrol members.
D. They give Scouts safe, supportive practice adapting to setbacks, solving problems under pressure, and persevering as a team.
choices: A. They guarantee that a Scout will never feel tired or frustrated again in adulthood.
B. They teach Scouts to quit an activity immediately whenever the first attempt fails.
C. They eliminate the need for empathy toward younger patrol members.
D. They give Scouts safe, supportive practice adapting to setbacks, solving problems under pressure, and persevering as a team.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. They give Scouts safe, supportive practice adapting to setbacks, solving problems under pressure, and persevering as a team.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Scouting challenges allow youth to face manageable obstacles with patrol support, building confidence and resilience as they adapt and recover from setbacks (p. 28).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While preparing for a high-adventure trek, a patrol leader notices a Scout becoming overwhelmed when trying to memorize 15 wilderness safety rules all at once. Using cognitive psychology principles of working memory, what teaching strategy works best?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While preparing for a high-adventure trek, a patrol leader notices a Scout becoming overwhelmed when trying to memorize 15 wilderness safety rules all at once. Using cognitive psychology principles of working memory, what teaching strategy works best?
options: A. Read all 15 rules faster without pausing so they enter long-term memory immediately.
B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
C. Skip practice and rely only on passive re-reading right before the trek.
D. Test the Scout on all 15 rules simultaneously while playing loud background distractions.
choices: A. Read all 15 rules faster without pausing so they enter long-term memory immediately.
B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
C. Skip practice and rely only on passive re-reading right before the trek.
D. Test the Scout on all 15 rules simultaneously while playing loud background distractions.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Use chunking and spaced practice: group the 15 rules into 3 meaningful categories (such as S.T.O.P. or ABCDE) and practice retrieving them across multiple hands-on scenarios.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Human working memory holds only a few chunks at once; grouping items into meaningful frameworks and practicing active recall builds durable neural pathways.
