patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the universal international distress call in Morse code, and what pattern of audible or visual signals is recognized worldwide as an emergency call for help?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the universal international distress call in Morse code, and what pattern of audible or visual signals is recognized worldwide as an emergency call for help?
options: A. Four short flashes followed by two long whistle blasts, repeated once every hour.
B. SOS in Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots), or three of any signal such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of light.
C. A single continuous horn blast lasting ten seconds or waving a green flag overhead.
D. Two short whistle blasts repeated every thirty seconds, which means all clear in wilderness navigation.
choices: A. Four short flashes followed by two long whistle blasts, repeated once every hour.
B. SOS in Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots), or three of any signal such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of light.
C. A single continuous horn blast lasting ten seconds or waving a green flag overhead.
D. Two short whistle blasts repeated every thirty seconds, which means all clear in wilderness navigation.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. SOS in Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots), or three of any signal such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of light.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Three of anything (three whistle blasts, three fires or smoke columns, three light flashes) and Morse code SOS (three dots, three dashes, three dots) are universally recognized emergency distress signals.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When constructing a large ground-to-air distress symbol in an open clearing, what does a giant letter "V" communicate to search aircraft?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When constructing a large ground-to-air distress symbol in an open clearing, what does a giant letter "V" communicate to search aircraft?
options: A. The party has found safe shelter and requires no assistance
B. The group is moving north toward the nearest paved road
C. The survivors on the ground require general search-and-rescue assistance
D. A helicopter can safely land directly on top of the marked spot
choices: A. The party has found safe shelter and requires no assistance
B. The group is moving north toward the nearest paved road
C. The survivors on the ground require general search-and-rescue assistance
D. A helicopter can safely land directly on top of the marked spot
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. The survivors on the ground require general search-and-rescue assistance
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): In international ground-to-air emergency signaling, a large V constructed on open ground means "Require assistance," while an X means "Require medical assistance" (p. 8).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How is a dash timed relative to a dot when transmitting a clear message in international Morse code?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How is a dash timed relative to a dot when transmitting a clear message in international Morse code?
options: A. Three times the duration of a single dot, with three-dot pauses between letters
B. Twice the duration of a single dot, with no pause needed between individual letters
C. Five times the duration of a single dot, sent only over electrical telegraph wires
D. Equal in length to a dot, distinguished only by using a higher audio pitch
choices: A. Three times the duration of a single dot, with three-dot pauses between letters
B. Twice the duration of a single dot, with no pause needed between individual letters
C. Five times the duration of a single dot, sent only over electrical telegraph wires
D. Equal in length to a dot, distinguished only by using a higher audio pitch
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Three times the duration of a single dot, with three-dot pauses between letters
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In international Morse code timing, a dash is three times as long as a dot, the pause between letters is three dot-lengths, and the pause between words is seven dot-lengths (p. 6).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Because semaphore uses the same arm angles for the letters A through J as it does for the digits 1 through 0, how does a sender indicate that numbers are being transmitted?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Because semaphore uses the same arm angles for the letters A through J as it does for the digits 1 through 0, how does a sender indicate that numbers are being transmitted?
options: A. Switch from red-and-yellow flags to blue-and-white flags before signaling numbers
B. Wave both flags in a continuous figure-eight above the head during each digit
C. Kneel on one knee so the receiver knows the clock positions represent digits
D. Send the dedicated "numerals" position first, then send the "letters" signal when returning to text
choices: A. Switch from red-and-yellow flags to blue-and-white flags before signaling numbers
B. Wave both flags in a continuous figure-eight above the head during each digit
C. Kneel on one knee so the receiver knows the clock positions represent digits
D. Send the dedicated "numerals" position first, then send the "letters" signal when returning to text
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Send the dedicated "numerals" position first, then send the "letters" signal when returning to text
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): In semaphore, letters and numbers share the same arm angles, so the sender must flash the "numerals" signal before sending digits and the "letters" (or "J") signal to return to text (p. 8).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does standard six-dot Braille distinguish a capital letter from a lowercase letter?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does standard six-dot Braille distinguish a capital letter from a lowercase letter?
options: A. By embossing the raised dots twice as large as standard lowercase dots
B. By placing a special capital-indicator cell (dot 6) immediately before the letter
C. By inverting the six-dot cell upside down for every uppercase character
D. By using an eight-dot cell for capitals and a four-dot cell for lowercase letters
choices: A. By embossing the raised dots twice as large as standard lowercase dots
B. By placing a special capital-indicator cell (dot 6) immediately before the letter
C. By inverting the six-dot cell upside down for every uppercase character
D. By using an eight-dot cell for capitals and a four-dot cell for lowercase letters
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. By placing a special capital-indicator cell (dot 6) immediately before the letter
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): In Braille, capital letters use the same cell patterns as lowercase letters but are preceded by a special cell with a single dot in position 6 (the capital indicator) (p. 6).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When a troop leader raises the silent Scout sign during an assembly or hike, what action should Scouts take?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When a troop leader raises the silent Scout sign during an assembly or hike, what action should Scouts take?
options: A. Form two parallel lines for an immediate equipment inspection
B. Scatter immediately to take cover from approaching severe weather
C. Come to quiet attention and listen to the leader speaking
D. Double-time jog toward the leader to form a tight semicircle
choices: A. Form two parallel lines for an immediate equipment inspection
B. Scatter immediately to take cover from approaching severe weather
C. Come to quiet attention and listen to the leader speaking
D. Double-time jog toward the leader to form a tight semicircle
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Come to quiet attention and listen to the leader speaking
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Raising the Scout sign silently alerts the troop or patrol to come to attention and stop talking, following the principle that the signal is passed along visually without shouting (p. 7).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which traditional woodcraft trail sign is used to warn following hikers of "Danger" or "Caution ahead"?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which traditional woodcraft trail sign is used to warn following hikers of "Danger" or "Caution ahead"?
options: A. Three rocks stacked vertically or three clumps of grass tied together
B. A single small pebble balanced on top of a larger base rock with a side stone on the right
C. Two twigs crossed in an X shape directly across the center of the footpath
D. A forked stick driven upright into the dirt with a longer stick resting in the fork
choices: A. Three rocks stacked vertically or three clumps of grass tied together
B. A single small pebble balanced on top of a larger base rock with a side stone on the right
C. Two twigs crossed in an X shape directly across the center of the footpath
D. A forked stick driven upright into the dirt with a longer stick resting in the fork
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Three rocks stacked vertically or three clumps of grass tied together
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In traditional woodcraft trail signs, three rocks stacked on top of one another or three tufts of grass tied together warn hikers of danger or important caution ahead (p. 7).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When directing a heavy-equipment or crane operator, what does extending both arms horizontally with palms down and moving them rapidly back and forth mean?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When directing a heavy-equipment or crane operator, what does extending both arms horizontally with palms down and moving them rapidly back and forth mean?
options: A. Raise the load slowly while swinging the boom to the operator's left
B. Lower the boom while holding the load height constant
C. Shut down the engine and secure the cab for the end of the shift
D. Execute an immediate Emergency Stop of all equipment movement
choices: A. Raise the load slowly while swinging the boom to the operator's left
B. Lower the boom while holding the load height constant
C. Shut down the engine and secure the cab for the end of the shift
D. Execute an immediate Emergency Stop of all equipment movement
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Execute an immediate Emergency Stop of all equipment movement
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): In standard heavy-equipment and crane hand signaling, extending both arms horizontally with palms down and moving them back and forth signals an immediate "Emergency Stop" (p. 9).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: On a standard topographical map, what do symbols and lines printed in brown ink represent?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: On a standard topographical map, what do symbols and lines printed in brown ink represent?
options: A. Unpaved backcountry dirt roads and seasonal four-wheel-drive tracks
B. Contour lines and relief features showing terrain elevation and shape
C. Dense woodland canopy, national forest boundaries, and scrub brush
D. Intermittent desert streams, dry washes, and seasonal marshlands
choices: A. Unpaved backcountry dirt roads and seasonal four-wheel-drive tracks
B. Contour lines and relief features showing terrain elevation and shape
C. Dense woodland canopy, national forest boundaries, and scrub brush
D. Intermittent desert streams, dry washes, and seasonal marshlands
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Contour lines and relief features showing terrain elevation and shape
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): On standard U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) topographical maps, brown is used for contour lines representing terrain elevation and relief features, while blue represents water and green represents vegetation (p. 9).

pamphlet_excerpts: Common Foot Friction Blisters: In skating, blisters are most likely to occur on the feet (p. 89).
Early Hot Spot Detection: Skaters should be attentive to any tenderness or sensitive areas ("hot spots") that indicate the start of a blister (p. 89).
Boot Lacing and Sock Adjustments: You may be able to adjust lacing or socks to avoid friction on the sensitive area (p. 89).
Recognizing Physical Fatigue Limits: Listen to your body and quit for the day (p. 89).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Adjust Laces and Socks: You may be able to adjust lacing or socks to avoid friction on the sensitive area (p. 89).
Step 2 - Stop Skating When Fatigued: Listen to your body and quit for the day (p. 89).
Step 3 - Apply Preventive Protective Tape: If you have no choice but to continue the activity, follow preventive steps such as taping and the use of commercial skin tougheners (p. 89).
Step 4 - Monitor and Treat for Shock: When a person is injured or under great stress, the circulatory system may fail to provide enough blood to all parts of the body (p. 89).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While skating on an outdoor winter pond, a skater breaks through thin ice into frigid water 30 feet from shore. How should your patrol respond safely?
quiz_item.question: While skating on an outdoor winter pond, a skater breaks through thin ice into frigid water 30 feet from shore. How should your patrol respond safely?
options: A. Skate out to the edge of the ice hole in a group to pull the skater up by both hands.

B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight, and extend a long reach/throw aid (branch, hockey stick, or rope) while coaching the skater to kick horizontally onto firm ice and roll away from the hole.
C. Instruct the skater to remove their skates and winter jacket in the water before trying to climb out.
D. Have one Scout walk upright to the rim of the broken ice hole carrying a heavy wooden bench.
choices: A. Skate out to the edge of the ice hole in a group to pull the skater up by both hands.

B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight, and extend a long reach/throw aid (branch, hockey stick, or rope) while coaching the skater to kick horizontally onto firm ice and roll away from the hole.
C. Instruct the skater to remove their skates and winter jacket in the water before trying to climb out.
D. Have one Scout walk upright to the rim of the broken ice hole carrying a heavy wooden bench.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight, and extend a long reach/throw aid (branch, hockey stick, or rope) while coaching the skater to kick horizontally onto firm ice and roll away from the hole.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Walking or skating up to an ice breakthrough hole causes the ice edge to collapse under rescuers; follow Reach-Throw protocol and keep clothing/skates on for buoyancy and traction.

requirements.lead_text: Working under the supervision of an experienced adult, do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Working under the supervision of an experienced adult, do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Ice Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety and courtesy guidelines for ice skating. (2) Discuss preparations that must be taken when skating outdoors on natural ice. Explain how to make an ice rescue. (3) Discuss the parts and functions of the different types of ice skates. (4) Describe the proper way to carry ice skates at the rink and for travel. (5) Describe how to store ice skates for long periods of time, such as seasonal storage. (6) Skate forward at least 40 feet and come to a complete stop. Use either a two-foot snowplow stop or a one-foot snowplow stop. (7) After skating forward, glide forward on two feet, then on one foot, first right and then left. (8) Starting from a T position, stroke forward around the test area, avoiding the use of toe picks if wearing figure skates. (9) Glide backward on two feet for at least two times the skater's height. (10) Skate backward for at least 20 feet on two skates. (11) After gaining forward speed, glide forward on two feet, making a turn of 180 degrees around a cone, first to the right and then to the left. (12) Perform forward crossovers in a figure-eight pattern. (13) Explain to your counselor the safety considerations for participating in an ice-skating race. (14) Perform a hockey stop. (b) Option B, Roller Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and etiquette guidelines for roller skating. (2) Discuss the parts of a roller skate and their functions. (3) Describe five essential steps to good roller skate care. (4) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet in both directions around the rink and demonstrate proper techniques for stopping. (5) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (6) Perform a forward crossover. (7) Skate backward for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 15 feet on one skate. (8) Skate forward in a slalom pattern for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 20 feet on one skate. (9) Skate backward in a slalom pattern for at least 15 feet on two skates. (10) Shuttle skate once around the rink, bending twice along the way, without stopping. (11) Perform a series of two consecutive spins on skates, OR hop, skip, and jump on skates for at least 10 feet. (12) Perform a stepover. (13) While skating, dribble a basketball at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position, OR push a hockey ball with a stick at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position. (c) Option C, In-Line Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and courtesy guidelines for in-line skating. (2) Describe the parts of an in-line skate and their functions. (3) Describe the required and recommended safety equipment for in-line skating. (4) Explain four essential steps to good in-line skate care. (5) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet. (6) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (7) Stop on command on flat pavement using the heel brake. (8) Perform a forward crossover. (9) Perform a series of forward, linked swizzles for at least 40 feet. (10) Skate backward for at least 40 feet in a series of linked, backward swizzles. (11) From a strong pace, perform a lunge turn around an object predetermined by your counselor. (12) Perform a mohawk. (13) Perform a series of at least four one-footed downhill slaloms on pavement with a gentle slope. (14) Describe how to pass a pedestrian or another skater from behind. (15) Describe at least three ways to avoid an unforeseen obstacle while skating. (16) Describe two ways to get on and off a curb, and demonstrate at least one of these methods. (d) Option D, Skateboarding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the history and evolution of skateboarding. (2) Describe the benefits of skateboarding (physical fitness, balance, coordination, perseverance, and creativity). (3) Explain the safety rules and courtesy guidelines for skateboarding, including right-of-way and communication signals and warnings. (4) Explain the protective gear needed to skate safely, including helmet, knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards, and show how to wear them correctly. (5) Describe the two main styles of skateboarding (street and vert), and describe common skatepark features (ramps, manual pad, rails, spine, etc.). (6) Explain skateboard anatomy (deck, trucks, wheels, hardware, etc.). (7) Build a board by assembling all pieces (deck, wheels, trucks, hardware, and grip tape) in the proper order. (8) Explain skateboard maintenance (cleaning, adjusting bolts, and replacing parts). (9) Explain the difference between regular and goofy stance, and demonstrate your preferred stance. (10) Demonstrate how to push, cruise, and carve on flat ground. (11) Show at least two braking and stopping techniques. (12) Do a basic ollie and at least one variation. (13) Show how to drop-in from coping. (14) Demonstrate THREE skateboarding tricks from the following types: (a) Flat ground tricks (b) Flip and shove-it tricks (c) Grind and slide tricks (d) Air and grab tricks (e) Footplant tricks

sub_requirements.label: (a)
sub_requirements.text: Option A, Ice Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety and courtesy guidelines for ice skating. (2) Discuss preparations that must be taken when skating outdoors on natural ice. Explain how to make an ice rescue. (3) Discuss the parts and functions of the different types of ice skates. (4) Describe the proper way to carry ice skates at the rink and for travel. (5) Describe how to store ice skates for long periods of time, such as seasonal storage. (6) Skate forward at least 40 feet and come to a complete stop. Use either a two-foot snowplow stop or a one-foot snowplow stop. (7) After skating forward, glide forward on two feet, then on one foot, first right and then left. (8) Starting from a T position, stroke forward around the test area, avoiding the use of toe picks if wearing figure skates. (9) Glide backward on two feet for at least two times the skater's height. (10) Skate backward for at least 20 feet on two skates. (11) After gaining forward speed, glide forward on two feet, making a turn of 180 degrees around a cone, first to the right and then to the left. (12) Perform forward crossovers in a figure-eight pattern. (13) Explain to your counselor the safety considerations for participating in an ice-skating race. (14) Perform a hockey stop.

(2) Discuss preparations that must be taken when skating outdoors on natural ice. Explain how to make an ice rescue. (3) Discuss the parts and functions of the different types of ice skates. (4) Describe the proper way to carry ice skates at the rink and for travel. (5) Describe how to store ice skates for long periods of time, such as seasonal storage. (6) Skate forward at least 40 feet and come to a complete stop. Use either a two-foot snowplow stop or a one-foot snowplow stop. (7) After skating forward, glide forward on two feet, then on one foot, first right and then left. (8) Starting from a T position, stroke forward around the test area, avoiding the use of toe picks if wearing figure skates. (9) Glide backward on two feet for at least two times the skater's height. (10) Skate backward for at least 20 feet on two skates. (11) After gaining forward speed, glide forward on two feet, making a turn of 180 degrees around a cone, first to the right and then to the left. (12) Perform forward crossovers in a figure-eight pattern. (13) Explain to your counselor the safety considerations for participating in an ice-skating race. (14) Perform a hockey stop.

sub_requirements.text: Option B, Roller Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and etiquette guidelines for roller skating. (2) Discuss the parts of a roller skate and their functions. (3) Describe five essential steps to good roller skate care. (4) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet in both directions around the rink and demonstrate proper techniques for stopping. (5) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (6) Perform a forward crossover. (7) Skate backward for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 15 feet on one skate. (8) Skate forward in a slalom pattern for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 20 feet on one skate. (9) Skate backward in a slalom pattern for at least 15 feet on two skates. (10) Shuttle skate once around the rink, bending twice along the way, without stopping. (11) Perform a series of two consecutive spins on skates, OR hop, skip, and jump on skates for at least 10 feet. (12) Perform a stepover. (13) While skating, dribble a basketball at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position, OR push a hockey ball with a stick at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position.

sub_requirements.text: Option C, In-Line Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and courtesy guidelines for in-line skating. (2) Describe the parts of an in-line skate and their functions. (3) Describe the required and recommended safety equipment for in-line skating. (4) Explain four essential steps to good in-line skate care. (5) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet. (6) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (7) Stop on command on flat pavement using the heel brake. (8) Perform a forward crossover. (9) Perform a series of forward, linked swizzles for at least 40 feet. (10) Skate backward for at least 40 feet in a series of linked, backward swizzles. (11) From a strong pace, perform a lunge turn around an object predetermined by your counselor. (12) Perform a mohawk. (13) Perform a series of at least four one-footed downhill slaloms on pavement with a gentle slope. (14) Describe how to pass a pedestrian or another skater from behind. (15) Describe at least three ways to avoid an unforeseen obstacle while skating. (16) Describe two ways to get on and off a curb, and demonstrate at least one of these methods.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, In-Line Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and courtesy guidelines for in-line skating. (2) Describe the parts of an in-line skate and their functions. (3) Describe the required and recommended safety equipment for in-line skating. (4) Explain four essential steps to good in-line skate care. (5) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet. (6) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (7) Stop on command on flat pavement using the heel brake. (8) Perform a forward crossover. (9) Perform a series of forward, linked swizzles for at least 40 feet. (10) Skate backward for at least 40 feet in a series of linked, backward swizzles. (11) From a strong pace, perform a lunge turn around an object predetermined by your counselor. (12) Perform a mohawk. (13) Perform a series of at least four one-footed downhill slaloms on pavement with a gentle slope. (14) Describe how to pass a pedestrian or another skater from behind. (15) Describe at least three ways to avoid an unforeseen obstacle while skating. (16) Describe two ways to get on and off a curb, and demonstrate at least one of these methods.

sub_requirements.label: (d)
sub_requirements.text: Option D, Skateboarding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the history and evolution of skateboarding. (2) Describe the benefits of skateboarding (physical fitness, balance, coordination, perseverance, and creativity). (3) Explain the safety rules and courtesy guidelines for skateboarding, including right-of-way and communication signals and warnings. (4) Explain the protective gear needed to skate safely, including helmet, knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards, and show how to wear them correctly. (5) Describe the two main styles of skateboarding (street and vert), and describe common skatepark features (ramps, manual pad, rails, spine, etc.). (6) Explain skateboard anatomy (deck, trucks, wheels, hardware, etc.). (7) Build a board by assembling all pieces (deck, wheels, trucks, hardware, and grip tape) in the proper order. (8) Explain skateboard maintenance (cleaning, adjusting bolts, and replacing parts). (9) Explain the difference between regular and goofy stance, and demonstrate your preferred stance. (10) Demonstrate how to push, cruise, and carve on flat ground. (11) Show at least two braking and stopping techniques. (12) Do a basic ollie and at least one variation. (13) Show how to drop-in from coping. (14) Demonstrate THREE skateboarding tricks from the following types: (a) Flat ground tricks (b) Flip and shove-it tricks (c) Grind and slide tricks (d) Air and grab tricks (e) Footplant tricks.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option D, Skateboarding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the history and evolution of skateboarding. (2) Describe the benefits of skateboarding (physical fitness, balance, coordination, perseverance, and creativity). (3) Explain the safety rules and courtesy guidelines for skateboarding, including right-of-way and communication signals and warnings. (4) Explain the protective gear needed to skate safely, including helmet, knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards, and show how to wear them correctly. (5) Describe the two main styles of skateboarding (street and vert), and describe common skatepark features (ramps, manual pad, rails, spine, etc.). (6) Explain skateboard anatomy (deck, trucks, wheels, hardware, etc.). (7) Build a board by assembling all pieces (deck, wheels, trucks, hardware, and grip tape) in the proper order. (8) Explain skateboard maintenance (cleaning, adjusting bolts, and replacing parts). (9) Explain the difference between regular and goofy stance, and demonstrate your preferred stance. (10) Demonstrate how to push, cruise, and carve on flat ground. (11) Show at least two braking and stopping techniques. (12) Do a basic ollie and at least one variation. (13) Show how to drop-in from coping. (14) Demonstrate THREE skateboarding tricks from the following types: (a) Flat ground tricks (b) Flip and shove-it tricks (c) Grind and slide tricks (d) Air and grab tricks (e) Footplant tricks.

pamphlet_excerpts: Parallel Skate Alignment Posture: Roller Skating. keeping the skates pressed together (p. 49).
Gradual Weight Transfer Control: Slowly transfer your body weight to the right skate (p. 49).
Wheel Angle Braking Friction: The friction of the right skate on the skating surface is the braking factor, since the wheels are notin a position to roll (p. 49).
Slide Friction Stopping Variations: There are several variations on this stopping method, all of them using slide friction (p. 49).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Angle Trailing Skate to Brake: The friction of the right skate on the skating surface is the braking factor, since the wheels are notin a position to roll (p. 49).
Step 2 - Apply Controlled Slide Friction: There are several variations on this stopping method, all of them using slide friction (p. 49).
Step 3 - Anticipate Forward Stopping Momentum: You will notice a tendency to lunge forward while stopping (p. 49).
Step 4 - Brace Back and Lean Away: Try to resist by supporting your body with a firm back and leaning slightly away from your direction of travel until your skates come (p. 49).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Which safety rule applies specifically to preparing for outdoor ice skating on a frozen pond, lake, or river?
quiz_item.question: Which safety rule applies specifically to preparing for outdoor ice skating on a frozen pond, lake, or river?
options: A. A thin layer of overnight frost on a pond guarantees safe skating across the entire surface
B. Ice is always thickest directly underneath low bridges and where streams flow into a lake
C. Natural ice must be verified for safe thickness, and skaters should never skate alone on frozen water bodies
D. Driving a heavy vehicle onto the pond is the safest way for Scouts to test unknown ice thickness
choices: A. A thin layer of overnight frost on a pond guarantees safe skating across the entire surface
B. Ice is always thickest directly underneath low bridges and where streams flow into a lake
C. Natural ice must be verified for safe thickness, and skaters should never skate alone on frozen water bodies
D. Driving a heavy vehicle onto the pond is the safest way for Scouts to test unknown ice thickness
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Natural ice must be verified for safe thickness, and skaters should never skate alone on frozen water bodies
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Before skating on natural outdoor ice, you must verify that the ice thickness is checked and approved by local authorities, never skate alone, and stay clear of thin ice near inflows, bridges, or dark snow-covered patches (p. 49).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While skating on an outdoor winter pond, a skater breaks through thin ice into frigid water 30 feet from shore. How should your patrol respond safely?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While skating on an outdoor winter pond, a skater breaks through thin ice into frigid water 30 feet from shore. How should your patrol respond safely?
options: A. Skate out to the edge of the ice hole in a group to pull the skater up by both hands.

B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight, and extend a long reach/throw aid (branch, hockey stick, or rope) while coaching the skater to kick horizontally onto firm ice and roll away from the hole.
C. Instruct the skater to remove their skates and winter jacket in the water before trying to climb out.
D. Have one Scout walk upright to the rim of the broken ice hole carrying a heavy wooden bench.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While sailing a centerboard dinghy under BSA Safety Afloat rules, what are the three most important safety actions regarding lifejackets, the boom, and a capsize?
quiz_item.question: While sailing a centerboard dinghy under BSA Safety Afloat rules, what are the three most important safety actions regarding lifejackets, the boom, and a capsize?
options: A. Store your PFD under the foredeck, stand on the gunwale during a jibe, and swim away from the hull if the boat capsizes.
B. Tie the mainsheet in a hard knot to the cleat so your hands are free, and dive under the sail if the boat turtles.
C. Always wear a properly fitted USCG-approved PFD, watch for the boom swinging across the cockpit during tacks and especially jibes, and stay with the floating sailboat if it capsizes.
D. Remove the centerboard when sailing upwind in strong gusts so the boat cannot heel over.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Which part of a small sailboat provides lateral resistance in the water to keep the boat from sliding sideways when sailing across or into the wind?
quiz_item.question: Which part of a small sailboat provides lateral resistance in the water to keep the boat from sliding sideways when sailing across or into the wind?
options: A. The centerboard or daggerboard lowered through the trunk into the water
B. The forestay wire attached from the bow to the front of the mast
C. The outhaul line used to pull the clew of the mainsail toward the end of the boom
D. The transom board located across the stern of the hull
choices: A. The centerboard or daggerboard lowered through the trunk into the water
B. The forestay wire attached from the bow to the front of the mast
C. The outhaul line used to pull the clew of the mainsail toward the end of the boom
D. The transom board located across the stern of the hull
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. The centerboard or daggerboard lowered through the trunk into the water
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The centerboard or daggerboard extends below the hull to provide lateral resistance that counteracts the sideways push of the wind, preventing leeway when sailing upwind (p. 18).

Explain how choosing the proper clothing, footwear, and personal gear will help keep you comfortable and safe while sailing.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: According to the navigation rules of the road, what happens when two sailboats approach each other on opposite tacks?
quiz_item.question: According to the navigation rules of the road, what happens when two sailboats approach each other on opposite tacks?
options: A. Both boats must immediately drop their sails and wait for the other to pass
B. The boat on the starboard tack must give way and steer behind the port-tack boat
C. Whichever boat has the larger mainsail automatically holds the right-of-way
D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
choices: A. Both boats must immediately drop their sails and wait for the other to pass
B. The boat on the starboard tack must give way and steer behind the port-tack boat
C. Whichever boat has the larger mainsail automatically holds the right-of-way
D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): When two sailboats approach on opposite tacks, the vessel on the port tack (wind coming over the port side) is the give-way vessel and must steer clear of the vessel on the starboard tack (p. 22).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How can a sailor accurately identify the wind direction before leaving the dock or beach?
quiz_item.question: How can a sailor accurately identify the wind direction before leaving the dock or beach?
options: A. Looking only at the direction the underwater weeds are leaning near the dock pilings
B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
C. Checking which way the rudder blade floats when the boat is tied tightly to a slip
D. Waiting until the sails are fully sheeted in at the dock to see which way the boat capsizes
choices: A. Looking only at the direction the underwater weeds are leaning near the dock pilings
B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
C. Checking which way the rudder blade floats when the boat is tied tightly to a slip
D. Waiting until the sails are fully sheeted in at the dock to see which way the boat capsizes
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Ripples and darker patches of water (cat's-paws), onshore flags, mooring boats pointing into the breeze, and masthead wind indicators all reveal wind direction before you launch (p. 26).

requirements.lead_text: Following the Scouting America Safety Afloat plan, show that you and a buddy can sail a boat properly. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Following the Scouting America Safety Afloat plan, show that you and a buddy can sail a boat properly. Do the following: (a) Prepare a boat for sailing, including a safety inspection. (b) Get underway from a dock, mooring, or beach. (c) Properly set sails for a round-trip course approved by your counselor that will include running, beating, and reaching, the basic points of sail. While sailing, demonstrate good helmsmanship skills. (d) Change direction by tacking; change direction by jibing. (e) Demonstrate getting out of irons. (f) Demonstrate the safety position. (g) Demonstrate capsize procedures and the rescue of a person overboard. Note: Capsize procedures should be conducted under the close supervision of the counselor. A rescue boat should be standing by to assist, if necessary, and to tow the capsized craft to shore. Self-bailing boats are acceptable for this requirement. Extreme care should be taken to avoid personal injury and damage to the boat or equipment. (h) Demonstrate the procedure to take after running aground. (i) Accept a single line or side tow and maneuver the craft being towed safely for 20 boat lengths. (j) Upon returning to the dock, mooring, or beach, properly secure all equipment, furl or stow sails, and prepare the craft for unattended docking or beaching overnight or longer.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do you recover a small sailboat that has stalled head-to-wind in irons?
quiz_item.question: How do you recover a small sailboat that has stalled head-to-wind in irons?
options: A. Pulling the mainsheet and jib sheet as tight as possible while keeping the rudder centered
B. Dropping the anchor immediately and waiting for the wind direction to shift 90 degrees
C. Backing the jib or mainsail to one side and steering the rudder so the bow swings clear of the no-sail zone
D. Raising the centerboard completely out of the trunk and paddling backward toward the dock
choices: A. Pulling the mainsheet and jib sheet as tight as possible while keeping the rudder centered
B. Dropping the anchor immediately and waiting for the wind direction to shift 90 degrees
C. Backing the jib or mainsail to one side and steering the rudder so the bow swings clear of the no-sail zone
D. Raising the centerboard completely out of the trunk and paddling backward toward the dock
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Backing the jib or mainsail to one side and steering the rudder so the bow swings clear of the no-sail zone
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): When a boat is stuck in irons (pointed directly into the no-sail zone with zero headway), backing the jib or boom to one side while positioning the tiller lets the wind push the bow off the wind onto a tack (p. 31).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What routine maintenance step should be performed after taking a small sailboat out of the water, especially after sailing in salt or brackish water?
quiz_item.question: What routine maintenance step should be performed after taking a small sailboat out of the water, especially after sailing in salt or brackish water?
options: A. Scrubbing the sails with harsh chlorine bleach and steel wool after every outing
B. Leaving the drain plug tightly sealed all winter so snowmelt fills the cockpit for weight
C. Painting over stainless steel rigging wires and turnbuckles to seal in moisture
D. Rinsing the hull, sails, and hardware with fresh water and removing the drain plug so the hull drains completely
choices: A. Scrubbing the sails with harsh chlorine bleach and steel wool after every outing
B. Leaving the drain plug tightly sealed all winter so snowmelt fills the cockpit for weight
C. Painting over stainless steel rigging wires and turnbuckles to seal in moisture
D. Rinsing the hull, sails, and hardware with fresh water and removing the drain plug so the hull drains completely
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Rinsing the hull, sails, and hardware with fresh water and removing the drain plug so the hull drains completely
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Salt crystals, grit, and dirt corrode metal fittings, stiffen lines, and abrade gelcoat, while removing the drain plug lets trapped bilge or rainwater drain out during storage (p. 38).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: On which point of sail does the wind blow at a right angle (90 degrees) to the side of the boat, often providing the fastest and easiest sailing angle for most small boats?
quiz_item.question: On which point of sail does the wind blow at a right angle (90 degrees) to the side of the boat, often providing the fastest and easiest sailing angle for most small boats?
options: A. Head-to-wind inside the no-sail zone
B. Beam reach with the wind blowing perpendicular to the hull's side
C. Dead run with the wind blowing directly over the stern
D. In irons with both sails luffing completely
choices: A. Head-to-wind inside the no-sail zone
B. Beam reach with the wind blowing perpendicular to the hull's side
C. Dead run with the wind blowing directly over the stern
D. In irons with both sails luffing completely
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Beam reach with the wind blowing perpendicular to the hull's side
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): On a beam reach, the wind blows at roughly a 90-degree angle across the side (beam) of the hull, generating optimal aerodynamic lift across the sails with minimal leeway (p. 40).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While sailing a centerboard dinghy under BSA Safety Afloat rules, what are the three most important safety actions regarding lifejackets, the boom, and a capsize?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While sailing a centerboard dinghy under BSA Safety Afloat rules, what are the three most important safety actions regarding lifejackets, the boom, and a capsize?
options: A. Store your PFD under the foredeck, stand on the gunwale during a jibe, and swim away from the hull if the boat capsizes.
B. Tie the mainsheet in a hard knot to the cleat so your hands are free, and dive under the sail if the boat turtles.
C. Always wear a properly fitted USCG-approved PFD, watch for the boom swinging across the cockpit during tacks and especially jibes, and stay with the floating sailboat if it capsizes.
D. Remove the centerboard when sailing upwind in strong gusts so the boat cannot heel over.
choices: A. Store your PFD under the foredeck, stand on the gunwale during a jibe, and swim away from the hull if the boat capsizes.
B. Tie the mainsheet in a hard knot to the cleat so your hands are free, and dive under the sail if the boat turtles.
C. Always wear a properly fitted USCG-approved PFD, watch for the boom swinging across the cockpit during tacks and especially jibes, and stay with the floating sailboat if it capsizes.
D. Remove the centerboard when sailing upwind in strong gusts so the boat cannot heel over.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Always wear a properly fitted USCG-approved PFD, watch for the boom swinging across the cockpit during tacks and especially jibes, and stay with the floating sailboat if it capsizes.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Sailing safety requires wearing a USCG-approved PFD at all times, keeping heads low and controlling the mainsheet when the boom crosses during tacks and jibes, and staying with a capsized hull.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: What must a Scout demonstrate to pass the Scouting America swimmer test before participating in small-boat sailing requirements?

B. Diving headfirst into shallow water and sprinting 25 yards to the dock
C. Jumping feetfirst into deep water, swimming 75 yards forward, 25 yards resting backstroke, and floating
D. Floating in a lifejacket for five minutes without completing any unassisted distance swim
choices: A. Swimming 50 yards using any stroke and treading water for 30 seconds
B. Diving headfirst into shallow water and sprinting 25 yards to the dock
C. Jumping feetfirst into deep water, swimming 75 yards forward, 25 yards resting backstroke, and floating

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Jumping feetfirst into deep water, swimming 75 yards forward, 25 yards resting backstroke, and floating
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The Scouting America swimmer test requires jumping feetfirst into water over the head, swimming 75 yards with a strong forward stroke, swimming 25 yards using an easy resting backstroke, and floating on the back (p. 6).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which part of a small sailboat provides lateral resistance in the water to keep the boat from sliding sideways when sailing across or into the wind?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which part of a small sailboat provides lateral resistance in the water to keep the boat from sliding sideways when sailing across or into the wind?
options: A. The centerboard or daggerboard lowered through the trunk into the water
B. The forestay wire attached from the bow to the front of the mast
C. The outhaul line used to pull the clew of the mainsail toward the end of the boom
D. The transom board located across the stern of the hull
choices: A. The centerboard or daggerboard lowered through the trunk into the water
B. The forestay wire attached from the bow to the front of the mast
C. The outhaul line used to pull the clew of the mainsail toward the end of the boom
D. The transom board located across the stern of the hull
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. The centerboard or daggerboard lowered through the trunk into the water
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The centerboard or daggerboard extends below the hull to provide lateral resistance that counteracts the sideways push of the wind, preventing leeway when sailing upwind (p. 18).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: According to the navigation rules of the road, what happens when two sailboats approach each other on opposite tacks?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the navigation rules of the road, what happens when two sailboats approach each other on opposite tacks?
options: A. Both boats must immediately drop their sails and wait for the other to pass
B. The boat on the starboard tack must give way and steer behind the port-tack boat
C. Whichever boat has the larger mainsail automatically holds the right-of-way
D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
choices: A. Both boats must immediately drop their sails and wait for the other to pass
B. The boat on the starboard tack must give way and steer behind the port-tack boat
C. Whichever boat has the larger mainsail automatically holds the right-of-way
D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. The boat on the port tack must give way and steer clear of the starboard-tack boat
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): When two sailboats approach on opposite tacks, the vessel on the port tack (wind coming over the port side) is the give-way vessel and must steer clear of the vessel on the starboard tack (p. 22).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How can a sailor accurately identify the wind direction before leaving the dock or beach?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How can a sailor accurately identify the wind direction before leaving the dock or beach?
options: A. Looking only at the direction the underwater weeds are leaning near the dock pilings
B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
C. Checking which way the rudder blade floats when the boat is tied tightly to a slip
D. Waiting until the sails are fully sheeted in at the dock to see which way the boat capsizes
choices: A. Looking only at the direction the underwater weeds are leaning near the dock pilings
B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
C. Checking which way the rudder blade floats when the boat is tied tightly to a slip
D. Waiting until the sails are fully sheeted in at the dock to see which way the boat capsizes
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Observing water ripples, flags onshore, moored boats weather-vaning, and masthead telltales
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Ripples and darker patches of water (cat's-paws), onshore flags, mooring boats pointing into the breeze, and masthead wind indicators all reveal wind direction before you launch (p. 26).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do you recover a small sailboat that has stalled head-to-wind in irons?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do you recover a small sailboat that has stalled head-to-wind in irons?
options: A. Pulling the mainsheet and jib sheet as tight as possible while keeping the rudder centered
B. Dropping the anchor immediately and waiting for the wind direction to shift 90 degrees
C. Backing the jib or mainsail to one side and steering the rudder so the bow swings clear of the no-sail zone
D. Raising the centerboard completely out of the trunk and paddling backward toward the dock
choices: A. Pulling the mainsheet and jib sheet as tight as possible while keeping the rudder centered
B. Dropping the anchor immediately and waiting for the wind direction to shift 90 degrees
C. Backing the jib or mainsail to one side and steering the rudder so the bow swings clear of the no-sail zone
D. Raising the centerboard completely out of the trunk and paddling backward toward the dock
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Backing the jib or mainsail to one side and steering the rudder so the bow swings clear of the no-sail zone
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): When a boat is stuck in irons (pointed directly into the no-sail zone with zero headway), backing the jib or boom to one side while positioning the tiller lets the wind push the bow off the wind onto a tack (p. 31).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which knot is known as the king of knots on a sailboat because it forms a fixed loop that never slips under load yet unties easily afterward?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which knot is known as the king of knots on a sailboat because it forms a fixed loop that never slips under load yet unties easily afterward?
options: A. Bowline knot
B. Square (reef) knot
C. Clove hitch
D. Figure-eight stopper knot
choices: A. Bowline knot
B. Square (reef) knot
C. Clove hitch
D. Figure-eight stopper knot
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Bowline knot
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The bowline forms a secure, fixed loop that will not slip under heavy load and remains easy to untie after bearing the strain of a jib sheet or towline (p. 36).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What routine maintenance step should be performed after taking a small sailboat out of the water, especially after sailing in salt or brackish water?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What routine maintenance step should be performed after taking a small sailboat out of the water, especially after sailing in salt or brackish water?
options: A. Scrubbing the sails with harsh chlorine bleach and steel wool after every outing
B. Leaving the drain plug tightly sealed all winter so snowmelt fills the cockpit for weight
C. Painting over stainless steel rigging wires and turnbuckles to seal in moisture
D. Rinsing the hull, sails, and hardware with fresh water and removing the drain plug so the hull drains completely
choices: A. Scrubbing the sails with harsh chlorine bleach and steel wool after every outing
B. Leaving the drain plug tightly sealed all winter so snowmelt fills the cockpit for weight
C. Painting over stainless steel rigging wires and turnbuckles to seal in moisture
D. Rinsing the hull, sails, and hardware with fresh water and removing the drain plug so the hull drains completely
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Rinsing the hull, sails, and hardware with fresh water and removing the drain plug so the hull drains completely
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Salt crystals, grit, and dirt corrode metal fittings, stiffen lines, and abrade gelcoat, while removing the drain plug lets trapped bilge or rainwater drain out during storage (p. 38).

B. Beam reach with the wind blowing perpendicular to the hull's side
C. Dead run with the wind blowing directly over the stern
D. In irons with both sails luffing completely
choices: A. Head-to-wind inside the no-sail zone

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Beam reach with the wind blowing perpendicular to the hull's side
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): On a beam reach, the wind blows at roughly a 90-degree angle across the side (beam) of the hull, generating optimal aerodynamic lift across the sails with minimal leeway (p. 40).

pamphlet_excerpts: RICE Treatment for Sprains: R = Rest I = Ice C = Compression E = Elevation Sprains and Strains Sprains are relatively common snow-sports (p. 22).
Causes of Joint Sprains: Sprains are caused by twisting, wrenching, or lifting movements that tear or stretch tissues surrounding a joint (p. 22).
Sudden Pain and Swelling: Such an injury causes sudden pain and swelling at the joint (p. 22).
Joint Tenderness and Discoloration: There may be some discoloration, and the joint will likely be tender to the touch and very painful when moved (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Sudden Joint Swelling: Such an injury causes sudden pain and swelling at the joint (p. 22).
Step 2 - Check for Joint Tenderness: There may be some discoloration, and the joint will likely be tender to the touch and very painful when moved (p. 22).
Step 3 - Elevate and Apply Cold: Elevate the injured joint, and apply cold compresses for no more than 20 minutes at a time (p. 22).
Step 4 - Distinguish Strains from Sprains: The term strain usually refers to a less severe joint or muscle injury where tissues are not torn but may have been overextended oroverstressed (p. 22).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Downhill (Alpine) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate each of the required skills. (1) Show how to wax and maintain your skis and use/maintain your release bindings. Explain the international DIN standard and what it means to skiers. (2) Explain the American Teaching System and a basic snowskiing progression. (3) Discuss the different types of Alpine skis. Demonstrate two ways to carry skis and poles safely and easily. (4) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (5) On a gentle slope, demonstrate some of the beginning maneuvers learned in skiing. Include the straight run, gliding wedge, wedge stop, sidestep, and herringbone maneuvers. (6) On slightly steeper terrain, show linked wedge turns. (7) On a moderate slope, demonstrate five to 10 christies. (8) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (9) Demonstrate the ability to ski in varied conditions, including changes in pitch and snow conditions. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (10) Name the major ski organizations in the United States and explain their functions. (b) Option B, Cross-Country (Nordic) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show your ability to select, use, and maintain equipment for cross-country skiing in safety and comfort. (2) Explain the reasons for common rules, including no walking on ski trails, one-way ski direction, no pets, and no skiing on snowmobile trails. (3) Discuss classic, skating, touring, and telemark skis. (4) Discuss the basic principles of waxing for cross-country ski touring. (5) Discuss the differences between cross-country, backcountry/ski touring, ski mountaineering, and downhill/telemark skiing. (6) List the items you would take on a one-day ski tour. (7) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass. (8) On a gentle, packed slope, show some basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the straight run, traverse, side slip, step turn, wedge stop, and wedge turn maneuvers. (9) On a cross-country trail, demonstrate effective propulsion by showing proper weight transfer from ski to ski, pole timing, rhythm, flow, and glide. (10) Demonstrate your ability, on a 4-mile tour, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive skiers may complete a 1-mile tour with prior approval from their counselor. (11) Demonstrate several methods of dealing with steep hills or difficult conditions. Include traverses and kick turns going uphill and downhill, sidesteps, and pole drag. (c) Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (11) Name the major snowboarding organizations in the United States and explain their functions. (d) Option D, Snowshoeing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name the parts of a snowshoe. (2) Explain how to choose the correct size of snowshoe. (3) Describe the different types of snowshoes and their specialized uses. Discuss factors to consider when choosing a snowshoe. (4) Explain how to properly care for and maintain snowshoes. (5) List the items you would take on a one-day snowshoe hike. (6) Describe areas that are best for snowshoeing. Discuss some advantages and dangers of backcountry snowshoeing. (7) Discuss the benefits of snowshoeing. (8) Demonstrate the most efficient ways to break trail, climb uphill, travel downhill, and traverse a slope. (9) Demonstrate your ability, on a 2-mile snowshoe hike, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive snowshoers may complete a 1-mile hike with prior approval from their counselor. (10) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass.

Include the straight run, gliding wedge, wedge stop, sidestep, and herringbone maneuvers. (6) On slightly steeper terrain, show linked wedge turns. (7) On a moderate slope, demonstrate five to 10 christies. (8) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (9) Demonstrate the ability to ski in varied conditions, including changes in pitch and snow conditions. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (10) Name the major ski organizations in the United States and explain their functions.

sub_requirements.text: Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (11) Name the major snowboarding organizations in the United States and explain their functions.

sub_requirements.text: Option D, Snowshoeing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name the parts of a snowshoe. (2) Explain how to choose the correct size of snowshoe. (3) Describe the different types of snowshoes and their specialized uses. Discuss factors to consider when choosing a snowshoe. (4) Explain how to properly care for and maintain snowshoes. (5) List the items you would take on a one-day snowshoe hike. (6) Describe areas that are best for snowshoeing. Discuss some advantages and dangers of backcountry snowshoeing. (7) Discuss the benefits of snowshoeing. (8) Demonstrate the most efficient ways to break trail, climb uphill, travel downhill, and traverse a slope. (9) Demonstrate your ability, on a 2-mile snowshoe hike, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive snowshoers may complete a 1-mile hike with prior approval from their counselor. (10) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass.

pamphlet_excerpts: Versatile All-Mountain Ski Designs: All-mountain skis come in a variety of flexes and side cuts (p. 37).
High-Speed Hard-Snow Racing Skis: Racing skis are designed for high speeds and hard snow (p. 37).
Stiff Flex High-Speed Stability: They generally have a stiff flex that can make turning more difficult, but that makes the ski more stable at higher speeds (p. 37).
Side Cut Turn Radius: Racing skis are specialized for turning around gates, and the side cut determines how wide a turn the skis can make (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Select Appropriate Ski Flex: They generally have a stiff flex that can make turning more difficult, but that makes the ski more stable at higher speeds (p. 37).
Step 2 - Evaluate Ski Side Cut: Racing skis are specialized for turning around gates, and the side cut determines how wide a turn the skis can make (p. 37).
Step 3 - Use Twin-Tips for Parks: Twin-tip skis are turned up at the tip and the tail and are designed for performing on jumps, rails, and half-pipes (p. 37).
Step 4 - Adapt Equipment to Terrain: They can be skied all over the mountain, but their design makes many conditions outside the terrain park more challenging (p. 37).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While skiing down an intermediate alpine trail, you approach a slower snowboarder ahead of you who suddenly begins a wide turn across the run. Under the Alpine Responsibility Code, who has the right-of-way and what must you do?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While skiing down an intermediate alpine trail, you approach a slower snowboarder ahead of you who suddenly begins a wide turn across the run. Under the Alpine Responsibility Code, who has the right-of-way and what must you do?
options: A. Shout 'On your left!' and pass at high speed since uphill skiers have momentum.
B. The downhill rider ahead always has the right-of-way; you must adjust your speed and steer clear to avoid them regardless of their turn.
C. Stop in the middle of a blind rollover just above the snowboarder and wait.
D. Cut sharply across the tips of the snowboarder's board to claim the center line of the groomer.
choices: A. Shout 'On your left!' and pass at high speed since uphill skiers have momentum.
B. The downhill rider ahead always has the right-of-way; you must adjust your speed and steer clear to avoid them regardless of their turn.
C. Stop in the middle of a blind rollover just above the snowboarder and wait.
D. Cut sharply across the tips of the snowboarder's board to claim the center line of the groomer.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. The downhill rider ahead always has the right-of-way; you must adjust your speed and steer clear to avoid them regardless of their turn.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Under Your Responsibility Code in the Snow Sports Merit Badge Pamphlet, downhill skiers/riders cannot see behind them, so uphill traffic bears full responsibility for avoiding collisions and must never stop where obstructed from above.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: At an Alpine ski resort, what is the standard method for alerting ski patrol when you lack direct phone or radio contact at an accident scene?
options: A. Send a group member to the bottom of the nearest lift to inform the lift operator
B. Wave your ski poles toward the nearest chairlift tower
C. Carry the injured skier down to the base lodge first-aid station
D. Wait at the trail merge until a roving patroller passes by
choices: A. Send a group member to the bottom of the nearest lift to inform the lift operator
B. Wave your ski poles toward the nearest chairlift tower
C. Carry the injured skier down to the base lodge first-aid station
D. Wait at the trail merge until a roving patroller passes by
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Send a group member to the bottom of the nearest lift to inform the lift operator
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): At Alpine resorts, a common reporting method is sending someone from your group to the bottom of the nearest lift to inform a lift attendant of the exact location and injuries (p. 19).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do farming and land-management practices like contour plowing, cover crops, and vegetated riparian buffers along streams protect soil and water resources?
quiz_item.question: How do farming and land-management practices like contour plowing, cover crops, and vegetated riparian buffers along streams protect soil and water resources?
options: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
B. They strip away the organic O and A soil horizons so rainwater can flow rapidly over bare subsoil into rivers.
C. They compact clay particles into an impermeable crust that prevents groundwater aquifers from recharging.
D. They channel agricultural runoff directly into storm drains to speed up stream erosion downstream.
choices: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
B. They strip away the organic O and A soil horizons so rainwater can flow rapidly over bare subsoil into rivers.
C. They compact clay particles into an impermeable crust that prevents groundwater aquifers from recharging.
D. They channel agricultural runoff directly into storm drains to speed up stream erosion downstream.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. They slow down surface water runoff, anchor the nutrient-rich topsoil (A horizon) with plant roots, and filter out sediment and fertilizers before runoff reaches streams.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Contour farming, cover crops, and streamside buffer strips reduce water velocity, hold topsoil in place against wind and water erosion, and trap sediment and nutrient pollution.

Step 3 - Assess Estuary Fishery Impacts: It has caused oysters to disappear from the Chesapeake Bay, affecting commercial fisheries (p. 39).
Step 4 - Account for Reservoir Sedimentation: When flood-prevention and other types of reservoirs are built, allowance must be made for the sedimentation (p. 39).

Municipal Water Supply Risks: The damage to a city's water supply can be devastating (p. 45).
Limits of Vegetative Cover: Plant cover is important in controlling runoff, but in many instances it is not possible to keep plants growing on the land (p. 45).
Shaping Land for Runoff: Sometimes the surface of the land needs to be shaped to guide and control runoff (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Maintain Protective Plant Cover: Plant cover is important in controlling runoff, but in many instances it is not possible to keep plants growing on the land (p. 45).
Step 2 - Shape Slopes and Terraces: Sometimes the surface of the land needs to be shaped to guide and control runoff (p. 45).
Step 3 - Build Water-Retarding Check Dams: Small dams and other types of water-retarding structures often must be built to control runoff so that the land and the water are not damaged (p. 45).
Step 4 - Identify Community Conservation Problems: Learning more about soil and water conservation will help you become aware of some of the conservation problems your community might face (p. 45).

pamphlet_excerpts: Natural Purification Through Evaporation: Evaporation is one of nature's ways of purifying water, because most of the dissolved substances in it, such as the salt inseawater, remain behind (p. 30).
Atmospheric Water from Reactions: Chemical reactions return small amounts of water to the atmosphere (p. 30).
Respiration and Fuel Combustion: People, animals, and plants return some through the process of respiration (breathing), and the combustion, or burning, of fuels in cars (p. 30).
Solar-Driven Ocean Evaporation: Let's begin with the sea, where the sun's energy draws up into the atmosphere most of the water that travels through thehydrologic cycle (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Trace Biological Water Return: People, animals, and plants return some through the process of respiration (breathing), and the combustion, or burning, of fuels in cars (p. 30).
Step 2 - Track Solar Ocean Evaporation: Let's begin with the sea, where the sun's energy draws up into the atmosphere most of the water that travels through thehydrologic cycle (p. 30).
Step 3 - Follow Moisture-Laden Wind Masses: Much of the moisture evaporated into the air soon falls back into the sea during storms, but winds eventually do carryair masses with moisture (p. 30).
Step 4 - Observe Condensed Atmospheric Vapor: A small part of the moisture, or water vapor, in the air at any time might be visible to us as clouds, fog, or mist (p. 30).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Support Aerobic Bacterial Digestion: Both processes depend on biological action and both require oxygen (p. 78).
Step 2 - Aerate Effluent with Oxygen: The oxygen is supplied through aeration, that is, by spraying the effluent into the air or by pumping air (p. 78).
Step 3 - Route Effluent to Filters: In one process, the effluent goes from the primary settling tank to a trickling filter (p. 78).
Step 4 - Decompose Waste Over Stones: There, it passes slowly over stones or other material where biological growths decompose the waste left in the effluent (p. 78).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Make a trip to TWO of the following places. Write a report of more than 500 words about the soil and water and energy conservation practices you saw. (1) An agricultural experiment (2) A managed forest or woodlot, range, or pasture (3) A wildlife refuge or a fish or game management area (4) A conservation-managed farm or ranch (5) A managed watershed (6) A waste-treatment plant (7) A public drinking water treatment plant (8) An industry water use installation (9) A desalinization plant (b) Plant 100 trees, bushes, and/or vines for a good purpose. (c) Seed an area of at least one-fifth acre for some worthwhile conservation purposes, using suitable grasses or legumes alone or in a mixture. (d) Study a soil survey report. Describe the things in it. Using tracing paper and a pen, trace over any of the soil maps, and outline an area with three or more different kinds of soil. List each kind of soil by full name and map symbol. (e) Make a list of places in your neighborhood, camps, school ground, or park that have erosion, sedimentation, or pollution problems. Describe how these could be corrected through individual or group action. (f) Carry out any other soil and water conservation project approved by your counselor.

B. To replace all topsoil with gravel pathways for farm machinery
C. To block sunlight from reaching adjacent row crops
D. To keep strips of land in permanent vegetation that slow runoff and trap sediment and pollutants
choices: A. To speed up rainwater drainage into nearby creeks
B. To replace all topsoil with gravel pathways for farm machinery
C. To block sunlight from reaching adjacent row crops
D. To keep strips of land in permanent vegetation that slow runoff and trap sediment and pollutants
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. To keep strips of land in permanent vegetation that slow runoff and trap sediment and pollutants
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Conservation buffers are small areas or strips kept in permanent vegetation that control erosion and pollution by breaking up and slowing runoff, sediment, and pollutants (p. 49).
