patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why must you inspect oxygen regulators, hoses, and torch fittings to ensure they are completely free of oil and grease before connecting them?
options: A. Grease clogs the ground clamp and reduces electrical conductivity
B. Oil makes the torch handle slippery and harder to aim
C. Pure oxygen can react violently with oil or grease and explode
D. Lubricant turns the welding arc flame from blue to yellow
choices: A. Grease clogs the ground clamp and reduces electrical conductivity
B. Oil makes the torch handle slippery and harder to aim
C. Pure oxygen can react violently with oil or grease and explode
D. Lubricant turns the welding arc flame from blue to yellow
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Pure oxygen can react violently with oil or grease and explode
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Pressurized oxygen reacts violently with hydrocarbons, so all regulators, hoses, and fittings must be tight and completely free of oil or grease to prevent fires or explosions (p. 21).

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in whitewater activities, including branches and trees in water along a shore and stretching across the stream, rocks, hydraulics over ledges or low-head dams, strong wind, low water or air temperature, and thunder and lightning storms. Explain what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review with your counselor the prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for the following injuries or illnesses that could occur while participating in whitewater activities: cold-water shock; hypothermia; head, neck, and back injuries; heat-related illnesses; sunburn; dehydration; blisters; bruises; cuts; sprains and strains; shoulder dislocation; and submersion injuries. (c) Discuss with your counselor the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy and the American Whitewater safety guidelines, including the use of helmet and life jackets.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: If your canoe, kayak, or raft capsizes in moving whitewater rapids deeper than knee height, why must you never attempt to stand up on the riverbed?
quiz_item.question: If your canoe, kayak, or raft capsizes in moving whitewater rapids deeper than knee height, why must you never attempt to stand up on the riverbed?
options: A. Standing up scares downstream paddlers into dropping their throw bags.
B. River rocks are too slippery to push your boat upstream against the current.
C. Standing upright causes your lifejacket to lose buoyancy when splashed.

D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
choices: A. Standing up scares downstream paddlers into dropping their throw bags.
B. River rocks are too slippery to push your boat upstream against the current.
C. Standing upright causes your lifejacket to lose buoyancy when splashed.

D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Foot entrapment in swift current is a deadly whitewater hazard; swimmers must assume the defensive whitewater swim position on their back with feet at the surface pointed downstream to fend off rocks until reaching an eddy.

pamphlet_excerpts: Lateral Ferrying Across Current: Upstream (forward) ferries and downstream (back) ferries move you sideways across the current (p. 30).
Upstream Ferry Angle: In an upstream ferry, you face upstream and paddle forward with your bow at an angle to the current (p. 30).
Bow Direction Movement: You move across the current in the direction your bowis pointing (p. 30).
Downstream Back-Paddling Ferry: To perform a downstream ferry, you face downstream and back paddle with your stern pointed upstream at an angle to the current (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Point Bow Toward Target: You move across the current in the direction your bowis pointing (p. 30).
Step 2 - Angle Stern Into Current: To perform a downstream ferry, you face downstream and back paddle with your stern pointed upstream at an angle to the current (p. 30).
Step 3 - Backpaddle Across the Stream: You move across the current in the direction your stern is facing (p. 30).
Step 4 - Turn Boat Facing Upstream: To perform a successful upstream ferry, begin by turning your boat until it faces upstream (p. 30).

quiz_item.question: When performing a downstream ferry across a fast current, how should you position and propel your craft?
options: A. Face upstream and paddle backward so the water pushes the bow sideways.
B. Face downstream and backpaddle with your stern angled upstream toward your target bank.
C. Position the boat perpendicular to the current and use high braces on the upstream side.
D. Point the bow directly downstream and paddle forward at twice the speed of the river.
choices: A. Face upstream and paddle backward so the water pushes the bow sideways.
B. Face downstream and backpaddle with your stern angled upstream toward your target bank.
C. Position the boat perpendicular to the current and use high braces on the upstream side.
D. Point the bow directly downstream and paddle forward at twice the speed of the river.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Face downstream and backpaddle with your stern angled upstream toward your target bank.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): To execute a downstream ferry, you face downstream and backpaddle while holding your stern at an angle to the current, moving laterally in the direction your stern points (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Backstrokes for Speed Control: Canoeists and kayakers use backstrokes to back paddle, that is, to slow or reverse the forward motion of the boat (p. 56).
Stopping in River Eddies: As you paddle downstream, you will want to stop in an eddy to rest or to scout a rapid below (p. 56).
Downstream Eddy Turn Maneuver: The maneuver to enter an eddy while heading downstream is called an eddy turn (p. 56).
Exiting via Peel Out: Later you will learn how to exit an eddy using a peel (p. 56).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Execute Clean Eddy Turns: The maneuver to enter an eddy while heading downstream is called an eddy turn (p. 56).
Step 2 - Practice Eddy Peel Outs: Later you will learn how to exit an eddy using a peel (p. 56).
Step 3 - Master Moving Water Transitions: When you have learned how to move in and out of eddies with confidence and ease, you will have passed a major whitewater skills milestone (p. 56).
Step 4 - Control Momentum in Current: Entering an eddy while moving downstream in a boat can be challenging, especially if the current is fast (p. 56).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Option A, Tandem Canoeist. Do ALL of the following strokes and techniques on calm water: (1) Demonstrate the following strokes in the bow: cross forward, bow draw, cross bow draw, bow pry, and sculling draw. (2) Demonstrate the following strokes in the stern: stern draw, stern pry, sculling draw, and forward with stern pry. (3) Demonstrate a high brace, low brace, and righting pry. (b) Option B, Solo Canoeist. Do ALL of the following strokes and techniques on calm water: (1) Demonstrate the following strokes: cross forward, bow draw, cross bow draw, stern draw, pry, stern pry, sculling draw, and forward with stern pry. (2) Demonstrate a high brace, low brace, and righting pry. (c) Option C, Solo Kayaker. Do ALL of the following strokes and techniques on calm water: (1) Demonstrate the following strokes: bow draw, rudder, and sculling draw. (2) Demonstrate a high brace and low brace.

pamphlet_excerpts: Knee Pressure Boat Tilt: In the peel out, note how both paddlers use their left knees to lean into and tilt the boat into the turn (p. 50).
Offside Peel Out Mechanics: An offside peel out incorporates all the same features of the on side peel out except that the turning strokes are different (p. 50).
Opposite Kayak Blade Turn: For kayakers, the opposite paddle blade is used for the turning stroke (p. 50).
Solo Canoe Turning Strokes: After crossing the eddy line, solo canoeists can use avariety of turning strokes, including a forward sweep or crossbow draw (p. 50).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Engage Opposite Kayak Blade: For kayakers, the opposite paddle blade is used for the turning stroke (p. 50).
Step 2 - Apply Cross-Bow Draw: After crossing the eddy line, solo canoeists can use avariety of turning strokes, including a forward sweep or crossbow draw (p. 50).
Step 3 - Coordinate Tandem Turning Strokes: Tandem canoeists use a combination of a cross-bowdraw in the bow while the stern paddler does a low bracing reverse sweep or simply powers (p. 50).
Step 4 - Keep Paddle Shaft Vertical: The paddle shaft should be vertical and move in a path 2 to 3 feet long next to the side of the boat (p. 50).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do tandem canoeists coordinate their strokes when executing an offside peel out across an eddy line?
quiz_item.question: How do tandem canoeists coordinate their strokes when executing an offside peel out across an eddy line?
options: A. Both paddlers switch sides simultaneously and perform reverse J-strokes.
B. The bow paddler stops paddling completely while the stern paddler rudders hard against the current.
C. Both paddlers lean toward the upstream gunwale and drag their paddles behind the stern.
D. The bow paddler uses a cross-bow draw while the stern paddler performs a low bracing reverse sweep or powers forward.
choices: A. Both paddlers switch sides simultaneously and perform reverse J-strokes.
B. The bow paddler stops paddling completely while the stern paddler rudders hard against the current.
C. Both paddlers lean toward the upstream gunwale and drag their paddles behind the stern.
D. The bow paddler uses a cross-bow draw while the stern paddler performs a low bracing reverse sweep or powers forward.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. The bow paddler uses a cross-bow draw while the stern paddler performs a low bracing reverse sweep or powers forward.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): In an offside peel out, tandem canoeists tilt the boat into the turn with their knees while the bow paddler uses a cross-bow draw and the stern paddler executes a low bracing reverse sweep or powers forward (p. 50).

pamphlet_excerpts: Six Rapid Difficulty Classes: Here are the six classifications used for the International Scale of River Difficulty (p. 34).
Class I Moving Water: Fast-moving water with riffles and small waves (p. 34).
Class II Clear Channels: Straightforward rapids with wide, clear channels (p. 34).
Maneuvering Around Medium Waves: Some maneuvering may be required, but rocks and medium-size waves are easily avoided by trainedpaddlers (p. 34).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Wide Clear Channels: Straightforward rapids with wide, clear channels (p. 34).
Step 2 - Maneuver Around River Rocks: Some maneuvering may be required, but rocks and medium-size waves are easily avoided by trainedpaddlers (p. 34).
Step 3 - Recognize Class III Waves: Rapids with moderate, irregular waves that may swamp an open canoe (p. 34).
Step 4 - Prepare for Group Assistance: Some risk to swimmers; group assistance may be necessary (p. 34).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why must whitewater canoes and kayaks be outfitted with extra flotation bags or foam blocks before running rapids?
quiz_item.question: Why must whitewater canoes and kayaks be outfitted with extra flotation bags or foam blocks before running rapids?
options: A. To increase the weight of the boat so strong winds cannot blow it sideways.
B. To displace water so the craft rides high and is much easier to rescue if it flips.
C. To stiffen the keel line so the boat tracks straighter across calm pools.
D. To replace the need for paddlers to wear personal flotation devices in Class I water.
choices: A. To increase the weight of the boat so strong winds cannot blow it sideways.
B. To displace water so the craft rides high and is much easier to rescue if it flips.
C. To stiffen the keel line so the boat tracks straighter across calm pools.
D. To replace the need for paddlers to wear personal flotation devices in Class I water.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. To displace water so the craft rides high and is much easier to rescue if it flips.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Extra flotation installed in a whitewater boat keeps a swamped or capsized hull riding high in the water, preventing heavy waterlogged pinning and simplifying rescues (p. 39).

pamphlet_excerpts: Pre-Launch Gear Inspection: Before you head out on the river, always double-check that you have both personal and group essentials necessary for a safe whitewater outing (p. 12).
Waterproofing Dry Essentials: Items that need to stay dry include food, spare clothing, first-aidkits, maps, sleeping bags, tents, and other camping equipment (p. 12).
Securing Gear Inside Gunwales: Use cam straps, bungee cords, and pieces of rope to secure items and equipment so they will not fall out past the gunwales if you capsize (p. 12).
Eliminating Rope Entrapment Hazards: Itis vital that your lashing does not pose an entrapment hazard (p. 12).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Lash Dry Bags Securely: Use cam straps, bungee cords, and pieces of rope to secure items and equipment so they will not fall out past the gunwales if you capsize (p. 12).
Step 2 - Tuck Loose Strap Ends: Itis vital that your lashing does not pose an entrapment hazard (p. 12).
Step 3 - Maintain Close Buddy Contact: Buddies either ride in the same boat or stay near each other in single-person craft (p. 12).
Step 4 - Verify Group Skill Proficiency: SKILL PROFICIENCY Everyone in an activity afloat must have sufficient knowledge and skill to participate safely (p. 12).

B. The helmet chinstrap is required to hold your whistle in place when signaling from land.
C. Taking a helmet off ashore voids the manufacturer's safety certification.
D. Wet, uneven shoreline boulders make slips and falls common right next to fast water.
choices: A. It shields your eyes from glare so you can see the riverbed clearly.
B. The helmet chinstrap is required to hold your whistle in place when signaling from land.
C. Taking a helmet off ashore voids the manufacturer's safety certification.
D. Wet, uneven shoreline boulders make slips and falls common right next to fast water.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Wet, uneven shoreline boulders make slips and falls common right next to fast water.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Shoreline rocks along rapids are often wet, mossy, and treacherous, so wearing your helmet while scouting ashore protects your head if you slip and fall (p. 26).

requirements.lead_text: Wearing a proper lifejacket and being appropriately dressed for the weather and water conditions, perform the following skills in moving water in a properly equipped whitewatercraft of your choice (tandem canoe, solo canoe, or solo kayak). requirements.req_text: Wearing a proper life jacket and being appropriately dressed for the weather and water conditions, perform the following skills in moving water in a properly equipped whitewater craft of your choice (tandem canoe, solo canoe, or solo kayak). If a tandem canoe is used, the skills must be demonstrated from both the bow and stern positions. (a) Launch and land. (b) Paddle forward in a straight line at least 10 boat lengths. (c) Backpaddle in a straight line at least five boat lengths. (d) Ferry upstream from both sides of the river. (e) Ferry downstream from both sides of the river. (f) Eddy turn from both sides of an eddy. (g) Peel out from both sides of an eddy.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What happens if you set too wide an angle to the current when attempting an upstream ferry across fast water?
quiz_item.question: What happens if you set too wide an angle to the current when attempting an upstream ferry across fast water?
options: A. The boat will shoot upstream faster than the surrounding river flow.
B. The current will catch the upstream side of the bow, spinning the boat broadside or pushing it downstream.
C. The stern will automatically lock into the nearest eddy without paddling.
D. The hull will rise onto a plane and skip over submerged rocks.
choices: A. The boat will shoot upstream faster than the surrounding river flow.
B. The current will catch the upstream side of the bow, spinning the boat broadside or pushing it downstream.
C. The stern will automatically lock into the nearest eddy without paddling.

Step 3 - Open Bag Mouth Halfway: Be sure that the mouth of the bag is only halfway open (p. 71).
Step 4 - Alert Swimmer Before Throwing: Get the attention of the person in the water by yelling, "Rope!" or giving a single blast of your whistle (p. 71).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What is the proper technique for a swimmer in whitewater to hold a throw rope while being pendulumed to shore?
quiz_item.question: What is the proper technique for a swimmer in whitewater to hold a throw rope while being pendulumed to shore?
options: A. Tie a bowline loop around the waist and swim headfirst toward the rescuer.
B. Wrap the rope three times around the dominant wrist and float face down.
C. Hold the rope with both hands at chest level, feed it over the shoulder opposite the shore to which you are being pulled, and float on your back with feet downstream.
D. Clip the end of the throw rope directly to the front zipper of the lifejacket.
choices: A. Tie a bowline loop around the waist and swim headfirst toward the rescuer.
B. Wrap the rope three times around the dominant wrist and float face down.
C. Hold the rope with both hands at chest level, feed it over the shoulder opposite the shore to which you are being pulled, and float on your back with feet downstream.
D. Clip the end of the throw rope directly to the front zipper of the lifejacket.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Hold the rope with both hands at chest level, feed it over the shoulder opposite the shore to which you are being pulled, and float on your back with feet downstream.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A swimmer receiving a throw rope should never wrap or tie the line around their body, and instead should float on their back holding the rope over the shoulder opposite the rescuer so the current swings them to shore without pulling their face underwater (p. 72).

requirements.lead_text: Participate in one or more whitewater trips using either a canoe or kayak on a Class I and/or Class II river. The trip(s) must involve at least six hours of paddling time. For each trip:
requirements.req_text: Participate in one or more whitewater trips using either a canoe or kayak on a Class I and/or Class II river. The trip(s) must involve at least six hours of paddling time. For each trip: (a) Help to prepare a written plan, specifying the route (put-ins and takeouts), schedule, equipment, safety precautions, and emergency procedures. (b) Determine local rules and obtain permission from landowners and land managers in advance. (c) Explain what steps have been taken to comply with Scouting America Safety Afloat and the American Whitewater safety guidelines. (d) Show how to protect personal and group equipment from water and how to load and secure the containers in boats to be used in the trip. Execute the plans with other paddlers. (e) Explain to your counselor how well your plans worked for each trip taken.

pamphlet_excerpts: Matching Group Capabilities: Consult with your counselor to make sure that the course is within the capabilities of all participants and that the equipment you will be using (p. 44).
Written Route Float Plan: Research and prepare a float plan that specifies your route (p. 44).
Realistic River Time Schedule: Set up a schedule in which you determine how much time you will need to safely float the stretch of river you selected (p. 44).
Pre-Trip Emergency Briefings: Double-check your equipment and review safety precautions and emergency procedures (p. 44).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Calculate Safe Paddling Time: Set up a schedule in which you determine how much time you will need to safely float the stretch of river you selected (p. 44).
Step 2 - Inspect Equipment Before Launch: Double-check your equipment and review safety precautions and emergency procedures (p. 44).
Step 3 - Map Emergency Evacuation Points: Identify your options in the event of a problem with equipment, a sudden change in weather, or a medical emergency (p. 44).
Step 4 - Follow Safety Afloat Rules: A review of the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy and the American whitewater safety guidelines will help you with these tasks (p. 44).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Which elements must be included when preparing a written plan for a whitewater trip?
quiz_item.question: Which elements must be included when preparing a written plan for a whitewater trip?
options: A. Only the names of the boats and the brand of paddles used by each participant.
B. A pledge to run every rapid without scouting or portaging to stay on schedule.
C. A map of Class V rapids for novice paddlers to test their limits.
D. The route with put-ins and takeouts, schedule, equipment list, safety precautions, and emergency procedures for weather, gear, or medical issues.
choices: A. Only the names of the boats and the brand of paddles used by each participant.
B. A pledge to run every rapid without scouting or portaging to stay on schedule.
C. A map of Class V rapids for novice paddlers to test their limits.
D. The route with put-ins and takeouts, schedule, equipment list, safety precautions, and emergency procedures for weather, gear, or medical issues.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. The route with put-ins and takeouts, schedule, equipment list, safety precautions, and emergency procedures for weather, gear, or medical issues.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A complete whitewater trip plan specifies the route (put-ins and takeouts), time schedule, required equipment, safety precautions, and emergency contingency procedures (p. 44).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: If your canoe, kayak, or raft capsizes in moving whitewater rapids deeper than knee height, why must you never attempt to stand up on the riverbed?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: If your canoe, kayak, or raft capsizes in moving whitewater rapids deeper than knee height, why must you never attempt to stand up on the riverbed?
options: A. Standing up scares downstream paddlers into dropping their throw bags.
B. River rocks are too slippery to push your boat upstream against the current.
C. Standing upright causes your lifejacket to lose buoyancy when splashed.

D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
choices: A. Standing up scares downstream paddlers into dropping their throw bags.
B. River rocks are too slippery to push your boat upstream against the current.
C. Standing upright causes your lifejacket to lose buoyancy when splashed.

D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Your foot can wedge between rocks on the riverbed while the force of the current pushes your body downstream and holds your head underwater (foot entrapment); instead, float on your back with feet up and pointed downstream.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Foot entrapment in swift current is a deadly whitewater hazard; swimmers must assume the defensive whitewater swim position on their back with feet at the surface pointed downstream to fend off rocks until reaching an eddy.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When performing a downstream ferry across a fast current, how should you position and propel your craft?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When performing a downstream ferry across a fast current, how should you position and propel your craft?
options: A. Face upstream and paddle backward so the water pushes the bow sideways.
B. Face downstream and backpaddle with your stern angled upstream toward your target bank.
C. Position the boat perpendicular to the current and use high braces on the upstream side.
D. Point the bow directly downstream and paddle forward at twice the speed of the river.
choices: A. Face upstream and paddle backward so the water pushes the bow sideways.
B. Face downstream and backpaddle with your stern angled upstream toward your target bank.
C. Position the boat perpendicular to the current and use high braces on the upstream side.
D. Point the bow directly downstream and paddle forward at twice the speed of the river.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Face downstream and backpaddle with your stern angled upstream toward your target bank.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): To execute a downstream ferry, you face downstream and backpaddle while holding your stern at an angle to the current, moving laterally in the direction your stern points (p. 30).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which maneuver does a paddler use to leave the main downstream current and come to a stop in the calm water behind an obstacle?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which maneuver does a paddler use to leave the main downstream current and come to a stop in the calm water behind an obstacle?
options: A. An upstream ferry
B. A peel out
C. An eddy turn
D. A portage carry
choices: A. An upstream ferry
B. A peel out
C. An eddy turn
D. A portage carry
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. An eddy turn
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Entering an eddy while paddling downstream to rest or scout a rapid below is called an eddy turn, whereas exiting the eddy is called a peel out (p. 56).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do tandem canoeists coordinate their strokes when executing an offside peel out across an eddy line?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do tandem canoeists coordinate their strokes when executing an offside peel out across an eddy line?
options: A. Both paddlers switch sides simultaneously and perform reverse J-strokes.
B. The bow paddler stops paddling completely while the stern paddler rudders hard against the current.
C. Both paddlers lean toward the upstream gunwale and drag their paddles behind the stern.
D. The bow paddler uses a cross-bow draw while the stern paddler performs a low bracing reverse sweep or powers forward.
choices: A. Both paddlers switch sides simultaneously and perform reverse J-strokes.
B. The bow paddler stops paddling completely while the stern paddler rudders hard against the current.
C. Both paddlers lean toward the upstream gunwale and drag their paddles behind the stern.
D. The bow paddler uses a cross-bow draw while the stern paddler performs a low bracing reverse sweep or powers forward.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. The bow paddler uses a cross-bow draw while the stern paddler performs a low bracing reverse sweep or powers forward.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): In an offside peel out, tandem canoeists tilt the boat into the turn with their knees while the bow paddler uses a cross-bow draw and the stern paddler executes a low bracing reverse sweep or powers forward (p. 50).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: According to the International Scale of River Difficulty, which characteristics define a Class II rapid?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the International Scale of River Difficulty, which characteristics define a Class II rapid?
options: A. Flat, slow-moving water with no riffles, rocks, or obstructions.
B. Straightforward rapids with wide, clear channels where medium-size waves and rocks are easily avoided by trained paddlers.
C. Long, violent rapids with constricted passages that require expert scouting and carry high risk to swimmers.
D. Moderate, irregular waves that routinely swamp open canoes and require tight, complex maneuvers in fast current.
choices: A. Flat, slow-moving water with no riffles, rocks, or obstructions.
B. Straightforward rapids with wide, clear channels where medium-size waves and rocks are easily avoided by trained paddlers.
C. Long, violent rapids with constricted passages that require expert scouting and carry high risk to swimmers.
D. Moderate, irregular waves that routinely swamp open canoes and require tight, complex maneuvers in fast current.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Straightforward rapids with wide, clear channels where medium-size waves and rocks are easily avoided by trained paddlers.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Class II (Novice) rapids feature straightforward channels that are evident without scouting, requiring some maneuvering around rocks and medium waves that trained paddlers can easily avoid (p. 34).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do you properly confirm that you are safe when a teammate asks "Are you OK?" by pointing to the top of their helmet?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do you properly confirm that you are safe when a teammate asks "Are you OK?" by pointing to the top of their helmet?
options: A. Return the exact same signal by touching the top of your helmet.
B. Wave your paddle side to side above your head and blow three whistle blasts.
C. Hold your paddle horizontally across your chest and nod your head.
D. Point your paddle blade downstream toward the next eddy.
choices: A. Return the exact same signal by touching the top of your helmet.
B. Wave your paddle side to side above your head and blow three whistle blasts.
C. Hold your paddle horizontally across your chest and nod your head.
D. Point your paddle blade downstream toward the next eddy.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Return the exact same signal by touching the top of your helmet.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Under the American Whitewater Universal River Signals, you confirm that you are OK by returning the same helmet-tap signal back to the person asking (p. 33).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why must whitewater canoes and kayaks be outfitted with extra flotation bags or foam blocks before running rapids?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why must whitewater canoes and kayaks be outfitted with extra flotation bags or foam blocks before running rapids?
options: A. To increase the weight of the boat so strong winds cannot blow it sideways.
B. To displace water so the craft rides high and is much easier to rescue if it flips.
C. To stiffen the keel line so the boat tracks straighter across calm pools.
D. To replace the need for paddlers to wear personal flotation devices in Class I water.
choices: A. To increase the weight of the boat so strong winds cannot blow it sideways.
B. To displace water so the craft rides high and is much easier to rescue if it flips.
C. To stiffen the keel line so the boat tracks straighter across calm pools.
D. To replace the need for paddlers to wear personal flotation devices in Class I water.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. To displace water so the craft rides high and is much easier to rescue if it flips.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Extra flotation installed in a whitewater boat keeps a swamped or capsized hull riding high in the water, preventing heavy waterlogged pinning and simplifying rescues (p. 39).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the most critical safety rule when using cam straps or cords to secure dry bags and equipment inside a whitewater boat?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the most critical safety rule when using cam straps or cords to secure dry bags and equipment inside a whitewater boat?
options: A. Leave 10 feet of slack in every rope so bags can float alongside the hull after a capsize.
B. Tie every piece of gear directly to the paddler's lifejacket buckle.
C. Secure items tightly so nothing falls past the gunwales or creates a loose loop that could cause an entrapment hazard.
D. Place heavy coolers on top of the thwarts to raise the boat's center of gravity.
choices: A. Leave 10 feet of slack in every rope so bags can float alongside the hull after a capsize.
B. Tie every piece of gear directly to the paddler's lifejacket buckle.
C. Secure items tightly so nothing falls past the gunwales or creates a loose loop that could cause an entrapment hazard.
D. Place heavy coolers on top of the thwarts to raise the boat's center of gravity.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Secure items tightly so nothing falls past the gunwales or creates a loose loop that could cause an entrapment hazard.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): All equipment must be lashed snugly inside the hull using cam straps or cords so items cannot fall past the gunwales or create loose loops that could entangle a swimmer (p. 12).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why should you always keep your whitewater helmet fastened on your head while scouting a rapid on foot along the shore?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why should you always keep your whitewater helmet fastened on your head while scouting a rapid on foot along the shore?
options: A. It shields your eyes from glare so you can see the riverbed clearly.
B. The helmet chinstrap is required to hold your whistle in place when signaling from land.
C. Taking a helmet off ashore voids the manufacturer's safety certification.
D. Wet, uneven shoreline boulders make slips and falls common right next to fast water.
choices: A. It shields your eyes from glare so you can see the riverbed clearly.
B. The helmet chinstrap is required to hold your whistle in place when signaling from land.
C. Taking a helmet off ashore voids the manufacturer's safety certification.
D. Wet, uneven shoreline boulders make slips and falls common right next to fast water.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Wet, uneven shoreline boulders make slips and falls common right next to fast water.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Shoreline rocks along rapids are often wet, mossy, and treacherous, so wearing your helmet while scouting ashore protects your head if you slip and fall (p. 26).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What happens if you set too wide an angle to the current when attempting an upstream ferry across fast water?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What happens if you set too wide an angle to the current when attempting an upstream ferry across fast water?
options: A. The boat will shoot upstream faster than the surrounding river flow.
B. The current will catch the upstream side of the bow, spinning the boat broadside or pushing it downstream.
C. The stern will automatically lock into the nearest eddy without paddling.
D. The hull will rise onto a plane and skip over submerged rocks.
choices: A. The boat will shoot upstream faster than the surrounding river flow.
B. The current will catch the upstream side of the bow, spinning the boat broadside or pushing it downstream.
C. The stern will automatically lock into the nearest eddy without paddling.
D. The hull will rise onto a plane and skip over submerged rocks.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. The current will catch the upstream side of the bow, spinning the boat broadside or pushing it downstream.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): In fast current, a narrow ferry angle is required because if your bow is angled too wide against strong flow, the water overwhelms your strokes and spins the bow downstream (p. 46).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the proper technique for a swimmer in whitewater to hold a throw rope while being pendulumed to shore?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the proper technique for a swimmer in whitewater to hold a throw rope while being pendulumed to shore?
options: A. Tie a bowline loop around the waist and swim headfirst toward the rescuer.
B. Wrap the rope three times around the dominant wrist and float face down.
C. Hold the rope with both hands at chest level, feed it over the shoulder opposite the shore to which you are being pulled, and float on your back with feet downstream.
D. Clip the end of the throw rope directly to the front zipper of the lifejacket.
choices: A. Tie a bowline loop around the waist and swim headfirst toward the rescuer.
B. Wrap the rope three times around the dominant wrist and float face down.
C. Hold the rope with both hands at chest level, feed it over the shoulder opposite the shore to which you are being pulled, and float on your back with feet downstream.
D. Clip the end of the throw rope directly to the front zipper of the lifejacket.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Hold the rope with both hands at chest level, feed it over the shoulder opposite the shore to which you are being pulled, and float on your back with feet downstream.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A swimmer receiving a throw rope should never wrap or tie the line around their body, and instead should float on their back holding the rope over the shoulder opposite the rescuer so the current swings them to shore without pulling their face underwater (p. 72).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While hiking back from a peak at dusk, your buddy pair realizes you missed a trail junction and are no longer sure where the main trail is. Following the BSA S.T.O.P. survival protocol, what should you do?
quiz_item.question: While hiking back from a peak at dusk, your buddy pair realizes you missed a trail junction and are no longer sure where the main trail is. Following the BSA S.T.O.P. survival protocol, what should you do?
options: A. Run downhill through the woods before total darkness falls to look for a road.
B. Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
C. Split up and hike in opposite directions to cover twice as much ground.
D. Climb an exposed cliff face after dark to check for distant highway lights.
choices: A. Run downhill through the woods before total darkness falls to look for a road.
B. Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
C. Split up and hike in opposite directions to cover twice as much ground.
D. Climb an exposed cliff face after dark to check for distant highway lights.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Moving randomly after losing the trail increases search radius exponentially and risks injury after dark; staying put with S.T.O.P., shelter, and 3-signal distress calls maximizes rapid rescue.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: According to the seven priorities of wilderness survival, which action comes immediately after maintaining a positive mental attitude and providing urgent first aid?
quiz_item.question: According to the seven priorities of wilderness survival, which action comes immediately after maintaining a positive mental attitude and providing urgent first aid?
options: A. Foraging for edible wild plants and berries before dark.
B. Seeking or building a shelter to protect against weather exposure.
C. Hiking downhill until you find a paved road or ranger station.
D. Rationing your remaining food supplies into equal daily portions.
choices: A. Foraging for edible wild plants and berries before dark.
B. Seeking or building a shelter to protect against weather exposure.
C. Hiking downhill until you find a paved road or ranger station.
D. Rationing your remaining food supplies into equal daily portions.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Seeking or building a shelter to protect against weather exposure.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): After positive mental attitude and first aid, shelter is the third priority of survival to protect your body from hypothermia or extreme heat (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Group Preparation Habits: Being Prepared as a Group Being Prepared as a Group Many people keep things to themselves (p. 21).
Speaking Up Without Fear: They don't want to hold up the team or are worried about what others will think of them (p. 21).
Early Blister Prevention: Remember, stopping for a few moments to deal with a hot spot on a heel can avoid bringing the group to a long halt later in the day when blisters break (p. 21).
Positive Survival Mindset: Most important is how you think about things when you are confronted with a survival situation (p. 21).

Step 2 - Control Thoughts Under Stress: Most important is how you think about things when you are confronted with a survival situation (p. 21).
Step 3 - Cultivate Will to Survive: Many survivors of wilderness emergencies have said that a willingness to survive is the key factor in getting through a difficult situation (p. 21).
Step 4 - Support Discouraged Group Members: You might assume that everyone has an equal desire to survive, but that is not always the case (p. 21).

quiz_item.question: Why should you carry your core personal survival kit on your person rather than stowing it deep inside a large frame backpack?
options: A. It keeps the survival kit warm so adhesive bandages do not freeze.
B. It ensures you still have life-saving gear if you are separated from your pack during a river crossing or side hike.
C. It prevents bears from smelling the metal tools inside your backpack.
D. It satisfies wilderness permit weight distribution rules in national forests.
choices: A. It keeps the survival kit warm so adhesive bandages do not freeze.
B. It ensures you still have life-saving gear if you are separated from your pack during a river crossing or side hike.
C. It prevents bears from smelling the metal tools inside your backpack.
D. It satisfies wilderness permit weight distribution rules in national forests.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. It ensures you still have life-saving gear if you are separated from your pack during a river crossing or side hike.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Keeping essential survival tools in your pockets or on your belt ensures they remain with you even if your main pack is lost or left behind (p. 55).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When improvising a natural survival shelter in cold weather, why is it critical to pile several inches of dry leaves, pine needles, or boughs on the floor?
quiz_item.question: When improvising a natural survival shelter in cold weather, why is it critical to pile several inches of dry leaves, pine needles, or boughs on the floor?
options: A. To elevate yourself high enough to see over surrounding brush.
B. To prevent conductive heat loss from your body into the cold ground.
C. To create smoke immediately if a spark lands inside the shelter.
D. To attract insects that can be used as emergency food.
choices: A. To elevate yourself high enough to see over surrounding brush.
B. To prevent conductive heat loss from your body into the cold ground.
C. To create smoke immediately if a spark lands inside the shelter.
D. To attract insects that can be used as emergency food.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. To prevent conductive heat loss from your body into the cold ground.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Lying directly on cold or damp soil drains body heat rapidly, so a thick ground mat of natural insulation is vital for preventing hypothermia (p. 43).

Practicing Before Emergencies: As with most survival skills, practicing when you are not in an emergency situation is the best way to become good (p. 31).
Matchless Ignition Tools: It is especially important to practice using fire-lighting methods other than matches and lighters, a magnifying lens, flint and steel, and fire (p. 31).
Campfire as Survival Tool: A good way to think about a campfire is to consider it a tool to be used for specific and important uses (p. 31).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Practice Matchless Fire Starting: It is especially important to practice using fire-lighting methods other than matches and lighters, a magnifying lens, flint and steel, and fire (p. 31).
Step 2 - Use Fire With Purpose: A good way to think about a campfire is to consider it a tool to be used for specific and important uses (p. 31).
Step 3 - Carry Backcountry Cooking Stoves: If you come to thebackcountry prepared not to need a fire, carrying a stove and fuel, for example, you can make an informed choice (p. 31).
Step 4 - Obey Open Flame Bans: Be mindful of any temporary bans against open flames in the area (p. 31).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Where is the best place to find dry tinder and kindling in a forest after a heavy rainstorm?
quiz_item.question: Where is the best place to find dry tinder and kindling in a forest after a heavy rainstorm?
options: A. Underneath rotting logs resting in low marshy hollows.
B. From dead branches still attached to standing trees and the dry inner core of split wood.
C. From freshly sprouted green ferns growing beside a creek.
D. Buried beneath two inches of saturated topsoil on a north-facing slope.
choices: A. Underneath rotting logs resting in low marshy hollows.
B. From dead branches still attached to standing trees and the dry inner core of split wood.
C. From freshly sprouted green ferns growing beside a creek.
D. Buried beneath two inches of saturated topsoil on a north-facing slope.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. From dead branches still attached to standing trees and the dry inner core of split wood.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Dead twigs off the ground dry out fastest, and splitting larger wet branches exposes dry interior wood fibers that catch sparks readily (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Long Range Mirror Flashes: When the sun is shining, the flash of light reflected with a signal mirror can be seen for miles (p. 36).
Sighting Mirror Targets: Sight a target through the hole in the center of the mirror or by looking just over the mirror's top edge (p. 36).
Nighttime Three Flash Signals: At night, use a flashlight to send groups of three flashes in the direction where you believe rescuers might be able tosee them (p. 36).
Aircraft Signal Flares: Flares can be found on airplanes and in some watercraft and motor vehicles and can be effective if you have a rescue aircraft in sight (p. 36).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Send Three Light Flashes: At night, use a flashlight to send groups of three flashes in the direction where you believe rescuers might be able tosee them (p. 36).
Step 2 - Save Flares Until Seen: Flares can be found on airplanes and in some watercraft and motor vehicles and can be effective if you have a rescue aircraft in sight (p. 36).
Step 3 - Conserve Brief Signal Flares: They are visible for only a short time, though, so save them for the right moment (p. 36).
Step 4 - Display Bright Gear Openly: Hanging brightly colored clothing or camping gear on tree branches can catch the rescuers' attention (p. 36).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Across the outdoors, what signal pattern is universally recognized as a call for help?
quiz_item.question: Across the outdoors, what signal pattern is universally recognized as a call for help?
options: A. One long continuous whistle blast every thirty minutes.
B. Any signal repeated in a series of three, such as three whistle blasts, three fires, or three flashes of light.
C. Flashing a flashlight rapidly ten times toward the northern horizon.
D. Arranging camp rocks into a small circle underneath dense tree cover.
choices: A. One long continuous whistle blast every thirty minutes.
B. Any signal repeated in a series of three, such as three whistle blasts, three fires, or three flashes of light.
C. Flashing a flashlight rapidly ten times toward the northern horizon.
D. Arranging camp rocks into a small circle underneath dense tree cover.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Any signal repeated in a series of three, such as three whistle blasts, three fires, or three flashes of light.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Three of anything (three whistle blasts, three light flashes, or three smoke columns) is the universal distress signal in the backcountry (p. 36).

pamphlet_excerpts: Priority of Hydration: Drink plenty of water (p. 40).
Hot Weather Dehydration: You can survive for days without food, but inhot weather without water, only hours (p. 40).
Cold Weather Fluid Loss: Dehydration happens in cold weather, too, even though you may not feel as thirsty (p. 40).
Clear Urine Hydration Check: The best rule is to drink plenty of water, enough so that your urine is clear, whenever you arein the outdoors (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Hydrate in Cold Climates: Dehydration happens in cold weather, too, even though you may not feel as thirsty (p. 40).
Step 2 - Maintain Clear Urine Output: The best rule is to drink plenty of water, enough so that your urine is clear, whenever you arein the outdoors (p. 40).
Step 3 - Collect Rain and Runoff: Ideally you will be able to find water where you are, from a lake, a stream, or melting snow, or by guiding rainwater down a tarp or tent fly (p. 40).
Step 4 - Check Rock Water Seeps: Water may have collected in depressions in rocks, in the crotches of trees, or in seeps along cliffs (p. 40).

quiz_item.question: What is the most reliable method for killing waterborne pathogens in water collected from a backcountry stream?
options: A. Letting the water sit in an open cup in the shade for twenty minutes.
B. Bringing the water to a rolling boil.
C. Pouring the water through a clean cotton bandana.
D. Stirring pine needles into the container to settle the sediment.
choices: A. Letting the water sit in an open cup in the shade for twenty minutes.
B. Bringing the water to a rolling boil.
C. Pouring the water through a clean cotton bandana.
D. Stirring pine needles into the container to settle the sediment.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Bringing the water to a rolling boil.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Bringing water to a rolling boil reliably destroys bacteria, viruses, and parasites that cause waterborne illness (p. 41).

pamphlet_excerpts: Predatory Wildlife Awareness: Protecting Yourself in the Wilderness Predatory Animals Be especially aware of the kinds of predatory animals you might meet during your adventures (p. 49).
Curious Wolves and Cougars: Wolves, coyotes, and cougars (or panthers and pumas) are curious (p. 49).
Slowly Backing Away: So, if you happen upon such an animal, face the creature and slowly retreat from the area (p. 49).
Looking Large to Predators: Make yourself as "big" as possible by waving your arms and clothing above your head (p. 49).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Face Predators and Retreat: So, if you happen upon such an animal, face the creature and slowly retreat from the area (p. 49).
Step 2 - Wave Arms Overhead Slowly: Make yourself as "big" as possible by waving your arms and clothing above your head (p. 49).
Step 3 - Throw Rocks When Cornered: If you have no escape or become cornered, throw rocks and sticks (p. 49).
Step 4 - Avoid Mothers With Young: Remember, no matter what kind of wild animal, give all wildlife a wide berth, especially young animals and their mother (p. 49).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why does the Wilderness Survival merit badge pamphlet advise against eating wild plants or hunting wildlife during most backcountry emergencies?
quiz_item.question: Why does the Wilderness Survival merit badge pamphlet advise against eating wild plants or hunting wildlife during most backcountry emergencies?
options: A. Most rescues occur before starvation becomes a threat, and foraging risks poisoning, injury, and wasted energy.
B. All plants growing above tree line contain lethal alkaloids.
C. Cooking wild plants extinguishes campfires and prevents smoke signaling.
D. Eating any solid food prevents your body from absorbing treated stream water.
choices: A. Most rescues occur before starvation becomes a threat, and foraging risks poisoning, injury, and wasted energy.
B. All plants growing above tree line contain lethal alkaloids.
C. Cooking wild plants extinguishes campfires and prevents smoke signaling.
D. Eating any solid food prevents your body from absorbing treated stream water.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Most rescues occur before starvation becomes a threat, and foraging risks poisoning, injury, and wasted energy.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Humans can survive weeks without food, whereas expending energy to hunt or risking accidental poisoning from wild plants endangers your survival (p. 51).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While hiking back from a peak at dusk, your buddy pair realizes you missed a trail junction and are no longer sure where the main trail is. Following the BSA S.T.O.P. survival protocol, what should you do?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While hiking back from a peak at dusk, your buddy pair realizes you missed a trail junction and are no longer sure where the main trail is. Following the BSA S.T.O.P. survival protocol, what should you do?
options: A. Run downhill through the woods before total darkness falls to look for a road.
B. Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
C. Split up and hike in opposite directions to cover twice as much ground.
D. Climb an exposed cliff face after dark to check for distant highway lights.
choices: A. Run downhill through the woods before total darkness falls to look for a road.
B. Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
C. Split up and hike in opposite directions to cover twice as much ground.
D. Climb an exposed cliff face after dark to check for distant highway lights.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Moving randomly after losing the trail increases search radius exponentially and risks injury after dark; staying put with S.T.O.P., shelter, and 3-signal distress calls maximizes rapid rescue.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: According to the seven priorities of wilderness survival, which action comes immediately after maintaining a positive mental attitude and providing urgent first aid?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the seven priorities of wilderness survival, which action comes immediately after maintaining a positive mental attitude and providing urgent first aid?
options: A. Foraging for edible wild plants and berries before dark.
B. Seeking or building a shelter to protect against weather exposure.
C. Hiking downhill until you find a paved road or ranger station.
D. Rationing your remaining food supplies into equal daily portions.
choices: A. Foraging for edible wild plants and berries before dark.
B. Seeking or building a shelter to protect against weather exposure.
C. Hiking downhill until you find a paved road or ranger station.
D. Rationing your remaining food supplies into equal daily portions.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Seeking or building a shelter to protect against weather exposure.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): After positive mental attitude and first aid, shelter is the third priority of survival to protect your body from hypothermia or extreme heat (p. 30).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What do the letters in the S.T.O.P. acronym instruct you to do the moment you realize you are lost?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What do the letters in the S.T.O.P. acronym instruct you to do the moment you realize you are lost?
options: A. Search, Track, Orient, and Proceed.
B. Signal, Travel, Observe, and Prepare.
C. Stop, Think, Observe, and Plan.
D. Shelter, Treat, Organize, and Patrol.
choices: A. Search, Track, Orient, and Proceed.
B. Signal, Travel, Observe, and Prepare.
C. Stop, Think, Observe, and Plan.
D. Shelter, Treat, Organize, and Patrol.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Stop, Think, Observe, and Plan.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Using the S.T.O.P. steps (Stop, Think, Observe, Plan) prevents panic and helps you assess your situation logically before acting (p. 22).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why should you carry your core personal survival kit on your person rather than stowing it deep inside a large frame backpack?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why should you carry your core personal survival kit on your person rather than stowing it deep inside a large frame backpack?
options: A. It keeps the survival kit warm so adhesive bandages do not freeze.
B. It ensures you still have life-saving gear if you are separated from your pack during a river crossing or side hike.
C. It prevents bears from smelling the metal tools inside your backpack.
D. It satisfies wilderness permit weight distribution rules in national forests.
choices: A. It keeps the survival kit warm so adhesive bandages do not freeze.
B. It ensures you still have life-saving gear if you are separated from your pack during a river crossing or side hike.
C. It prevents bears from smelling the metal tools inside your backpack.
D. It satisfies wilderness permit weight distribution rules in national forests.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It ensures you still have life-saving gear if you are separated from your pack during a river crossing or side hike.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Keeping essential survival tools in your pockets or on your belt ensures they remain with you even if your main pack is lost or left behind (p. 55).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When improvising a natural survival shelter in cold weather, why is it critical to pile several inches of dry leaves, pine needles, or boughs on the floor?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When improvising a natural survival shelter in cold weather, why is it critical to pile several inches of dry leaves, pine needles, or boughs on the floor?
options: A. To elevate yourself high enough to see over surrounding brush.
B. To prevent conductive heat loss from your body into the cold ground.
C. To create smoke immediately if a spark lands inside the shelter.
D. To attract insects that can be used as emergency food.
choices: A. To elevate yourself high enough to see over surrounding brush.
B. To prevent conductive heat loss from your body into the cold ground.
C. To create smoke immediately if a spark lands inside the shelter.
D. To attract insects that can be used as emergency food.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. To prevent conductive heat loss from your body into the cold ground.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Lying directly on cold or damp soil drains body heat rapidly, so a thick ground mat of natural insulation is vital for preventing hypothermia (p. 43).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Where is the best place to find dry tinder and kindling in a forest after a heavy rainstorm?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Where is the best place to find dry tinder and kindling in a forest after a heavy rainstorm?
options: A. Underneath rotting logs resting in low marshy hollows.
B. From dead branches still attached to standing trees and the dry inner core of split wood.
C. From freshly sprouted green ferns growing beside a creek.
D. Buried beneath two inches of saturated topsoil on a north-facing slope.
choices: A. Underneath rotting logs resting in low marshy hollows.
B. From dead branches still attached to standing trees and the dry inner core of split wood.
C. From freshly sprouted green ferns growing beside a creek.
D. Buried beneath two inches of saturated topsoil on a north-facing slope.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. From dead branches still attached to standing trees and the dry inner core of split wood.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Dead twigs off the ground dry out fastest, and splitting larger wet branches exposes dry interior wood fibers that catch sparks readily (p. 33).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Across the outdoors, what signal pattern is universally recognized as a call for help?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Across the outdoors, what signal pattern is universally recognized as a call for help?
options: A. One long continuous whistle blast every thirty minutes.
B. Any signal repeated in a series of three, such as three whistle blasts, three fires, or three flashes of light.
C. Flashing a flashlight rapidly ten times toward the northern horizon.
D. Arranging camp rocks into a small circle underneath dense tree cover.
choices: A. One long continuous whistle blast every thirty minutes.
B. Any signal repeated in a series of three, such as three whistle blasts, three fires, or three flashes of light.
C. Flashing a flashlight rapidly ten times toward the northern horizon.
D. Arranging camp rocks into a small circle underneath dense tree cover.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Any signal repeated in a series of three, such as three whistle blasts, three fires, or three flashes of light.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Three of anything (three whistle blasts, three light flashes, or three smoke columns) is the universal distress signal in the backcountry (p. 36).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the most reliable method for killing waterborne pathogens in water collected from a backcountry stream?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the most reliable method for killing waterborne pathogens in water collected from a backcountry stream?
options: A. Letting the water sit in an open cup in the shade for twenty minutes.
B. Bringing the water to a rolling boil.
C. Pouring the water through a clean cotton bandana.
D. Stirring pine needles into the container to settle the sediment.
choices: A. Letting the water sit in an open cup in the shade for twenty minutes.
B. Bringing the water to a rolling boil.
C. Pouring the water through a clean cotton bandana.
D. Stirring pine needles into the container to settle the sediment.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Bringing the water to a rolling boil.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Bringing water to a rolling boil reliably destroys bacteria, viruses, and parasites that cause waterborne illness (p. 41).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why does the Wilderness Survival merit badge pamphlet advise against eating wild plants or hunting wildlife during most backcountry emergencies?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why does the Wilderness Survival merit badge pamphlet advise against eating wild plants or hunting wildlife during most backcountry emergencies?
options: A. Most rescues occur before starvation becomes a threat, and foraging risks poisoning, injury, and wasted energy.
B. All plants growing above tree line contain lethal alkaloids.
C. Cooking wild plants extinguishes campfires and prevents smoke signaling.
D. Eating any solid food prevents your body from absorbing treated stream water.
choices: A. Most rescues occur before starvation becomes a threat, and foraging risks poisoning, injury, and wasted energy.
B. All plants growing above tree line contain lethal alkaloids.
C. Cooking wild plants extinguishes campfires and prevents smoke signaling.
D. Eating any solid food prevents your body from absorbing treated stream water.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Most rescues occur before starvation becomes a threat, and foraging risks poisoning, injury, and wasted energy.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Humans can survive weeks without food, whereas expending energy to hunt or risking accidental poisoning from wild plants endangers your survival (p. 51).

quiz_item.question: In wildland fire management, what are the three legs of the wildland fire behavior triangle, and what does the LCES safety protocol stand for?
options: A. Oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide; LCES stands for Ladders, Chainsaws, Engines, and Sprinklers.
B. Fuel, weather, and topography govern wildland fire behavior; LCES stands for Lookouts, Communications, Escape routes, and Safety zones.
C. Humidity, barometric pressure, and moonlight; LCES stands for Lighting, Containment, Evacuation, and Shelter.
D. Soil depth, tree height, and road width; LCES stands for Location, Compass, Elevation, and Slope.
choices: A. Oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide; LCES stands for Ladders, Chainsaws, Engines, and Sprinklers.
B. Fuel, weather, and topography govern wildland fire behavior; LCES stands for Lookouts, Communications, Escape routes, and Safety zones.
C. Humidity, barometric pressure, and moonlight; LCES stands for Lighting, Containment, Evacuation, and Shelter.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Fuel, weather, and topography govern wildland fire behavior; LCES stands for Lookouts, Communications, Escape routes, and Safety zones.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why do severe wildfires frequently lead to destructive flash floods and mudslides when rain falls months after the fire is out?
quiz_item.question: Why do severe wildfires frequently lead to destructive flash floods and mudslides when rain falls months after the fire is out?
options: A. Chemical fire retardants turn clay soils into impermeable concrete crusts
B. Surviving trees release excess groundwater through their damaged bark
C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
D. Ash deposits freeze the upper soil horizon and block snowmelt infiltration
choices: A. Chemical fire retardants turn clay soils into impermeable concrete crusts
B. Surviving trees release excess groundwater through their damaged bark
C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
D. Ash deposits freeze the upper soil horizon and block snowmelt infiltration
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): High-severity fires vaporize organic compounds that condense into a waxy, water-repellent soil layer while removing the plants and roots that normally absorb rainfall (p. 6).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How does a carefully executed prescribed burn help regenerate fire-dependent tree species such as lodgepole pine or longleaf pine?
quiz_item.question: How does a carefully executed prescribed burn help regenerate fire-dependent tree species such as lodgepole pine or longleaf pine?
options: A. It melts resin on serotinous cones to release seeds onto nutrient-rich mineral soil
B. It sterilizes the soil to prevent earthworms from eating tree roots
C. It boils sap inside mature trunks so they sprout new branches from the crown
D. It drives away all songbirds that would otherwise consume fallen pine needles
choices: A. It melts resin on serotinous cones to release seeds onto nutrient-rich mineral soil
B. It sterilizes the soil to prevent earthworms from eating tree roots
C. It boils sap inside mature trunks so they sprout new branches from the crown
D. It drives away all songbirds that would otherwise consume fallen pine needles
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. It melts resin on serotinous cones to release seeds onto nutrient-rich mineral soil
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Prescribed fire heat melts the waxy resin sealing serotinous cones while clearing surface litter so seeds fall directly onto nutrient-rich mineral soil (p. 9).

quiz_item.question: What is the primary mechanism that ignites most homes destroyed in the wildland-urban interface during a wildfire?
options: A. Underground root fires traveling through septic lines and foundations
B. Radiant heat shattering concrete driveways from a mile away
C. Direct contact with a fifty-foot wall of advancing crown flames
D. Windblown embers landing on flammable roofs, rain gutters, and porch vegetation
choices: A. Underground root fires traveling through septic lines and foundations
B. Radiant heat shattering concrete driveways from a mile away
C. Direct contact with a fifty-foot wall of advancing crown flames
D. Windblown embers landing on flammable roofs, rain gutters, and porch vegetation
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Windblown embers landing on flammable roofs, rain gutters, and porch vegetation
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Showers of wind-carried embers travel ahead of the main fire front and ignite dry needles in gutters, wood shake roofs, and mulch against home siding (p. 8).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why does a wildland fire typically spread much faster up a steep slope than across flat ground?
quiz_item.question: Why does a wildland fire typically spread much faster up a steep slope than across flat ground?
options: A. Atmospheric oxygen is denser near mountain ridges than in valley bottoms
B. Rising convective heat and closer flame angles preheat and dry the fuels upslope
C. Uphill tree roots pump flammable turpentine to the surface when warmed
D. Gravity pulls smoke downward, leaving clear air above the flame front
choices: A. Atmospheric oxygen is denser near mountain ridges than in valley bottoms
B. Rising convective heat and closer flame angles preheat and dry the fuels upslope
C. Uphill tree roots pump flammable turpentine to the surface when warmed
D. Gravity pulls smoke downward, leaving clear air above the flame front
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Rising convective heat and closer flame angles preheat and dry the fuels upslope
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): On a slope, flames tilt closer to the unburned vegetation above them, and rising hot air preheats and dehydrates upslope fuels so they ignite rapidly (p. 6).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In wildland firefighter safety, what do the letters in the critical acronym LCES stand for?
quiz_item.question: In wildland firefighter safety, what do the letters in the critical acronym LCES stand for?
options: A. Ladders, Chainsaws, Engines, and Sprinklers
B. Location, Compass, Elevation, and Slope
C. Lookouts, Communications, Escape Routes, and Safety Zones
D. Line Construction, Equipment Checks, Evacuation, and Shelter
choices: A. Ladders, Chainsaws, Engines, and Sprinklers
B. Location, Compass, Elevation, and Slope
C. Lookouts, Communications, Escape Routes, and Safety Zones

quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Lookouts, Communications, Escape Routes, and Safety Zones
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): LCES stands for Lookouts, Communications, Escape Routes, and Safety Zones, the four interrelated safety pillars maintained on every wildland fire (p. 7).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why do wildland firefighting crews always begin constructing a fireline from an established anchor point such as a road, stream, or burned area?
quiz_item.question: Why do wildland firefighting crews always begin constructing a fireline from an established anchor point such as a road, stream, or burned area?
options: A. To prevent the fire from wrapping around behind the crew and flanking their position
B. To keep heavy hand tools within fifty feet of the water tender at all times
C. To ensure the Incident Commander can see the entire crew from the base camp
D. To test whether the soil contains enough clay for bulldozer blades
choices: A. To prevent the fire from wrapping around behind the crew and flanking their position
B. To keep heavy hand tools within fifty feet of the water tender at all times
C. To ensure the Incident Commander can see the entire crew from the base camp
D. To test whether the soil contains enough clay for bulldozer blades
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. To prevent the fire from wrapping around behind the crew and flanking their position
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Starting from a secure barrier or anchor point keeps unburned fuel from igniting behind the firefighters and trapping them with an unanchored flank (p. 8).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What combination of working edges makes the Pulaski one of the most versatile hand tools in wildland firefighting?
quiz_item.question: What combination of working edges makes the Pulaski one of the most versatile hand tools in wildland firefighting?
options: A. A serrated chainsaw blade paired with a collapsible water nozzle
B. A wide leaf rake paired with a pointed post-hole digger
C. A flat snow shovel paired with a rubber-belted swatter
D. An axe bit for chopping wood paired with an adze hoe blade for trenching soil
choices: A. A serrated chainsaw blade paired with a collapsible water nozzle
B. A wide leaf rake paired with a pointed post-hole digger
C. A flat snow shovel paired with a rubber-belted swatter
D. An axe bit for chopping wood paired with an adze hoe blade for trenching soil
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. An axe bit for chopping wood paired with an adze hoe blade for trenching soil
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Developed by Ranger Ed Pulaski after the 1910 fires, the Pulaski combines an axe blade for chopping roots and brush with an adze hoe for grubbing down to mineral soil (p. 8).

requirements.lead_text: Taking Action. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Taking Action. Do ONE of the following: (a) Develop a fire readiness plan for a wildland area with which you are familiar. The plan should include a map showing available resources, water supplies, natural and manmade barriers, and access. The plan should discuss fuel loads, available fire apparatus, structure protection needs, values at risk, medical and evacuation considerations, and potential fire suppression tactics. (b) Visit with a state or federal forestry official or your local fire warden. Discuss the causes of and types of wildland fire that occur in your area. Discuss the prime fire season(s) in your area. Identify the agency responsible for wildland fire suppression in your area. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (c) Conduct a Firewise assessment of a home or a building in the wildland-urban interface, which could include a Scout camp building or facility. Identify potential risks and fire hazards. With your counselor's approval, complete a project to reduce the wildfire risk and increase the preparedness of the building. Write a brief report about what you did and learned from the assessment and project. (d) Meet with a Fire Prevention Specialist or a local fire official to learn about fire prevention efforts in your community. From what you learned, prepare a fire prevention message (skit, video, or billboard concept) and share with your counselor and troop (or other group approved by your counselor). (e) Meet with a meteorologist or someone familiar with fire weather and discuss the fire weather concerns and typical fire seasons that exist in your area. Discuss the conditions that lead to a Fire Weather Watch or a Red Flag Warning. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Establishing the Ten Standard Firefighting Orders and systematic fire behavior training

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why do severe wildfires frequently lead to destructive flash floods and mudslides when rain falls months after the fire is out?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why do severe wildfires frequently lead to destructive flash floods and mudslides when rain falls months after the fire is out?
options: A. Chemical fire retardants turn clay soils into impermeable concrete crusts
B. Surviving trees release excess groundwater through their damaged bark
C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
D. Ash deposits freeze the upper soil horizon and block snowmelt infiltration
choices: A. Chemical fire retardants turn clay soils into impermeable concrete crusts
B. Surviving trees release excess groundwater through their damaged bark
C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
D. Ash deposits freeze the upper soil horizon and block snowmelt infiltration
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Intense heat destroys root systems and creates hydrophobic soil layers that repel water
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): High-severity fires vaporize organic compounds that condense into a waxy, water-repellent soil layer while removing the plants and roots that normally absorb rainfall (p. 6).
